<a id="ek10937"></a>
## EK10937 — Withdrawn: m68k `Wait()` masks Paula interrupts during scheduler-list commit

The earlier candidate misread `0x4000` as enabling the Paula master interrupt. `INTENA` uses bit 15 as SET/CLR and bit 14 as master enable (`compiler/include/hardware/intbits.h:40-43`), so `0x4000` clears master interrupts and `0xC000` sets them. `m68k_VoluntarySwitch()` disables Paula master interrupts at `arch/m68k-all/exec/switch.S:54` before rechecking `tc_SigRecvd`, then sets `TS_WAIT` and links the task into `TaskWait` (`:60-75`); it re-enables interrupts only after those list writes (`:76-80`). The signal-check and queue-publication window claimed by the finding is therefore protected. EK10937 is withdrawn; no bug is established by that transition. Source-only.

## Coverage

`rom/exec/mmakefile.src` selects 169 generic Exec C sources plus initialization and support; `rom/kernel/mmakefile.src` selects 77 generic kernel C sources, with MMU allocation included when `USE_MMU=1`. The review examined task/ETask creation and teardown, scheduling and signals, message ports and I/O requests, semaphore arbitration, resident/library initialization, heap/pool/page allocation, interrupts and exception chains, and clock/bootstrap paths. Architecture manifests and representative overrides were checked for PC x86/x86-64, Unix hosted, m68k, AArch64 native, and RISC-V OpenSBI; architecture-specific findings name their target. No source review can establish that this list is exhaustive. The report deliberately excludes disk, filesystem, and DOS-library implementation defects already covered by the linked reports in [AROS.md](AROS.md).

## Findings

<a id="ek01"></a>
### EK01 — Withdrawn as duplicate of EK9883

The original `WaitIO()` unlocked-removal candidate is covered by the later EK9883 finding, which reconciles the shared message-port lock defect with the selected AHI-Handler and Wanderer callers and gives the concrete SMP list interleavings. EK01 is not a separate finding.

<a id="ek02"></a>
### EK02 — Signal allocation/free shift outside the 32-bit mask [medium impact, high confidence]

`rom/exec/allocsignal.c:96-113` computes `1L << signalNum` for an explicit number without verifying `0 <= signalNum < 32`; `rom/exec/freesignal.c:48-56` similarly shifts `1 << signalNum` for anything other than `-1`. Trigger: caller passes 32 or greater, or a negative value other than `-1`. Consequence: undefined C shift behavior, which can allocate/free the wrong bit or produce inconsistent signal masks. Generic Exec, all targets.

<a id="ek03"></a>
### EK03 — `AllocVec` and `AllocVecPooled` can wrap requested size [high impact, high confidence]

`rom/exec/allocvec.c:55-69` and `rom/exec/allocvecpooled.c:69-80` add a metadata word to caller-supplied `IPTR` size without an overflow check. Trigger: a request near the maximum representable size. Consequence: a small block can be returned for a large requested allocation, so the caller's ordinary write overruns it. Pool and system-heap variants share the root cause. Exact threshold depends on pointer width.

<a id="ek04"></a>
### EK04 — Releasing shared semaphore grants later readers ahead of a queued writer [medium impact, high confidence]

`rom/exec/releasesemaphore.c:130-160`: when the first waiter is shared, the code walks the entire wait queue and grants *every* shared request, including those after an exclusive request. Trigger: shared holder releases while queue order is reader, writer, reader. Consequence: later reader bypasses the writer; while a shared hold remains active, newly arriving shared requests also join it because `InternalObtainSemaphore()` admits a request when `ss_Owner == owner == NULL` without checking the wait queue (`rom/exec/semaphores.c:91-113`). A continuing reader stream can indefinitely delay an exclusive waiter. This ordering is reachable through the selected DOS list API: `LockDosList()` maps `LDF_ALL|LDF_READ` and `LDF_ALL|LDF_WRITE` to shared and exclusive acquisition of the same `di_DevLock` (`rom/dos/lockdoslist.c:60-66`); selected read traversal and `RemDosEntry()` use those modes (`rom/dos/getdeviceproc.c:120-130`; `rom/dos/remdosentry.c:53-84`). Generic Exec, including SMP.

<a id="ek05"></a>
### EK05 — `ChildWait` can erase the signal for a newly arrived child [high impact, high confidence; SMP]

`rom/exec/childwait.c:91-112` checks the child-message list under its spinlock, releases it, then calls `SetSignal(0, SIGF_CHILD)` before `Wait`. `Exec_CleanupETask` queues the child message and signals the parent after releasing the list locks (`rom/exec/exec_util.c:308-330`). A child can finish on another CPU after the empty list scan, publish its completion, and signal the parent before the parent clears `SIGF_CHILD`; the signal is then erased while the completion remains queued, and `ChildWait` can sleep indefinitely until another child signals. **Affected configurations and callers:** the configured `__AROSEXEC_SMP__` variants are x86-64 PC SMP and ARM32/AArch64 Raspberry Pi SMP (`configure.in:1669,2197`). The maintained POSIX `wait()` and `waitpid()` paths call `ChildWait()` for processes created with `NP_NotifyOnDeath` (`compiler/crt/posixc/wait.c:92-100`; `waitpid.c:113-149`; `__vfork.c:484`). Uniprocessor `Forbid` prevents the corresponding task transition. **Confidence:** high for the split predicate/clear sequence and producer ordering; the missed wake requires cross-CPU child completion in that interval. No task or SMP interleaving was run; source-only.

<a id="ek06"></a>
### EK06 — Failed task creation leaves a dangling caller-visible message-port pointer [medium impact, high confidence]

`rom/exec/newcreatetaska.c:207-235` writes `*msgPortPtr = mp` before `NewAddTask`; if the latter fails, `fail` frees the `MemList` containing `mp` (`:252-266`) but does not clear the caller's pointer. Trigger: `TASKTAG_TASKMSGPORT` supplied and context/ETask setup fails. Consequence: caller receives `NULL` for the task but a non-null pointer to freed memory.

A maintained consumer consequence is present in `rom/log/log.c:304-315`: `libInit()` stores the task result in `lebTask` but tests only `lrb_ServicePort`. If `NewAddTask()` fails after port publication, `lrb_ServicePort` remains non-NULL after its storage is freed, so `libInit()` returns `TRUE` although `log_Task()` never started. This leaves `log.resource` reported as initialized without a broadcaster. The apparent later stale-port dereferences are guarded: producer calls require non-NULL `lrb_Task` (`rom/log/log_event.c:215,295`), which the failed task cannot set, and the timer/DOS retry helpers are called only by that task. The confirmed caller consequence is therefore false-success, not a demonstrated use-after-free. The selected serial logger has the same unchecked-task-result pattern: when serial output is enabled, its `libInit()` stores `NewCreateTask()`'s result in `selrb_Task` but returns `TRUE` unconditionally (`rom/log/serial/seriallogger.c:181-193`); its port dereferences occur only in the task body, which does not run after creation fails. No task setup failure was induced; source-only.

<a id="ek07"></a>
### EK07 — CPU-affinity allocation failure is used as a mask [high impact, high confidence; PC SMP]

`rom/exec/exec_util.c:131-163` does not check `KrnAllocCPUMask()` before calling `KrnGetCPUMask` with the result. PC's implementation forwards that pointer to `core_APIC_GetMask` (`arch/all-pc/kernel/getcpumask.c:13-26`). Trigger: low memory during `InitETask` on an SMP PC with CPU affinity enabled. Consequence: null pointer dereference or a child task with invalid affinity. AArch64's mask setter ignores null, but silently loses inherited affinity.

<a id="ek08"></a>
### EK08 — Equal-version resident priority is ignored [medium impact, high confidence]

`rom/exec/initkicktags.c:53-73`: the replacement comment says an equal-version resident with higher priority should supersede the old one. The condition starts `OldRomTag->rt_Version >= RomTag->rt_Version`, which is already true on equality, so the priority comparison cannot affect that case. Trigger: merged KickTag resident with equal version and higher priority. Consequence: older resident remains selected after reset/merge.

<a id="ek09"></a>
### EK09 — `KrnRemIRQHandler(NULL)` dereferences null [medium impact, high confidence]

`rom/kernel/remirqhandler.c:52-56` reads `h->in_nr` before the following `if (h && ...)`. Trigger: a caller passes the `NULL` failure result from `KrnAddIRQHandler` to cleanup. A selected PC example is the i8042 keyboard HIDD: after successful controller setup, `i8042_kbd_controller_task()` stores the registration result at `arch/all-pc/hidds/i8042/i8042_kbdclass.c:248` but signals readiness without checking it (`:253`); the constructor checks `LEDSigBit`, not the IRQ token (`:320-325`), and later Dispose unconditionally removes `data->irq` (`:335-344`). The driver-level consequence—an accepted keyboard object without an IRQ handler and the conditional later disposal fault—is detailed in OD3345. The Efika override has the same ordering at `arch/ppc-chrp/efika/kernel/intr.c:151-154`; its timer stores the result without checking it at `timer_init.c:88`, then unconditionally removes it on expunge at `:153-159`. This trigger is conditional on registration returning NULL and expunge running; the Efika timer's `noexpunge` option limits ordinary reachability. Consequence: kernel fault instead of a harmless no-op. Generic and Efika implementations; selected callers include i386-PC/x86-64-PC i8042 and the optional Efika timer.

<a id="ek10"></a>
### EK10 — IRQ handler data update races with IRQ execution/removal [high impact, high confidence; SMP]

`rom/kernel/modifyirqhandler.c:63-73` uses local `Disable()` but no `kb_IntrSpinLock`. IRQ execution walks handlers under that lock in read mode (`rom/kernel/addirqhandler.c:154-173`), and removal takes it in write mode (`rom/kernel/remirqhandler.c:60-77`). Trigger: modify on one CPU while IRQ executes or removes the node on another. Consequence: handler can observe a mixed pair of old/new data pointers, or modifier can write into freed node memory.

<a id="ek11"></a>
### EK11 — The ninth exception handler is silently dropped on SMP [medium impact, high confidence; SMP]

`rom/kernel/addexceptionhandler.c:158-188` snapshots only eight handlers and logs, then skips further entries. `KrnAddExceptionHandler` imposes no matching limit (`:84-125`). Trigger: nine or more handlers register for an exception. Consequence: later handlers never run, even if the preceding eight decline to handle the exception. The code itself logs that a handler was dropped.

<a id="ek12"></a>
### EK12 — PC IRQ attribute mapping dereferences a failed allocation [high impact, high confidence; PC]

`arch/all-pc/kernel/modifyirq.c:45-61` allocates `IntrMapping` and immediately assigns its fields without testing for `NULL`. Trigger: low memory during `KrnModifyIRQA` for an unmapped IRQ. Consequence: kernel null dereference while configuring an interrupt. The ACPI IOAPIC MADT mapping paths contain the same pattern (`arch/all-pc/kernel/acpi_ioapic.c:811-821,860-870,925-935`), so this is grouped as one allocation-check failure class.

<a id="ek13"></a>
### EK13 — PC SMP startup uses an unchecked spinlock-array allocation [high impact, high confidence; PC SMP]

`arch/all-pc/kernel/smp.c:230-245` allocates `apicReadyLocks` and indexes it for each secondary CPU without a null check. Trigger: memory exhaustion during SMP bring-up. Consequence: boot-time null dereference instead of falling back to one CPU. Per-CPU schedule-data allocations at `:250-253` are also used without checks.

<a id="ek14"></a>
### EK14 — Fixed-address page allocation can read beyond the selected MemHeader map [conditional; `USE_MMU=1`]

The generic `mm_AllocPages()` scans the Exec MemHeader list and filters for matching physical attributes and enough free space (`rom/kernel/kernel_mm.c:33-41`). For a non-NULL requested address, it treats a header as a match when `addr >= mh->mh_Lower || addr + length <= mh->mh_Upper` (`:43-54`). The OR admits an earlier header solely because the requested address is above its lower bound, even when the requested range belongs to a later MemHeader. It then stops scanning after this first candidate.

The called `mm_AllocAbs()` aligns the address and rejects only addresses below `head->start`; it computes a page index from the selected header without checking that the index is below `head->size`, then reads `head->map[start]` (`rom/kernel/mm_linear.c:291-310`). A valid fixed-address `KrnAllocPages()` request into a later MemHeader can therefore be sent to an earlier compatible header and index beyond that header's map. A direct address beyond the selected header also reaches this missing upper-bound check. Depending on the out-of-range map contents, the allocator can continue into an invalid page-map traversal and attempt an invalid block-state update; `SetBlockState()` raises `AN_BadFreeAddr` for an oversized end but then continues unless the alert is fatal (`mm_linear.c:43-74`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a generic MMU allocator build has at least two MemHeaders; a public fixed-address request targets a range inside a later header; and an earlier header has compatible attributes, `mh_Free >= length`, and a `mm_linear` block header accepted by `GetBlockHeader()`. The OR selector may choose that earlier header, leading to an out-of-bounds map read and potentially invalid allocator metadata access instead of allocating from the containing region. The public `KrnAllocPages()` contract allows a supplied starting address whose requested region must be included (`rom/kernel/allocpages.c:20-31`). A caller that supplies an address outside the only selected region also reaches the unchecked map bound. **Affected configuration:** `USE_MMU=1` with the generic `rom/kernel/allocpages.c`/`kernel_mm.c`/`mm_linear.c` path; the hosted Unix allocation vector is a separate implementation. The checked-in production callers found use `addr == NULL`, so the fixed-address trigger is limited to external or future callers, and checked-in kernel startup does not establish a live generic allocator because `kb_PageSize` remains unset (EK639). **Confidence:** high for the OR selection and missing upper-bound check; actual allocator failure/corruption depends on memory-list order, out-of-range map contents, and an initialized generic MMU region. Require full-range containment in the selected MemHeader and reject any computed page index outside `head->size` before reading the map. No allocation, map access, or build was run; source-only; see the [coverage ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md).

<a id="ek15"></a>
### EK15 — Zero-page MMU region makes initialization write before its map [latent source defect; generic allocator currently disabled]

When a valid generic-MMU initialization reaches `mm_Init()` with a nonzero page size but a region too small to leave one usable page after metadata/map reservation, `head->size` becomes zero. The subsequent `do { head->map[--p] = ...; } while (p > 0)` decrements zero and writes before the map (`rom/kernel/mm_linear.c:399-424`).

This path is currently gated off in the checked-in source: `KrnInitMemory()` returns before `mm_Init()` whenever `kb_PageSize` is zero (`rom/kernel/initmemory.c:45-54`), and a source-wide C/assembly search found no assignment to `kb_PageSize` (`rom/kernel/kernel_base.h:106`; see EK639 coverage). The sole checked-in `KrnInitMemory()` caller is the excluded allocator debug test (`developer/debug/test/kernel/allocator.c:150`; `developer/debug/test/kernel/mmakefile.src:5-12`); it does not set the private kernel field. Thus `USE_MMU=1` alone does not establish a current maintained trigger.

**Consequence if enabled:** a small region with no usable pages makes initialization write to an invalid map index and corrupt memory. **Scope/confidence:** high for the `mm_Init()` zero-page defect; no maintained current path supplies the required nonzero page size, so this remains a latent conditional candidate rather than an established boot bug. No allocator operation or boot was run; source-only.

<a id="ek16"></a>
### EK16 — Zero-length page allocation underflows the state-map writer [latent source defect; generic allocator currently disabled]

With a nonzero `kb_PageSize` and an initialized generic linear allocator, `mm_Allocate()` rounds a zero-byte request to zero pages (`rom/kernel/mm_linear.c:144-149`). It can select a free block and pass `pages == 0` to `SetBlockState()` (`:238-264`). `SetBlockState()` enters its write loop unconditionally, decrements the exclusive end before storing, and writes `head->map[first - 1]` (`:43-74`); when `first` is zero this is before the map, and when `first` is positive it alters the preceding page's state.

The public `KrnAllocPages()` wrapper currently returns NULL while `kb_PageSize` is zero (`rom/kernel/allocpages.c:63-75`). The checked-in source tree contains no assignment that enables this generic page size, and the only checked-in `KrnInitMemory()` test caller is excluded from its target and does not set the field (see EK639 and the [generic allocator caller reconciliation](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7695)). Thus neither `USE_MMU=1` nor a public zero-length request alone establishes a current maintained trigger.

**Consequence if enabled:** a zero-length allocation can corrupt the page-state entry before its selected block and may return a non-NULL address despite allocating no pages. **Scope/confidence:** high for the zero-page state-map write when the generic allocator is enabled; no maintained current path enables it, so this remains a latent conditional candidate rather than an established runtime bug. No allocation, MMU operation or boot was run; source-only.

<a id="ek17"></a>
### EK17 — RISC-V virtual IRQ count arithmetic can wrap [medium impact, high confidence; OpenSBI RISC-V64]

`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/allocirq.c:32-51` checks `(base + count) > HW_IRQ_COUNT` and loops on `(irq + count) <= HW_IRQ_COUNT` using unchecked unsigned addition. Trigger: a very large `count` supplied to `KrnAllocIRQ(IRQTYPE_MSI, count)`. Consequence: a wrapped count bypasses the range check and can run off the `__virq_used` array during scan/marking. The API is normally called with small vector counts; this is an argument-validation candidate.

<a id="ek18"></a>
### EK18 — AArch64 affinity mask functions index beyond their one-word allocation [medium impact, high confidence; AArch64 native]

`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/alloccpumask.c:14-23` allocates one 32-bit word, while `getcpumask.c:19-22` and `cpuinmask.c:29` index it by `id >> 5` without validating the CPU ID. Trigger: an ID of 32 or greater passed to the exported mask APIs. Consequence: out-of-bounds write/read. The current native platform advertises at most four CPUs, so normal scheduler IDs should remain in range; this affects invalid or future-expanded IDs.

<a id="ek19"></a>
### EK19 — Boot panic formatting can overflow its fixed buffer [medium impact; high source confidence, trigger length unverified]

The generic formatter (`rom/kernel/kernel_panic.c:18-39`) and Android override (`arch/all-android/kernel/kernel_panic.c:17-45`) each prepend the 22-byte string `"Critical boot failure\n"` to a 1,024-byte buffer, then call unbounded `vsprintf()`. That leaves 1,002 bytes for the formatted output including its terminating NUL; output longer than 1,001 characters crosses the buffer end. The local `vsprintf()` implementation explicitly performs no destination-size check (`compiler/crt/stdc/vsprintf.c:28-40,53-60`).

Selected hosted callers pass host error text with `%s`: Unix passes the `hostlib_Open()` error when loading libc (`arch/all-unix/kernel/kernel_startup.c:145-150`); its selected hostlib provider obtains that text directly from `dlerror()` without imposing a length bound (`arch/all-unix/bootstrap/hostlib.c:14-18,20-30`). Android passes `hostlib_GetPointer()`/`hostlib_Open()` errors during alert setup (`arch/all-android/kernel/_displayalert.c:58-78`) and the missing `__page_size` lookup error (`arch/all-android/kernel/getpagesize.c:14-24`); the Android host-interface implementation that supplies those strings is outside this checkout. The checked-in panic caller census found no other dynamic `%s` input to these two implementations; the remaining selected calls use fixed text or scalar values.

If a selected host error plus its fixed message exceeds the 1,001-character output limit, `vsprintf()` writes past the buffer before alert display or debug output. This occurs during an already-failing startup and can corrupt nearby state or obscure the diagnostic. **Affected configuration:** hosted Unix and Android kernels using these selected panic implementations; other targets may define `KERNEL_PANIC_BUFFER` with different storage or size. **Confidence:** high for the buffer boundary, unbounded formatter, and unchecked host-string path; whether the external loader or Android host interface supplies a sufficiently long string remains unverified, so the overrun trigger is conditional. No host lookup failure or boot was induced; source-only. See the [panic error-string recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#panic-buffer-error-string-boundary-recheck-ek19).
## Limitations

This report identifies candidate bugs by reading source and build selections; none are runtime-confirmed. In particular, hardware-dependent triggers, available memory-region shapes, and external API call patterns should be validated before fixing lower-confidence cases. Stub functions intentionally supplied by `rom/kernel` and replaced by architecture builds were not treated as bugs solely because they return a default value.


<a id="ek738"></a>
EK738. **genmodule indexes past fixed argument arrays for a prototype with more than 64 parameters (build-tool correctness impact; high source confidence for extended or malformed `.conf` input).** `readsectionfunctionlist` declares `args[64]` and `regs[64]` on its stack (`tools/genmodule/config.c:1886`). While parsing each function parameter, it stores the start pointer at `args[argcount]` and increments `argcount` without checking the array capacity (`:1940-1947`); the following prototype scan and end check continue to use the just-indexed slot (`:1948-1976`). Thus a function declaration with a 65th parameter performs an out-of-bounds stack-array access before the later argument/register count comparison can reject a mismatch (`:2051-2058`). `genmodule` accepts an explicit configuration file with `-c` (`tools/genmodule/genmodule.c:100-109`) and is built as a host utility (`tools/genmodule/Makefile:12-22`); selected build rules invoke it with project `.conf` files (for example `compiler/crt/posixc/mmakefile.src:374` and `workbench/libs/gl/mmakefile.src:60`). A declaration over this undocumented limit can therefore corrupt parser-local state, abort generation, or produce invalid output. Reject excess arguments before indexing, and apply the same bound to register parsing. Trigger: a generator configuration contains a function prototype with at least 65 parameters. A source census of all 479 checked-in `.conf` files counted 5,120 `functionlist`, `methodlist`, and `cfunctionlist` declarations; the largest has 17 parameters. This confirms no checked-in over-limit declaration in those parser sections, so the finding remains conditional on custom or future configuration input. No generator was run; source-only.


<a id="ek739"></a>
EK739. **genmodule accepts a negative `.skip` and assigns duplicate or wrapped library-vector numbers (build-output correctness impact; high source confidence for invalid `.conf` input).** The parser's usage diagnostic says a positive number is expected, but it stores `strtol` directly in signed `int n` and adds it to unsigned `lvo` without rejecting negative values (`tools/genmodule/config.c:1716-1733`). For example, with the normal first LVO of 5, one function advances `lvo` to 6; `.skip -1` moves it back to 5, so the next function is assigned the same LVO as the preceding function (`:1667-1668,1927-1929`). Generation uses those stored values directly for `LVO...` constants (`tools/genmodule/writeincdefines.c:42-47`) and lays out function-table entries by comparing each stored LVO with the previous one (`tools/genmodule/writestart.c:1764-1769`), producing constants that collide with the preceding function while the emitted table still advances sequentially. More negative values can also wrap the unsigned LVO and distort generated vector layout. Trigger: an explicit or project `.conf` function-list section contains a negative `.skip`; a census of all 488 checked-in `.conf`/`.cfg` files found 305 numeric directives, none negative (maximum 285), so this remains a custom or future-input case. Reject values less than zero and check `strtol` range/errors before updating `lvo`. No generator was run; source-only.


<a id="ek736"></a>
EK736. **genmodule's default superclass overwrites a configured `superclass_field` (generated class behavior impact; high source confidence for configurations using this option).** Class configuration parsing accepts `superclass_field` and stores it separately from the optional static superclass (`tools/genmodule/config.c:953-963`). At class-section finalization, the intended “neither value supplied” test mistakenly checks `cl->superclass` twice (`:1475-1481`). If a configuration supplies only `superclass_field`, this condition still succeeds and the class-type switch assigns a static default such as `MUIC_Area`, `ROOTCLASS`, or `CLID_Root` (`:1482-1505`). Selected generators then test `cl->superclass` first and emit that static superclass, bypassing the requested base-structure field (`tools/genmodule/muisupport.c:108-120`; `boopsisupport.c:185-193`; `oopsupport.c:133-141`). The generated class therefore uses the default class even when the configuration intended to inherit from its runtime superclass field. Change the second null check to `cl->superclass_field`. Trigger: a genmodule class config specifies `superclass_field` without `superclass`. A repository-wide `.conf` search found no current in-tree use of this option; the defect affects project or external configurations that use the supported field. No generator output or class was built; source-only.


<a id="ek735"></a>
EK735. **genmodule derives its directory-trim index from `argv[1]`, corrupting some `-d`/`-l` paths and reading beyond empty arguments (conditional host build-generation failure; high source confidence).** `initconfig()` sets `argvit = argv + 1` once and never advances it. Both the `-d` and `-l` handlers test `optarg[strlen(*argvit)-1]`, then trim the final byte of `optarg` if that unrelated byte is `/` (`tools/genmodule/config.c:130-135,172-181`). In the selected GL stub rule, `-c` is the first option, so the test index is 1 (`workbench/libs/gl/mmakefile.src:56-61`). With `TOP=.`, the generated `GENDIR` begins `./`; that slash is mistaken for a trailing slash and the handler drops the final `l` from `.../workbench/libs/gl`. `make_output_path()` appends generated filenames to the truncated path (`tools/genmodule/writeutils.c:4-41`), while the rule expects the original directory and stamp, so this selected generation step can fail or place outputs at a different path. Default configure uses an absolute TOP; this relative-path trigger requires an override such as `TOP=.`. For either `-d ""` or `-l ""` with a two-character first option, the same expression reads `optarg[1]` beyond the empty string. If that read happens to compare equal to `/`, `strlen(optarg)-1` wraps and the trim writes before the string; if execution continues without trimming, writers that format `"%s/%s_start.c"` or stub filenames with the empty directory construct an absolute `/filename` output path (`tools/genmodule/writestart.c:93-99`; `writestubs.c:40-58`). Attached forms such as `-d./path` or `-l./path` also make the index derive from the combined option token and can read beyond the `optarg` string; selected build rules use separate option and argument tokens. Empty-directory and attached-form cases require explicit host-tool input, and no checked-in invocation was found. Check `optarg` for nonempty input and inspect its final character before trimming. No generation command or build was run; source-only.


<a id="ek8901"></a>
### EK8901 — GenModule dereferences failed allocations while deriving variadic aliases [conditional host include-generation failure]

The inline and defines writers derive aliases for variadic functions using unchecked allocations. For an `A`-suffixed name, each assigns `strdup(funclistit->name)` and immediately writes through the result (`tools/genmodule/writeincdefines.c:140-146`; `tools/genmodule/writeincinline.c:88-94`). Other recognition branches similarly mutate or copy an unchecked `strdup()`/`malloc()` result (`writeincdefines.c:148-200`; `writeincinline.c:96-149`). `newfunctionhead()` initializes `novararg` to false, so parsed argument-bearing functions reach the alias detection unless explicitly marked otherwise (`tools/genmodule/functionhead.c:18-34`).

The selected Exec config declares `NewCreateTaskA(struct TagItem *tags)` (`rom/exec/exec.conf:236`). Its name ends in `A`, so the ordinary `writeincludes` pass attempts to duplicate the name and then writes its terminator at the penultimate character to derive `NewCreateTask`; a failed `strdup()` is dereferenced immediately. `kernel-exec` depends on its generated includes through the `%build_module` rule and selected module include target (`rom/exec/mmakefile.src:91-94`; `config/make.tmpl:2210-2224,2428-2440`).

**Trigger and consequence:** host-memory exhaustion causes the specific alias `strdup()` to fail during Exec header generation. The GenModule process dereferences NULL rather than reporting allocation failure, terminating the generation command; the include target fails and the build cannot proceed. Equivalent failures exist in the other derived-alias allocations, including the optional dummy library's `printx(...,...)` varargs path. **Affected configuration:** Exec include generation when that function is processed; the additional `printx` path requires the explicit developer dummy-library target. **Confidence:** high for unchecked allocation results and the immediate write; occurrence requires the specific host allocation to fail. Check each derived-name allocation before mutation or copy and propagate a generation error. No allocation failure, generator, or build was run; source-only.

<a id="ek733"></a>
### EK733 — GenModule forms out-of-object suffix pointers for short argument-taking function names [conditional host build-generation failure]

Both generated-header writers test whether a function name ends in `TagList` by forming `name + strlen(name) - 7` before comparing it with `strcmp()` (`tools/genmodule/writeincdefines.c:131-158`; `tools/genmodule/writeincinline.c:79-109`). `strlen()` returns `size_t`, so names shorter than seven bytes underflow the subtraction and the resulting pointer is outside the string object. The writers reach this test for non-private functions with arguments when `novararg` is false; new function records default to that value (`tools/genmodule/functionhead.c:18-34`). The ordinary Exec function list includes four-character `Wait(ULONG signalSet)` and five-character `SetSR(ULONG newSR, ULONG mask)` (`rom/exec/exec.conf:97,126`).

The `kernel-exec` target is built through `%build_module` (`rom/exec/mmakefile.src:91-94`); the generated module Makefile selects the include writers, and the module include target depends on those generated headers (`config/make.tmpl:2243-2260,2428-2440`; `tools/genmodule/genmodule.c:39-49`). Thus a normal Exec include-generation pass reaches the invalid pointer comparisons. The optional `test-library-dummylib` target adds three-character argument-taking names `add` and `asl` (`developer/debug/test/library/dummy.conf:12-16`; `mmakefile.src:81-83`), which reach the same `TagList` comparison and, if it continues, also the four-character `Args` suffix comparison.

**Trigger and consequence:** generation of inline/defines headers for a selected config containing a non-private, argument-taking function shorter than seven characters (and with variadic detection enabled). The C behavior is undefined; depending on host compiler and memory layout, `strcmp()` can read before the function-name allocation, abort generation, or misclassify the wrapper and emit incorrect headers. This is a host build-tool defect, not an Exec runtime defect. **Affected configuration:** the `kernel-exec` include-generation target; the dummy-library case requires its explicit developer test target. **Confidence:** high for the underflow and out-of-object pointer formation; manifestation is host/compiler dependent. Check the name length before suffix arithmetic. No generator, build, or runtime operation was run; source-only.

<a id="ek574"></a>
### EK574 — A pthread TLS destructor can deadlock when it deletes a key [high functional impact; high source confidence for a destructor that calls `pthread_key_delete`]

`StarterFunc` acquires `tls_sem` in shared mode before iterating the active TLS keys, and keeps that shared hold while invoking each non-null per-thread destructor (`compiler/pthread/pthread_create.c:180-197`). The public `pthread_key_delete` implementation needs the same semaphore exclusively before it can clear the key's `used` and `destructor` fields (`compiler/pthread/pthread.c:201-223`). Exec's shared-semaphore implementation records shared ownership with a null owner; an exclusive request by that same task does not count as recursive ownership and is queued to wait for the shared holder to release (`rom/exec/semaphores.c:58-141`). The destructor cannot return and release the shared hold until `pthread_key_delete` returns, so the worker blocks forever during thread exit. POSIX explicitly requires `pthread_key_delete()` to be callable from a thread-specific-data destructor ([POSIX Programmer's Manual](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man3/pthread_key_delete.3p.html)). Snapshot the key/destructor state under the lock and release it around callbacks, while preserving safe key lifetime and reuse semantics. Trigger: a worker exits with a non-null value for a key whose destructor calls `pthread_key_delete` on an allocated key. No pthread workload or deadlock was run; source-only.


<a id="ek306"></a>
### EK306 — A different-task expunge can free a per-task library base while leaving its owner's slot pointing to it [high memory-integrity impact; high source confidence for generated per-task-base libraries with relative dependencies]

`InitLib` opens each configured `rellib` and stores the returned base in the library's resident base (`compiler/autoinit/functions.c:42-52`; `compiler/autoinit/libraries.c:77-109`). When that parent library is expunged, `_set_libexpunge` closes those dependencies in the task performing expunge (`functions.c:75-86`; `libraries.c:112-127`), which need not be the task that initialized the resident library. For a generated `pertaskbase` dependency, the selected `CloseLib` sees that `dupbase->task != FindTask(NULL)`, so it does not restore or clear the original owner's per-task slot; it then sets `dupbase->task = NULL` and frees that duplicate base (`tools/genmodule/writestart.c:1470-1502`). `FreeTaskStorageSlot` returns only the slot ID to the allocator and does not clear values in existing tasks' storage arrays (`rom/task/FreeTaskStorageSlot.c:29-66`; `SetTaskStorageSlot.c:119-122`). The owner task therefore retains a non-null slot value that points to freed memory. A later open of that dependency first reads its current-task slot and, if non-null, dereferences `dupbase->task`, `lib_Node.ln_Name`, and process return-address fields to decide whether to reuse it (`writestart.c:1320-1345`) before it can reject the stale duplicate. This is a use-after-free even though the generated comment anticipates a stale pointer. The checked-in `tiff.library` configuration declares per-task `jfif`, `z1`, `posixc` and `stdc` dependencies, and `png.library` declares per-task `z1` and `posixc` dependencies (`workbench/libs/tiff/tiff.conf:6-10`; `workbench/libs/png/png.conf:4-9`). Their module targets have explicit build rules, but the `workbench-libs-complete` and `workbench-datatypes-complete` catch-all declarations that could select these examples are commented out at this revision (`workbench/libs/mmakefile:11-62`; `workbench/classes/datatypes/mmakefile:3-21`); this source review does not establish default packaging or a currently selected runtime client. Trigger: task A loads a parent library whose resident relative-dependency base is opened in A; the parent is finally expunged by task B, which closes that dependency duplicate while A remains alive; A later opens the still-resident dependency again (or its task-slot ID is reused and a generated per-task base is opened). The open path can read the freed duplicate, fault, or make a decision from recycled memory. Clear the owner slot through a safe cross-task mechanism before freeing the base, or defer reclamation until the owner task can unwind its slot. No module expunge or subsequent open was run; source-only, and the specific concurrent task sequence remains conditional.


<a id="ek631"></a>
### EK631 — Task-resource slot IDs are permanently consumed when FreeTaskStorageSlot cannot allocate its free-list node [low task-resource capacity impact; high source confidence under allocation failure followed by later reuse]

`FreeTaskStorageSlot` allocates a `TaskStorageFreeSlot` record and returns immediately if that allocation fails, explicitly discarding the released ID (`rom/task/FreeTaskStorageSlot.c:45-53`). The allocator reuses only IDs represented by nodes in `trb_TaskStorageSlots`; when none are available it advances the tail sentinel to the next ID instead (`rom/task/AllocTaskStorageSlot.c:51-76`). The selected generated per-task-base expunge path ignores the void free result and sets `__pertaskslot` to zero (`tools/genmodule/writestart.c:1578-1582`); posixc's selected thread-hook expunge likewise clears its saved slot after calling `FreeTaskStorageSlot` (`compiler/crt/posixc/__threadhook.c:170-174`). Neither caller can retry the lost ID. A later load/reinitialization therefore allocates a new, higher slot ID, and `SetTaskStorageSlot` may have to grow each affected task's storage array to cover it (`rom/task/SetTaskStorageSlot.c:70-103`). Trigger: freeing a generated per-task or posixc worker slot while the record allocation fails, followed by later module reinitializations that need task storage. Repeated incidents monotonically consume IDs and can expand task-storage arrays or eventually make later slot publication fail; one incident only burns one ID and does not itself corrupt existing slots. Preserve failed IDs in a nonallocating fallback/free list or retain the slot ID for retry. No allocation failure or repeated load/unload was run; source-only.


<a id="ek714"></a>
**Caller scope:** a repository-wide direct-call search found no production in-tree `SetTaskAffinity()` caller. The only direct caller is the SMP affinity test, which changes a running spinner and races setter threads but does not force the dispatch/check-to-lock interleaving (`developer/debug/test/smp/smpaffinity.c:206-301`). The race is therefore an API-level defect whose practical trigger requires an external or indirect client to retarget a ready task concurrently with dispatch.
EK714. **SMP schedulers can launch a task on a CPU excluded by its newly set affinity mask (conditional scheduling-affinity violation; high source confidence on selected PC, ARM and AArch64 SMP).** `SetTaskAffinity()` changes an existing mask in place under `tc_SpinLock` (`rom/task/SetTaskAffinity.c:98-120`), but its reschedule kick is requested only when the task is already `TS_RUN`, not while it remains `TS_READY` (`:130-132`). The selected PC dispatcher tests the mask and removes the task under `TaskReadySpinLock` (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:304-322`), then later changes `TS_READY` to `TS_RUN` without taking the task lock or checking affinity again (`:344-370`). The setter does not take the ready-list lock. Interleaving: PC dispatch observes that CPU in the old mask and removes the ready task; the setter replaces the mask to exclude that CPU and returns while the task is still `TS_READY`; PC dispatch then launches it using its stale match. ARM and AArch64 have the same stale-eligibility window: `core_AffinityMatch` runs before the dispatcher takes the task lock, and the selected CPU is not checked again before transition to `TS_RUN` (`arch/arm-native/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:263-295,309-349`; `arch/aarch64-native/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:241-269,280-314`). A setter can win the task lock after eligibility was read but before dispatch obtains it; dispatch then launches using the stale result and the setter did not request a kick because it saw `TS_READY`. This can run a task outside the affinity requested by a completed setter until a later scheduling point. It affects ExecSMP builds using the selected PC, ARM or AArch64 scheduler when a task's existing mask is changed concurrently with dispatch. `QueryTaskTagList(TaskTag_CPUAffinity)` also reads the mutable mask without the setter's task lock and can return a partial snapshot; this remains a related unsynchronized-read effect. Recheck affinity while holding the task lock before launch, or publish immutable replacement masks with appropriate lifetime protection. The in-tree SMP affinity test migrates a running spinner and races setters, but reads back after setter threads finish; it does not force the dispatch/check-to-lock interleaving (`developer/debug/test/smp/smpaffinity.c:206-301`). No runtime interleaving was run; source-only.


<a id="ek333"></a>
EK333. **`logInitialise` dereferences a failed provider-handle allocation (conditional low-memory fault; high source confidence).** After `CreatePool` returns non-NULL, `logInitialise` assigns `AllocVecPooled` directly to `lpHandle` and immediately writes its fields without checking for NULL (`rom/log/log.c:143-153`). Exec documents `AllocVecPooled` as returning NULL on allocation failure (`rom/exec/allocvecpooled.c:25-36`). A successful pool creation does not guarantee this allocation: `CreatePool` allocates only the small pool-header block and leaves the first usable puddle allocation until the first `AllocPooled` call (`rom/exec/createpool.c:113-127,161-177,201-215`); that growth can fail independently. With the broadcaster running and a nonnull provider, failure of this first pooled allocation therefore reaches the `lpHandle->lrh_Node` write and faults inside `logInitialise`. The default x86-64 PC configuration selects log.resource and AHCI calls this API during initialization when `AROS_USE_LOGRES` is enabled (`rom/devs/ahci/ahci_init.c:87-93`; `arch/x86_64-pc/boot/mmakefile.src:34-35`); other selected callers also initialize providers. Check the handle allocation, delete the newly created pool on failure, and return NULL. Trigger requires `CreatePool`'s pool-header allocation to succeed and its first usable-puddle allocation to fail; no allocation failure or client initialization was induced. Source-only.


<a id="ek567"></a>
EK567. **`pthread_mutex_timedlock` acquires an uncontended mutex twice (conditional lock leak; high source confidence).** For a valid non-NULL absolute deadline, the function calls `pthread_mutex_trylock`; when it succeeds, the function does not return and instead proceeds to `_obtain_sema_timed` (`compiler/pthread/pthread.c:329-353`). That helper submits an exclusive `Procure` request (`:303-323`). Exec's `Procure` recognizes that the current task already owns the semaphore and increments `ss_NestCount` again before replying immediately (`rom/exec/procure.c:47-70`). The timed-lock call returns success with nesting count two, while one matching `pthread_mutex_unlock` invokes `ReleaseSemaphore` only once, leaving the semaphore owned and blocking other tasks (`compiler/pthread/pthread_mutex_unlock.c:26-43`; `rom/exec/releasesemaphore.c:62-82`). This affects the selected pthread library on AROS when `pthread_mutex_timedlock` is called with a non-expired deadline and an initially available mutex; recursive mutexes are also acquired twice. Return immediately when the trylock succeeds, and use the timed wait only after an `EBUSY` result. No pthread call or semaphore contention was run. Source-only.


EK736. **`superclass_field` is ignored when genmodule supplies its default superclass (conditional generated BOOPSI parent mismatch; high source confidence).** The parser rejects an explicitly supplied `superclass` together with `superclass_field`, but its defaulting condition checks `cl->superclass == NULL` twice instead of checking both fields (`tools/genmodule/config.c:1475-1505`). For a BOOPSI class whose configuration specifies only `superclass_field`, the static default is consequently stored in `cl->superclass`. The selected BOOPSI writer prefers `superclass` and emits `aMeta_SuperID`, so it never emits the configured runtime `aMeta_SuperPtr` expression (`tools/genmodule/oopsupport.c:127-145`; the same superclass branch is used by `boopsisupport.c:180-198` and `muisupport.c:76-98`). Generated class creation therefore uses the default parent instead of the base field's parent, which can make the class inherit the wrong methods/attributes. The trigger is a genmodule configuration using `superclass_field` without `superclass`; no in-tree `.conf` uses this option, so no checked-in generated module is claimed affected. Check `superclass == NULL && superclass_field == NULL` before selecting a default. No generated output or runtime class was built; source-only.


EK738. **A function prototype with more than 64 arguments overruns genmodule's parser arrays (conditional host-tool memory corruption; high source confidence).** `readsectionfunctionlist` stores each parsed parameter in local `args[64]` before any argument-count bound check; register specifications are similarly stored in `regs[64]` (`tools/genmodule/config.c:1886-1888,1940-1947,1994-2003`). A 65th argument writes beyond the corresponding stack array, and later parsing/generation can consume corrupted parser state or terminate abnormally. The parser is used by selected host genmodule invocations on module `.conf` input, but a census of all 479 checked-in `.conf` files counted 5,120 `functionlist`, `methodlist`, and `cfunctionlist` declarations, with a maximum of 17 parameters; this remains conditional on custom or future over-limit configuration. Reject before writing either array. No malformed configuration was run.

EK739. **Negative `.skip` values move generated library vectors backward and can duplicate an LVO (conditional generated ABI defect; high source confidence).** The function-list parser accepts any integer accepted by `strtol` after `.skip` and adds it directly to unsigned `lvo` without requiring a nonnegative value (`tools/genmodule/config.c:1663-1668,1713-1733`). For example, after a function advances the counter, `.skip -1` returns it to that function's LVO; the next parsed function receives that duplicate vector (`functionhead.h:31-40`; table emission in `tools/genmodule/writestart.c:1758-1788`). The generated module can expose two functions at the same vector or an incorrect table layout. A source census of all 488 checked-in `.conf`/`.cfg` files found 305 numeric `.skip` directives, all nonnegative (maximum 285); this requires custom or future negative input. Reject negative values and check LVO range before updating. No generated module was built.


<a id="ek117"></a>
EK117. **An EIST-capable Intel CPU can leave its governor uninitialized at low load and briefly over-report frequency on its first high-load update (conditional; high source confidence).** On the selected x86-64 PC path, `core_CPUFreqInit()` skips `x86_64_cpu_perf_init_core_intel()` when CPUID reports EIST, but still installs the setter and enables `PLATFORMF_CPUFREQ` (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:528-572`). The selected APIC allocation paths clear the per-core `CPUData` records (`arch/all-pc/kernel/apic.c:35`; ACPI enumeration uses `MEMF_CLEAR` at `arch/all-pc/kernel/acpi_apic.c:43`). The first low-load sample therefore selects low ratio zero and finds `cpu_PerfCurRatio` also zero; `core_CPUFreqUpdate()` returns before invoking the setter (`arch/all-pc/kernel/cpu_freq.c:27-39,66-98`). While samples stay below the down threshold, the per-core capability/current/min/max fields remain uninitialized and no configured low ratio is requested. On the first later high-load sample, target selection falls back to `0xff`; the Intel setter initializes the core and clamps that request to `cpu_PerfMaxRatio` before writing `MSR_IA32_PERF_CTL` (`kernel_cpu.c:399-435,474-497`), but the common updater stores the original target `0xff` as `cpu_PerfCurRatio` (`cpu_freq.c:91-98`). Until a later update stores the now-selected in-range target, `KATTR_CPUFrequencyKHz` scales `cpu_TSCFreq` by that overstated field (`arch/all-pc/kernel/getcpuattr.c:61-79`; public attribute declaration `compiler/include/aros/kernel.h:115`). **Trigger and consequence:** an EIST-present Intel CPU starts with low-load samples, then reaches a high-load sample; the first transition can temporarily over-report frequency when its maximum ratio is below `0xff`, while a low-load-only start delays governor initialization. **Affected configuration:** x86-64 PC with Intel EIST and CPU-frequency support enabled. Initialize each core before governor updates and record the setter’s clamped ratio. **Confidence:** high for the initialization, fallback, clamp, stored value and query math; no CPU, MSR or runtime load behavior was exercised.

<a id="ek144"></a>
EK144. **An empty ROM resident scan dereferences its NULL terminator while sorting (conditional early-boot failure; high source confidence).** When the resident scan finds no entries and the scanner can allocate its pointer array, `krnRomTagScanner()` writes `RomTag[0] = NULL` and then enters the bubble-sort loop without checking that `scanData.num` is at least two (`rom/kernel/kernel_romtags.c:294-329`). The condition `i < scanData.num - 1` underflows for the unsigned zero count, so the first iteration evaluates `RomTag[0]->rt_Pri` and dereferences the NULL terminator. The caller `krnPrepareExecBase()` would otherwise detect a missing `exec.library` and issue the documented panic, but the sort fails before that check (`rom/kernel/prepareexecbase.c:21-38`). **Trigger and consequence:** startup supplies scan ranges containing no resident tags, while the scanner's pointer-array allocation succeeds; boot then faults during resident sorting instead of taking the missing-Exec panic path. **Affected configuration:** maintained kernel startup targets using this shared resident scanner, conditional on an empty resident scan. No such reachable maintained boot range was established in the source review. **Confidence:** high for the zero-count underflow and NULL dereference; occurrence depends on startup memory contents/ranges. Return the empty list for normal missing-Exec handling or skip sorting for fewer than two residents. No boot was run; source-only; see the Exec/Kernel coverage ledger.

EK768. **An accepted OpenSBI timebase below 100 Hz produces a zero periodic timer interval (conditional timer-rearm failure; high source confidence, unsupported firmware input not established).** The FDT parser accepts any nonzero `timebase-frequency` value of at least four bytes without a lower-bound check (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_fdt.c:232-236`); startup selects that value when available and calls `krnTimerInit` with a fixed 100 Hz tick rate (`kernel_startup.c:559-560,722-729`). `krnTimerInit` computes `tick_interval = timebase_hz / tick_hz` with integer division, so values 1–99 yield zero; each timer trap then computes and rearms the next tick at the current time (`kernel_timer.c:248-260,284-295`). This can cause continuous immediate timer interrupts and prevent normal progress. The EFI fallback uses 10 MHz, and no supported OpenSBI device tree below 100 Hz was found; this remains conditional on firmware input. Reject too-low frequencies or enforce a nonzero interval. No timer was run.


<a id="ek277"></a>
EK277. **Concurrent parent and child exit can make child cleanup use a freed former parent (conditional ExecSMP lifetime and child-list corruption; high source confidence).** `NewAddTask` records the currently running task as the new task's parent (`rom/exec/newaddtask.c:181-190,268-272`), and `Exec_InitETask` links the child ETask into that parent's `et_Children` list under the parent's task lock (`rom/exec/exec_util.c:217-227`). During child teardown, `Exec_CleanupETask` reads `et->et_Parent` and caches the parent's ETask before taking any lock that prevents the parent's teardown from changing that relationship (`:271-277`). If the parent exits concurrently, its cleanup takes its own task lock and reparents each child to the grandparent by changing `child->et_Parent` and appending the child to the grandparent's list (`:279-298`), then can expunge and free the former parent's ETask (`:354-355,360-370`). The child cleanup still holds its cached former-parent pointer; it later takes that freed ETask's task lock, removes the child node, and may enqueue or signal through the former parent's task port (`:302-329`). If the child was moved to the grandparent's list, the child cleanup also performs that removal while holding the former parent's lock rather than the current parent's lock. This can access freed memory and mutate the grandparent's child list without its lock. `Forbid()` does not serialize these operations across CPUs on ExecSMP (`rom/exec/forbid.c:55-60`). The trigger is an ETask parent and one of its children exiting concurrently on different CPUs; ordinary task creation and teardown provide both paths. A child-exit cleanup should revalidate and pin its current parent under a lifetime-safe protocol, and parent teardown must transfer children atomically with respect to child cleanup. Affects selected ExecSMP configurations, including x86-64 PC and Raspberry Pi ARM32/AArch64 SMP builds. **Confidence:** high for the stale-parent dereference and wrong-list-lock sequence in the traced code; the cross-CPU overlap is conditional. No task exit or SMP interleaving was run; source-only.


<a id="ek8981"></a>
EK8981. **OpenLibrary can dispatch through a library base freed by a concurrent RemLibrary (conditional SMP use-after-free; high source confidence).** `OpenLibrary` protects `FindName` with the `LibList` read lock, then releases that lock before checking `lib_Version` and calling the library's Open vector (`rom/exec/openlibrary.c:73-91`). It retains only `Forbid()` on the calling CPU until the function returns (`:74,107`); Exec documents that Forbid is processor-local on ExecSMP (`rom/exec/forbid.c:58-60`). `RemLibrary` does not take the LibList write lock; it calls the target's Expunge vector under its own local `Forbid` (`rom/exec/remlibrary.c:64-79`). If OpenLibrary has obtained the pointer but has not yet called the Open vector, a concurrent RemLibrary can therefore see `lib_OpenCnt == 0` and expunge the object before OpenLibrary reads `lib_Version` or dispatches through its vector. The generic generated library expunge path removes and frees a zero-open-count base after its expunge hooks succeed (`tools/genmodule/writestart.c:1535-1589`). This has a selected direct caller: VMM closes its `MUIMasterBase` reference and calls `RemLibrary(MUIMasterBase)` during `Q_QUITBOTH`, protected only by local Forbid (`workbench/system/VMM/MUI/main.c:186-195`); muimaster's selected expunge hook succeeds (`workbench/libs/muimaster/muimaster_init-aros.c:94-114`). Hold a cross-core lifetime reference from list lookup through completion of the Open vector, and serialize expunge with that reference. **Affected configuration and trigger:** ExecSMP builds when a direct RemLibrary caller expunges a zero-open-count library after another CPU's OpenLibrary has looked up its base but before that OpenLibrary call reaches its Open vector; the selected VMM/MUI path provides a concrete expunge caller. Single-CPU builds are excluded. **Confidence:** high for the unpinned lookup/dispatch and zero-open-count expunge sequence; the overlap is conditional on concurrent ExecSMP scheduling. The VMM preferences application is selected in the Workbench:System aggregate; the caller still requires someone to launch it and issue the quit command. No library open, expunge, or SMP interleaving was run; source-only.


<a id="ek9019"></a>
EK9019. **PC task exception callbacks are not dispatched by the selected i386 or x86-64 task switchers (conditional unhandled exception signals; high source confidence).** `Signal()` sets `TF_EXCEPT` and requests rescheduling when it delivers a bit in the task’s exception mask; `SetExcept()` does the same when enabling a mask that intersects already-received signals (`rom/exec/signal.c:305-342`; `rom/exec/setexcept.c:69-87`). The shared PC scheduler treats `TF_EXCEPT` as a reschedule condition (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_scheduler.c:65-101`), but the selected i386 `cpu_Dispatch()` leaves its `Exception()` call commented as a TODO (`arch/i386-pc/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:44-46`), while x86-64 compiles the call out and prints an “unhandled exception” diagnostic instead (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:168-176`). `rom/exec/exception.c:54-80` is the selected routine that clears the flag, drains matching received exception bits, and calls `tc_ExceptCode`; no alternate selected PC caller was found. Therefore, when a task has an exception callback and receives a matching exception signal, the callback is skipped and the bit remains pending; x86-64 can repeat the diagnostic on dispatch. The checked-in test demonstrates callback setup and signaling (`developer/debug/test/exec/exceptiontest.c:34-47`). **Affected configuration and trigger:** i386-PC or x86-64-PC; a task configures `tc_ExceptCode`, enables a signal in `tc_SigExcept`, and receives that signal. **Confidence:** high for the dispatch omission and signal-state flow; no callback or task switch was run. Source-only; see the Exec/Kernel coverage ledger.

<a id="ek514"></a>
## EK514

EK514. **Android hosted cold reboot reuses the freed `KernelArgs` pointer.** The shared hosted bootstrap stores optional command-line text in the global `KernelArgs`; the Android JNI loader calls `bootstrap(0, NULL)` and obtains that text from its selected `AROSBootstrap_android.conf` configuration (`arch/all-hosted/bootstrap/bootstrap.c:66,163-168,216-218,274-299`; `arch/all-android/bootstrap/main.c:40-68`; `arch/all-unix/boot/mmakefile.src:13-14`). On non-warm child exit, Android's `childHandler` calls `Host_FreeMem()` before notifying Java (`arch/all-android/bootstrap/kickstart.c:53-73`); `Host_FreeMem` frees `KernelArgs` but does not set it to NULL (`arch/all-unix/bootstrap/memory.c:123-136`). Java handles cold-reboot status by calling `ColdBoot`, which invokes native `Load` again in the same process (`AROSBootstrap.java:120-146,351-357`; `:75-85`). If the reloaded config contains an `arguments` directive, `bootstrap()` sees the dangling non-NULL pointer, passes it to `join_string()` for `strlen`/`strcpy`, and may then `free()` it a second time (`bootstrap.c:278-299`; `:120-160`). If the directive is absent, the stale pointer is still placed in `KRN_CmdLine` (`:390-393`); the selected Unix kernel startup later reads it with `strstr` for `waitdebug` and `notlsf` options (`arch/all-unix/kernel/kernel_startup.c:161,180`). Clear `KernelArgs` when freeing it and rebuild the command-line tag from the current load's state. **Affected configuration and trigger:** Android-hosted builds on a cold reboot after a bootstrap configuration supplied `arguments`; on the next load, the same-process freed pointer is either dereferenced during argument concatenation or passed to kernel startup. The checked-in Android config has no `arguments` directive, so the trigger requires a custom config (or prior argument-bearing load); no cold reboot was performed. **Confidence:** high for the free-without-clear and same-process reload path; visible failure depends on the stated argument configuration and allocator reuse. Source-only.


<a id="ek285"></a>
## EK285

**OpenSBI FDT register lookup reads beyond its ancestor stack for deeply nested device nodes (conditional wrong parent-cell decoding or early driver fault; high source confidence).** `fdt_parent()` tracks ancestors in a fixed `stack[16]`, but continues incrementing `depth` after the stack fills. When the requested node is at depth 17 or greater (root depth 0), it returns `stack[depth - 1]` without checking that index; at depth 17 this reads `stack[16]` past the array (`arch/riscv-all/linklibs/fdt/fdt.c:254-288`). `FDT_GetReg()` and `FDT_GetRegNamed()` call the parent-cell helpers, so the uninitialized/out-of-bounds value is then treated as an FDT node while looking up `#address-cells` or `#size-cells` (`:296-334`). The OpenSBI I²C, UART, PCI host and RTC discovery paths use these register helpers (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/hidd/dwi2c/dwi2c_init.c:119-225`; `dwuart/dwuart_init.c:81-100`; `pcidt/pcidt_driverclass.c:650-670`; `battclock/battclock_init.c:82-92`). The explicitly buildable `workbench-devs-networks-dwmac-riscv64` target also links `fdt` and calls `FDT_GetReg()` for its controller and MDIO child (`workbench/devs/networks/dwmac/mmakefile.src:10-21`; `dwmac_dt.c:101-126,177-182`); the active `workbench-devs-networks` rule includes this CPU-specific DWMAC target (`workbench/devs/networks/mmakefile.src:3-15`), so it is selected in the corresponding RISC-V network aggregate. A sufficiently deep compatible device node can therefore decode its register address/size from an unrelated location or fault during early driver discovery. Bound the depth and return a defined failure when the ancestor stack cannot represent the tree, or use dynamically/iteratively bounded storage. **Affected configuration and trigger:** OpenSBI RISC-V builds selecting the shared FDT library and one of these device drivers, when firmware supplies a compatible node nested at depth 17 or greater. No firmware blob or device was used. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked stack index and selected register-helper callers; occurrence depends on the external tree depth and matching device node. Source-only.

<a id="ek779"></a>
## EK779 — OpenSBI FDT register decoding overflows its tuple-size check

`FDT_GetReg()` obtains parent `#address-cells` and `#size-cells`, adds them into a 32-bit `stride`, then checks `(index + 1) * stride * 4 > len` using unchecked `ULONG` arithmetic (`arch/riscv-all/linklibs/fdt/fdt.c:296-313`). It does not constrain the cell counts or detect overflow in the sum or byte-size product. For example, an address-cell count of `0x40000000` and a size-cell count of zero make the index-zero byte-size product wrap to zero, so a short `reg` property passes the check. `FDT_ReadCells()` then iterates the declared count from that property without checking the available length (`fdt.c:228-235,310-313`), reading beyond the property.

The selected OpenSBI DWI2C, DW UART, PCI host and BattClock discovery paths use `FDT_GetReg()` directly or through `FDT_GetRegNamed()` (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/hidd/dwi2c/dwi2c_init.c:119-225`; `dwuart/dwuart_init.c:81-100`; `pcidt/pcidt_driverclass.c:650-670`; `battclock/battclock_init.c:82-92`). **Trigger and consequence:** OpenSBI RISC-V firmware supplies malformed parent cell counts for a node with a short `reg` property, and a selected caller parses it. The cell reader can access beyond the property during hardware discovery, causing incorrect register data or a fault. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked 32-bit arithmetic and read loop; occurrence depends on malformed firmware data and a matching selected device node. Validate supported cell counts and use checked arithmetic before indexing or reading. No firmware blob, device, or build was used. Source-only; see the Exec/Kernel coverage ledger.## EK9099

<a id="ek9099"></a>
EK9099. **Concurrent `OpenDevice()` and dynamic-device expunge can use a freed device base on ExecSMP (conditional stale-vector dereference; high source confidence).** `OpenDevice()` looks up the device while holding the `DeviceList` read lock and `Forbid`, but releases the list lock before calling the device's Open vector (`rom/exec/opendevice.c:92-114,130-135`). `RemDevice()` invokes the expunge vector under only `Forbid()` (`rom/exec/remdevice.c:65-81`); on ExecSMP, `Forbid()` disables task switching only on its calling processor and does not serialize another CPU (`rom/exec/forbid.c:52-61`). Thus a second CPU can expunge the device after `OpenDevice()` obtains its pointer but before the Open-vector call. The checked-in dynamic USB class expunges call `RemDevice()` after dropping their reserved device-base open count, and their `devExpunge()` removes the node and frees the device base when the count reaches zero. All 17 USB class `dev.c` implementations with direct `RemDevice()` calls increment `lib_OpenCnt` only after `devOpen()` has begun; that count cannot pin a base still held only in `OpenDevice()`'s local pointer. The audited classes are asixeth, bluetooth, cdcacm, cdceth, davicometh, ethwrap, lan78xx, massstorage, moschipeth, palmpda, pegasuseth, printer, rawwrap, rndis, serialcp210x, serialpl2303 and stir4200. The two Bluetooth-class expunge paths have the same ordering; selected `btserial.device` provides a concrete caller (`rom/bluetooth/classes/btserial/btserial.class.c:79-112`; `rom/bluetooth/classes/btserial/dev.c:43-137,180-210`). An additional selected caller is the per-unit `printer.device`: `Printer_Unit()` publishes the newly allocated unit with `AddDevice()` before starting and handshaking with its worker (`workbench/devs/printer/driver.c:783-812`). If worker startup fails, it calls `RemDevice()` (`:850`); that per-unit expunge removes and frees the allocation when `lib_OpenCnt` is zero (`:144-166`). A direct `OpenDevice()` for the published unit name on another CPU can therefore hold the raw node pointer while this failure cleanup frees it, before the per-unit Open vector increments the count. This direct-open overlap is separate from OD1889's publication-before-ready behavior and OD4287's child surviving reply-port creation failure. A concurrent expunge can therefore free the vector target and its base before dispatch, or race the vector's first base dereference/count increment. The same missing lifetime/list serialization also affects list readers: `AddDevice()` inserts under the `DeviceList` write lock (`rom/exec/adddevice.c:62-69`), but `RemDevice()` invokes expunge without that lock and representative dynamic expunges call plain `Remove()` before freeing the base (`rom/exec/remdevice.c:65-81`; `rom/exec/remove.c:55-62`; `rom/usb/classes/printer/dev.c:158-180`). The selected `C:DevList` command holds the DeviceList read lock while traversing nodes and copying their fields and names (`workbench/c/DevList.c:58-90,103-142`; selected by `workbench/c/mmakefile.src:16`); concurrent expunge can rewire/free the current node or its name during that snapshot. This is the same removal/lifetime root cause, not a separate finding. Protect DeviceList removal with its write lock and retain a lifetime reference through Open dispatch. **Affected configuration and trigger:** an ExecSMP build with one of the dynamic device classes above selected and registered, or with the `workbench-devs-printer` module selected and a per-unit device published, while another CPU runs `OpenDevice()` or the selected `C:DevList` snapshot during expunge. For printer, the OpenDevice overlap requires its worker startup handshake to fail after publication; single-CPU scheduling is excluded by `Forbid()`. No open/expunge overlap or list snapshot race was run. **Confidence:** high for the generic lock interval, local-only Forbid semantics, missing removal lock, selected DevList read-locked traversal, enumerated USB/Bluetooth count/free orderings, and printer publication/rollback path; occurrence requires the stated concurrent timing or startup-failure condition. Source-only.


<a id="ek830"></a>
## EK830 — concurrent `RemTask()` calls can both clean up the same task

`RemTask()` checks the target's terminal state before asking the scheduler helper to mark/remove it (`rom/exec/remtask.c:68-75,97-112`). The check is outside the synchronization in the PC, ARM32, and AArch64 reschedule helpers. On ExecSMP, two CPUs can therefore pass it for the same live task. The PC helper serializes list updates but accepts a repeated `TS_REMOVED` request for a tombstoned task and returns no indication that another caller owns cleanup (`arch/all-pc/exec/platform_init.c:269-335`). ARM32/AArch64 similarly serialize the state/list mutation under `tc_SpinLock` but return no cleanup-owner result (`arch/arm-native/exec/platform_init.c:129-213`; AArch64 `:114-180`). Both callers then proceed through context deletion, ETask cleanup, and freeing the detached `tc_MemEntry` chain without another ownership check (`rom/exec/remtask.c:115-128,165-181`; `rom/exec/exec_util.c:238-270,354-370`). This can make one caller access or free resources already released by the other.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** ExecSMP, when two CPUs call `RemTask()` for the same live, non-current task and both pass the initial check before either transition completes. On x86-64 PC, selected `security.library` provides a root-authorized `secKill()` path for plain tasks; overlap with the target's own finalizer is conditional, and no schedule was observed (`rom/security/secKill.c:50-58`; `arch/x86_64-pc/boot/mmakefile.src:60-65`). **Consequence:** duplicate context/ETask/MemEntry cleanup can access freed objects or repeat frees. Make the terminal transition and cleanup ownership a single atomic claim, and let only its winner release task resources. **Confidence:** high for the precheck, serialized state transitions, and unconditional common cleanup; manifestation requires concurrent callers. No task teardown or SMP interleaving was run. Source-only; see the Exec/Kernel coverage ledger.


<a id="ek9138"></a>
## EK9138 — Realtime alarm fields are published without synchronization

`SetPlayerAttrsA()` writes `PLAYERF_ALARMSET` before storing a new `pl_AlarmTime`, and updates `pl_Task` and `pl_Reserved0` in separate tag cases without acquiring `RT_CONDUCTORS` (`workbench/libs/realtime/setplayerattrsa.c:195-229`). `Pulse()` traverses players and reads the alarm flag, deadline, signal bit, and task while holding that semaphore (`workbench/libs/realtime/pulse.c:76-78,126-151`). Under ExecSMP, Pulse can therefore observe a newly enabled alarm with the prior deadline or observe a mixed task/bit pair during a destination update. A newly created player has a cleared allocation; if it already has a conductor and signal destination, the old zero deadline can cause an early signal when a future alarm time is being published. For an already enabled alarm, a concurrent two-tag destination change can signal a different task or use a mismatched signal bit.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** ExecSMP with an external or future public API caller changing alarm time or signal destination while the Pulse task reads the same player; no checked-in setters for these alarm tags were found. **Consequence:** early alarm notification or delivery to the wrong task/bit. Publish the alarm fields under `RT_CONDUCTORS` using a consistent update protocol. **Confidence:** high for the unlocked writer/locked reader and store ordering; occurrence requires the stated overlap and signal destination. No alarm or interleaving was run. Source-only; see the Exec/Kernel coverage ledger.


<a id="ek8969"></a>
## EK8969 — POSIXC ordinary `execve()`/`execv()` preserves descriptors marked `FD_CLOEXEC`

`execve()` and `execv()` call `__exec_prepare()` and then `__exec_do()` (`compiler/crt/posixc/execve.c:51-56`; `execv.c:55-60`). Unless `PRETEND_CHILD` is set, `__exec_do()` selects `__exec_do_regular()`, which sets `EXEC_PARENT` and runs the target through DOS `RunCommand()` (`__exec.c:49-69,505-573`). The target POSIXC startup sees that flag and `__copy_fdarray()` copies each descriptor's `fdflags` and shared file-control-block pointer, incrementing the shared reference count (`__fdesc.c:692-718,767-779`). The regular path does not call `__close_on_exec_fdescs()`; the only call is in the separate pretend-child path (`__exec.c:486`; `__fdesc.c:799-818`). Thus a locally managed descriptor marked `FD_CLOEXEC` remains open in the newly executed program.

**Trigger and consequence:** successful ordinary `execve()` or `execv()` with a local descriptor whose close-on-exec flag is set; the new program inherits the descriptor contrary to the flag's purpose. **Confidence:** high for the path split and copied flag; no program was executed. Source-only; see the Exec/Kernel coverage ledger.

<a id="ek9139"></a>
## EK9139 — POSIXC reports success for socket `F_SETFD` but does not store `FD_CLOEXEC`

For descriptors owned by another subsystem, `fcntl()` takes the foreign-hook path. For AROSTCP sockets, that branch returns zero for both `F_GETFD` and `F_SETFD` without storing or retrieving descriptor flags (`compiler/crt/posixc/fcntl.c:94-110`). Local descriptors instead store the supplied flags and return them from `F_GETFD` (`fcntl.c:168-181`). The public `fd_hooks` table provides an `fdh_fcntl` hook, but AROSTCP registers it as NULL; the available hook path only implements status behavior through `FIONBIO` (`workbench/libs/fd/include/fd.h:40-45`; `workbench/network/stacks/AROSTCP/bsdsocket/api/amiga_fdhooks.c:191-234`). Thus setting `FD_CLOEXEC` on a socket appears to succeed but has no effect, and a later `F_GETFD` reports zero. **Affected configuration and trigger:** POSIXC integrated with AROSTCP's fd.library socket descriptors, when a caller uses `F_SETFD`/`F_GETFD` to manage `FD_CLOEXEC`; no maintained direct socket caller was found. **Consequence:** the close-on-exec state cannot be set or observed for these descriptors. **Confidence:** high for the hard-coded returns and absent socket hook; no socket or fcntl call was run. Source-only; see the Exec/Kernel coverage ledger.


<a id="ek9152"></a>
## EK9152 — taskless semaphore attempts leave an initialized semaphore permanently held [conditional]

`exec_init.c` calls the `PREINITLIB` set before allocating and publishing the bootstrap task (`rom/exec/exec_init.c:143-200`). Exec's resident comment requires the CPU to be in user mode for this initialization call (`exec_init.c:61-66`), so `CheckSemaphore()`'s supervisor-mode rejection does not block a valid pre-init call (`rom/exec/semaphores.c:17-48`). `InitSemaphore()` sets `ss_QueueCount` to -1, `ss_Owner` to NULL, and `ss_NestCount` to zero (`rom/exec/initsemaphore.c:45-59`). Before task publication, `AttemptSemaphore()` passes a NULL current task as its owner, and `AttemptSemaphoreShared()` explicitly passes NULL (`rom/exec/attemptsemaphore.c:53-57`; `attemptsemaphoreshared.c:53-56`). `InternalAttemptSemaphore()` lacks the taskless early return used by `InternalObtainSemaphore()` and increments the free semaphore to queue count zero, assigns the NULL owner, increments the nest count, and returns TRUE (`rom/exec/semaphores.c:50-62,164-195`). The matching `ReleaseSemaphore()` immediately returns when `GET_THIS_TASK` is NULL, without undoing either count (`rom/exec/releasesemaphore.c:56-63`). A later task's exclusive `ObtainSemaphore()` then sees the phantom queue entry and waits; there is no task owner that can release it. Shared acquisitions may join the NULL-owner state but cannot remove the phantom nesting level.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** a `PREINITLIB` callback calls either attempt API on an initialized, free semaphore before the bootstrap task is published. The only maintained registration in this snapshot is PC `Exec_X86PreInit()` (`arch/all-pc/exec/platform_init.c:429-443`), which only registers a shutdown callback and does not call either semaphore API; therefore no current default startup path is claimed. **Consequence:** the attempt reports success, its paired pre-init release has no effect, and later exclusive users of that semaphore can wait indefinitely. **Confidence:** high for the state transition and release mismatch; low for current in-tree reachability, which was not found. Reject taskless attempts before mutating semaphore state. No startup or semaphore operation was run; source-only; see the [coverage ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#taskless-preinitlib-attemptsemaphore-ek9152).

<a id="ek9154"></a>
## EK9154 — POSIXC socket `F_SETFL` silently ignores `O_ASYNC`

The public POSIXC `fcntl()` contract says `F_SETFL` may change `O_NONBLOCK`, `O_APPEND`, and `O_ASYNC` (`compiler/crt/posixc/fcntl.c:44-57`). For descriptors owned by another subsystem, the socket branch reads the requested flags but forwards only `O_NONBLOCK` through `FIONBIO`; it ignores the `fdh_ioctl()` result and returns success (`fcntl.c:94-129`). Its `F_GETFL` path likewise reports only `O_NONBLOCK` (`:101-108`). The selected AROSTCP socket fd hook implements only `FIONBIO`, while AROSTCP's own socket ioctl implementation supports `FIOASYNC` by toggling `SS_ASYNC` and socket-buffer async flags (`workbench/network/stacks/AROSTCP/bsdsocket/api/amiga_fdhooks.c:166-190,205-232`; `amiga_generic.c:196-205`).

Thus `fcntl(socket_fd, F_SETFL, flags | O_ASYNC)` reports success without enabling asynchronous notification, and a later `F_GETFL` cannot report that flag. **Affected configuration and trigger:** POSIXC with AROSTCP's `ENABLE_FDLIBRARY` socket integration, when a caller uses `O_ASYNC` on a socket; no maintained direct caller was found. **Consequence:** applications may believe asynchronous socket notification is enabled when it is not. Forward `O_ASYNC` to the socket's `FIOASYNC` handling and report it from `F_GETFL`, or return an unsupported-operation error. **Confidence:** high for the POSIXC flag contract, socket-hook behavior, and AROSTCP capability; no socket or notification was used. Source-only; see the Exec/Kernel coverage ledger.

<a id="ek9147"></a>
## EK9147 — m68k software `UMult64` pairs the wrong operand halves

The 68000/68010/68060 software fallback for `UMult64` computes incorrect partial products. It copies the two input registers, swaps the copies to expose their high words, then uses `mulu %d5,%d1` for the low-word product; both operands there are the second input’s low word, so it squares that half instead of multiplying the inputs (`arch/m68k-all/utility/umult64.s:46-77`). The remaining partial products also do not implement the documented `ac`, `ad`, `bc`, and `bd` terms. For example, the source arithmetic for `UMult64(2,3)` yields 9 instead of 6.

The m68k Utility manifest includes this assembly implementation, and the same-basename generic C object is excluded when the architecture object is linked (`arch/m68k-all/utility/mmakefile.src:5-14`; `rom/utility/mmakefile.src:35-47`; `config/make.tmpl:2106-2109,2142-2143`). `UtilityM68K_ArchInit()` replaces the vector with the native 020 implementation on 68020/030/040, but leaves the software fallback on 68000/68010 and 68060 (`arch/m68k-all/utility/utility_archinit.c:27-39`).
