Both selected PowerPC `Supervisor()` overrides call `SuperState()`, invoke the supplied callback, and then unconditionally call `UserState(stack)` (`arch/ppc-sam440/exec/supervisor.c:16-25`; `arch/ppc-chrp/exec/supervisor.c:16-25`). The corresponding `UserState()` implementations ignore the token and unconditionally set `MSR_PR` (`arch/ppc-sam440/exec/userstate.c:12-21`; `arch/ppc-chrp/exec/userstate.c:12-21`). If `Supervisor()` is called while already in supervisor mode, `SuperState()` leaves the caller privileged (its syscall clears an already-clear `MSR_PR`), the callback returns to that context, and the unconditional `UserState()` changes the processor to user mode. `Supervisor()` then returns in a less privileged mode than its caller had before the call.

The documented `Supervisor()` interface describes running a callback under supervisor privilege but does not require a user-mode caller (`rom/exec/supervisor.c:14-34`). The selected code therefore violates mode preservation for an already-supervisor caller. This is distinct from EK9050, which covers the separate `SuperState()` return-token contract for direct user-mode callers. Caller review found Sam440's selected `Processor_Init()` call is reached after kernel startup sets `MSR_PR` and therefore starts in user mode; the apparent Sam440 ATA call is in a commented-out build edge; no ordinary CHRP caller or selected in-tree supervisor-mode caller was established (`arch/ppc-sam440/processor/processor_init.c:26`; `rom/exec/exec_init.c:270-279`; `arch/ppc-sam440/kernel/kernel_startup.c:649`; `arch/ppc-sam440/ata/mmakefile.src:7-17`).

The same conditional mode loss is also present through three selected Efika kernel.resource vectors. `KrnSetProtection()`, `KrnUnmapGlobal()`, and `KrnVirtualToPhysical()` in `arch/ppc-chrp/efika/kernel/mmu.c:367-490` save the entry MSR with `goSuper()` and then call `goUser(msr)`. The selected `kernel_intern.h:85-87` declares `goUser()` without a parameter and implements it as `wrmsr(rdmsr() | MSR_PR)`, so the passed value is not restored and a supervisor-mode entry is demoted. `KrnMapGlobal()` instead restores its saved value with `wrmsr(msr)` (`mmu.c:403-423`). A checkout-wide direct-caller census found the selected Efika PCI driver and CHRP cache/RTAS call paths, but did not establish one invoking these vectors while already supervisor; these remain conditional public-kernel-API cases, grouped under this existing mode-preservation finding.

**Trigger and consequence:** either a client calls `Supervisor()` from supervisor mode on PowerPC CHRP/Efika or Sam440, or a supervisor-mode caller invokes one of the three Efika MMU vectors above. On return it unexpectedly resumes in user mode, so subsequent privileged instructions or data accesses can fault. **Affected configuration:** PowerPC CHRP/Efika and Sam440 Exec builds selecting these overrides, plus Efika kernel.resource clients using the three vectors; practical in-tree supervisor-mode callers were not found, so these remain conditional API cases. **Confidence:** high for the unconditional mode change in source; impact requires an already-supervisor caller. Preserve the entry privilege state and restore it rather than unconditionally selecting user mode. No privilege transition or build was exercised. Source-only; see the [PowerPC Supervisor wrapper caller census](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7719).

<a id="ek565"></a>
### EK565 — `pthread_setschedprio()` rejects every requested priority due to a reversed range predicate (API always fails; high source confidence).

`pthread_setschedprio()` validates the requested priority with `prio < sched_get_priority_max(SCHED_NORMAL) || prio > sched_get_priority_min(SCHED_NORMAL)` and returns `EINVAL` when that expression is true (`compiler/pthread/pthread.c:1014-1022`). The selected bounds are 2 and -2 (`compiler/pthread/sched.c:24-40`), so the predicate is true for every integer: values below 2 satisfy the first clause, and values at least 2 satisfy the second. The function returns before resolving the thread or calling `SetTaskPri()`, making it impossible to change any thread's priority through this API.

The pthread implementation is included in the selected pthread link library (`compiler/pthread/mmakefile.src:7-12,15-38`). A repository-wide C/C++ caller search found only the declaration and definition, so no checked-in client impact is claimed. **Trigger and consequence:** any client calls the exported function with any priority and receives `EINVAL`; the thread priority remains unchanged. **Affected configuration:** clients linking the selected AROS pthread link library. **Confidence:** high for the fixed bounds, reversed predicate and unconditional early return; practical impact depends on an external client using the API. Reverse the comparisons so values outside the inclusive `[-2, 2]` range are rejected. No pthread call was run; source-only.

<a id="ek570"></a>
### EK570 — `pthread_exit()` longjmps through an unset jump buffer on the initial thread.

The pthread initializer reserves slot zero for the current main task and initializes its cleanup list, but does not establish `threads[0].jmp` (`compiler/pthread/pthread.c:1217-1231`). `pthread_self()` maps that task to slot zero (`pthread_self.c:29-43`; `pthread.c:80-93`). In contrast, the only `setjmp(inf->jmp)` is in the worker `StarterFunc()` path after `pthread_create()` starts a child (`pthread_create.c:105-138`). If the initial thread calls `pthread_exit()`, it resolves slot zero, records the return value, runs cleanup handlers, then calls `longjmp(inf->jmp, 1)` without a prior `setjmp()` for that buffer (`pthread_exit.c:26-43`). This is an invalid nonlocal jump and can terminate or corrupt the initial task instead of completing the thread exit path.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** an application using the selected AROS pthread link library calls `pthread_exit()` from its initial thread. No checked-in caller was found; the trigger is external use of the public API. **Confidence:** high that the initial slot has no established jump point and the exported exit path uses it unconditionally; the resulting control flow is undefined by the C `setjmp`/`longjmp` contract. Provide a dedicated initial-thread exit path rather than using the worker trampoline's jump buffer. No pthread call was run; source-only.


<a id="ek569"></a>
### EK569 — Detaching a pthread during or after completion leaves its slot live and makes process exit wait forever.

When a joinable worker finishes, `StarterFunc()` sets `inf->finished` and signals its waiter but leaves `inf->task` and the rest of the slot intact (`compiler/pthread/pthread_create.c:203-209`). A later `pthread_detach()` accepts the still-populated slot and only sets `inf->detached = TRUE` (`compiler/pthread/pthread.c:942-960`). `pthread_join()` then rejects that slot because it is detached and cannot perform its normal `memset()` cleanup (`compiler/pthread/pthread_join.c:34-53`). The detached-worker cleanup that clears the slot only runs at the end of `StarterFunc()` when the worker observes `detached` before its completion branch; it does not run again after detach is applied to an already-finished worker.

At process exit, `__pthread_Exit_Func()` waits in a loop while every detached slot's `inf->task` is non-NULL (`compiler/pthread/pthread.c:1234-1255`). Thus the sequence “worker completes as joinable; parent detaches it; parent exits” leaves a permanent non-NULL task pointer and stalls the exit hook indefinitely.

A second valid timing reaches the same state: while a joinable worker is completing, `StarterFunc()` reads `inf->detached` as false at its branch (`pthread_create.c:203`). If the parent calls `pthread_detach()` after that read but before the worker returns from the branch, detach only writes `TRUE` (`pthread.c:942-960`); the worker still records `finished` and signals without clearing the slot. On an ExecSMP target those unsynchronized accesses can overlap on separate CPUs. The exit hook then sees the detached flag and waits on the retained task pointer. No separate finding is needed because both triggers share the missed completion cleanup and exit wait.

The pthread link-library target includes the implementation (`compiler/pthread/mmakefile.src:7-38`). No checked-in caller of `pthread_detach()` was found, so practical triggers are external clients using either the completed-unjoined lifecycle or detaching a running worker during this completion window.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** clients linking the selected AROS pthread link library; a joinable worker is detached after it has completed but before join, or concurrently after its completion branch has read the joinable state, and the parent process exits. **Confidence:** high for the sequential state transitions and retained task pointer; the additional race requires the stated overlap on ExecSMP. Clear/reap an already-finished slot when detach is called, synchronize detach with worker completion, or make the exit hook recognize completed slots and avoid waiting on stale task pointers. No pthread, concurrent detach, or process-exit operation was run; source-only.

<a id="ek588"></a>
### EK588 — Concurrent first use of POSIX `flock()` can publish duplicate named semaphores on ExecSMP (conditional advisory-lock bypass; high source confidence).

`flock()` builds a semaphore name from the file's full path, then wraps `FindSemaphore()` and, on a miss, allocation plus `AddSemaphore()` in `Forbid()` (`compiler/crt/posixc/flock.c:116-165`). On ExecSMP, the Exec contract explicitly states that `Forbid()` applies only to the calling processor (`rom/exec/forbid.c:48-66`). `FindSemaphore()` takes the semaphore-list spinlock only while searching (`rom/exec/findsemaphore.c:52-59`); `AddSemaphore()` takes it separately while inserting and does not reject an existing name (`rom/exec/addsemaphore.c:69-82`). Therefore two CPUs can both search and miss before either inserts, then publish two semaphores with the same `FLOCK(path)` name. Each caller subsequently obtains its own semaphore, so two exclusive locks on the same file can both report success instead of excluding each other.

The `flock()` API documentation itself promises only one holder of an exclusive lock for a given file (`compiler/crt/posixc/flock.c:47-70`). **Affected configuration and trigger:** POSIXC on ExecSMP; two CPUs make the first `flock()` call for the same canonical path concurrently, and both searches complete before either insertion. **Confidence:** high for the unprotected lookup-plus-create interval, duplicate-name insertion, and separate subsequent lock objects; the race requires that interleaving. Use a cross-CPU lock around the complete find-or-create transaction or provide atomic named-semaphore creation. No file operation, lock or concurrent call was run; source-only.

<a id="ek589"></a>
### EK589 — POSIX `flock()` mutates its process-shared lock-record list without synchronization (conditional list corruption or lost cleanup records; high source confidence).

POSIXC maintains a single `file_locks` list shared across library opens so locks can be released during library cleanup (`compiler/crt/posixc/flock.c:256-303`; `__posixc_intbase.h:99-100`). After acquiring a file semaphore, `flock()` calls `AddToList()`; unlock calls `RemoveFromList()` (`flock.c:172-219`). `AddToList()` allocates a node and mutates the shared list with `AddHead()`, while `RemoveFromList()` traverses it with `ForeachNodeSafe()`, removes a matching node and frees it (`:225-254`). None of these accesses uses a semaphore or spinlock protecting `file_locks`; the per-file semaphore protects file-lock ownership, not this global bookkeeping list.

On ExecSMP, callers on separate CPUs can concurrently insert nodes or traverse/remove nodes. Interleaving `AddHead()` pointer updates can lose entries or corrupt the list; a removal can also invalidate a node another traversal has cached. Later unlock or expunge cleanup can then miss records, operate on stale list state, or fail to release recorded semaphores. This is separate from EK592, where allocation failure causes the already-acquired semaphore not to be recorded at all.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** POSIXC on ExecSMP with concurrent `flock()` lock/unlock operations from threads or processes, including operations on different files. **Confidence:** high for the shared list, unsynchronized pointer mutations and existence of concurrent public call paths; the precise corruption outcome depends on interleaving. Protect the entire shared list with a cross-CPU synchronization primitive. No concurrent file-lock operation or library cleanup was run; source-only.

<a id="ek590"></a>
### EK590 — POSIXC initialization dereferences a failed lock-list allocation (conditional library initialization fault; high source confidence).

The selected POSIXC `flock.c` library-init hook allocates the global `file_locks` list and immediately initializes it without checking allocation success (`compiler/crt/posixc/flock.c:262-269`). `NEWLIST()` writes the list head/tail fields through the supplied pointer (`compiler/include/exec/lists.h:85-104`), so if `AllocMem()` returns NULL during low-memory library initialization, the hook dereferences NULL instead of reporting initialization failure. The hook is selected through the POSIXC link-library source list and registered with `ADD2INITLIB(__init_flocks, 1)` (`compiler/crt/posixc/mmakefile.src:78`; `flock.c:302`).

**Affected configuration and trigger:** a client links/opens POSIXC while memory allocation fails for the small `MinList` object. Initialization can fault before the library is usable. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked allocation and immediate `NEWLIST()` writes; the trigger is allocation failure at that point. Check the allocation and return an initialization failure before list setup. No allocation failure or library initialization was induced; source-only.

<a id="ek591"></a>
### EK591 — Closing the last descriptor does not release its POSIX `flock()` lock (conditional permanent lock retention; high source confidence).

A successful `flock(fd, LOCK_SH/LOCK_EX)` stores the acquired semaphore in the global `file_locks` list, with each record containing only the semaphore pointer (`compiler/crt/posixc/flock.c:192-219,225-235`). The normal `close(fd)` implementation decrements the FCB reference count and, when it reaches zero, closes the DOS handle and frees the FCB; it does not call `flock(..., LOCK_UN)` or otherwise remove the corresponding semaphore (`compiler/crt/posixc/close.c:75-115`). The lock record has no FCB/descriptor association, and the flock implementation removes it only on explicit `LOCK_UN` or library expunge cleanup (`flock.c:172-185,276-303`).

Consequently, if a task closes the final descriptor while still running and omits `LOCK_UN`, the advisory semaphore remains owned; a different task trying to obtain an exclusive lock for the same path can block or fail nonblocking until the lock is explicitly released or cleanup occurs. Duplicated descriptors share the FCB, so the trigger is closing the last descriptor referencing it, not closing one duplicate while others remain (`__fdesc.h:15-30,57-66`; `close.c:75-115`). This describes the current source behavior; no claim is made about what the kernel does to semaphore ownership when the owning task later exits.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** clients using POSIXC `flock()`; a task acquires a lock, closes the last descriptor for that file without `LOCK_UN`, and remains alive while another task requests a conflicting lock. **Confidence:** high that close frees the FCB without releasing/removing the semaphore and that lock records are independent of descriptors; blocking impact follows the selected Exec semaphore calls. Associate lock cleanup with final shared-FCB close or explicitly release the held lock at that point. No descriptor close or competing lock was run; source-only.

<a id="ek592"></a>
### EK592 — `flock()` reports success when it cannot record the acquired semaphore for cleanup (conditional lost cleanup record; high source confidence).

After a blocking or nonblocking shared/exclusive semaphore acquisition succeeds, `flock()` calls `AddToList(sem)` but ignores its return value and returns success (`compiler/crt/posixc/flock.c:192-219`). `AddToList()` allocates a `FlockNode` and returns `-1` when `AllocMem()` fails; only a successful allocation adds the semaphore to the process-shared `file_locks` list (`flock.c:225-235`). Thus low memory at this point leaves the caller holding a successfully acquired lock with no record for `__unlock_flocks()` to release at library expunge (`flock.c:276-303`). A caller that later performs explicit `LOCK_UN` can still find and release the named semaphore; the defect is specifically the silently lost cleanup bookkeeping, not an inability to explicitly unlock. If the client does not explicitly unlock, the missing node prevents library-expunge cleanup from discovering the semaphore, potentially leaving it retained after the library's lock-record cleanup. This is distinct from EK589's concurrent list corruption, EK590's list-initialization allocation failure, and EK591's final-descriptor close path.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** POSIXC clients using `flock()` when `AllocMem(sizeof(struct FlockNode), ...)` fails immediately after a successful `LOCK_SH` or `LOCK_EX`; `flock()` nevertheless returns 0. **Confidence:** high for ignored allocation failure and missing expunge record; subsequent semaphore lifetime depends on whether the client explicitly unlocks and on later cleanup. Propagate the bookkeeping failure and release the just-acquired semaphore before returning an error. No allocation failure or lock operation was induced; source-only.

<a id="ek600"></a>
### EK600 — Failed per-task POSIXC `OpenLib` frees its duplicate base without unwinding completed open hooks (conditional descriptor/resource leak; high source confidence).

For `pertaskbase,rellinklib`, generated `OpenLib` creates and publishes a duplicate base, opens its relative libraries, then runs the `OPENLIB` symbol set with failure testing enabled. If any hook returns false, the failure branch restores the old per-task base, calls `__freebase(newlib)`, decrements the root library's open count, and returns NULL; it does not call the `CLOSELIB` symbol set or close the relative libraries (`tools/genmodule/writestart.c:1357-1399`). `set_call_libfuncs()` stops at the first failing hook and does not undo earlier successful hooks (`compiler/libinit/libinit.c:24-50`).

A concrete partial-state path is POSIXC's `__init_fd()` hook: when initializing a vfork/exec child descriptor table, `__copy_fdarray()` allocates entries and increments shared FCB `opencount` values one by one, then returns failure if a later slot or descriptor allocation fails (`compiler/crt/posixc/__fdesc.c:692-718,765-776`; hook registration at `:845-846`). The generated failure branch frees only the duplicate base storage, leaving those copied descriptors and reference increments without `__exit_fd()` cleanup. Other previously successful POSIXC hooks likewise receive no close callback, so their resources are also unreleased on a later hook failure. This is distinct from EK8934, which concerns failure while opening relative libraries before the OPENLIB hooks begin.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** task-local POSIXC bases generated with `pertaskbase,rellinklib`; an `OPENLIB` hook fails after earlier hooks have changed state. The descriptor-copy instance requires a vfork/exec-parent path and a later slot/descriptor allocation failure after at least one copied entry. **Confidence:** high for the missing rollback and partial descriptor-copy ownership increments; the trigger is conditional on hook failure. Run completed close hooks in reverse order and close opened relative libraries before freeing the duplicate base. No library open, descriptor copy, allocation failure, or vfork/exec operation was run; source-only.

<a id="ek603"></a>
### EK603 — pthread timed waits clear pending Ctrl-D/Ctrl-E signals when signal allocation fails (conditional signal loss; high source confidence).

The selected pthread wait paths use fixed break-signal bits when private signal allocation fails, and clear those bits before waiting without preserving the previous state. `OpenTimerDevice()` substitutes `SIGB_TIMER_FALLBACK` (`SIGBREAKB_CTRL_D`) after `AllocSignal(-1)` fails, then calls `SetSignal(SIGF_TIMER_FALLBACK, 0)` (`compiler/pthread/pthread.c:129-153`; `pthread_intern.h:79-80`). This helper is used by `_obtain_sema_timed()` and `_pthread_cond_timedwait()` (`pthread.c:267-271`; `pthread_cond_timedwait.c:61-64`), so a pending Ctrl-D can be consumed by timed mutex or timed condition waits. Separately, `_pthread_cond_timedwait()` tries to allocate its own waiter signal; on failure it substitutes `SIGB_COND_FALLBACK` (`SIGBREAKB_CTRL_E`) and clears it with `SetSignal(SIGF_COND_FALLBACK, 0)` (`pthread_cond_timedwait.c:124-132`; `pthread_intern.h:77-78`). Thus condition waits can also consume a pending Ctrl-E. Exec's `SetSignal(newSignals, signalMask)` clears the selected task bits when called with zero mask (`rom/exec/setsignal.c:22-83`). Neither fallback path checks or preserves the returned previous signal state. The timer fallback and condition fallback may both be reached by one timed condition wait under signal exhaustion. No separate condition-wakeup correctness defect is claimed: condition waits may return spuriously and callers must recheck their predicate.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** clients using the selected AROS pthread library when the task has no allocatable signal bits and has Ctrl-D pending on entry to a timed mutex/condition wait, or Ctrl-E pending on entry to a condition wait. **Confidence:** high for both fallback selections and unconditional clears; loss requires the stated signal state and allocation failure. Preserve pending task signals or use a fallback mechanism that does not consume caller-owned state. No signal exhaustion or pthread wait was induced; source-only.

<a id="ek604"></a>
### EK604 — Concurrent lazy initialization exposes a pthread condition variable before its waiter list is ready (conditional invalid-list access; high source confidence).

`PTHREAD_COND_INITIALIZER` sets the semaphore to `NULL_SEMAPHORE` and the waiter list to `NULL_MINLIST` (`compiler/pthread/pthread.h:345-347`). Both `_pthread_cond_timedwait()` and `_pthread_cond_broadcast()` detect an invalid semaphore and lazily call `pthread_cond_init()` (`pthread_cond_timedwait.c:42-46`; `pthread_cond_broadcast.c:34-38`). Initialization calls `InitSemaphore(&cond->semaphore)` first and only afterward initializes `cond->waiters` with `NEWLIST()` (`pthread_cond_init.c:36-55`). A first-use thread can therefore finish `InitSemaphore()` and be preempted before `NEWLIST()`. A concurrent wait/signal/broadcast sees a valid semaphore, skips initialization, and accesses the still-null waiter list: the wait path uses `AddTail()`, while signal/broadcast traverses it with `ForeachNode()` (`pthread_cond_timedwait.c:136-140`; `pthread_cond_broadcast.c:40-45`). These list operations expect initialized sentinels and may dereference invalid pointers. The issue is specifically concurrent lazy use of a statically initialized condition; concurrent explicit `pthread_cond_init()` is not needed for the trigger.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** clients using the selected pthread library where multiple tasks first use the same `PTHREAD_COND_INITIALIZER` object concurrently, with one task paused between semaphore initialization and waiter-list initialization. **Confidence:** high for the unsynchronized publication ordering and uninitialized-list access; the fault depends on the interleaving. Use an atomic once-state that publishes the object only after both members are initialized. No condition-variable operation or interleaving was run; source-only.

<a id="ek607"></a>
### EK607 — `sem_unlink()` destroys and frees a named semaphore still referenced by open handles or waiters (conditional use-after-free; high source confidence).

`sem_open()` returns the same named `sem_t *` to callers and maintains no open-reference count; `sem_close()` is a no-op (`compiler/pthread/semaphore.c:53-110`). `sem_unlink()` finds that object, calls `sem_destroy()`, removes it from the name list, and frees it immediately (`:117-151`). POSIX unlink semantics leave an already-open semaphore usable until its references are closed, but this implementation invalidates every previously returned pointer at unlink time.

The waiter case is especially unsafe: `sem_timedwait()` increments `waiters_count`, then waits on `count_nonzero` while the condition wait releases `sem->lock` (`semaphore.c:223-252`; `pthread_cond_timedwait.c:136-145`). During that wait, `sem_destroy()` can acquire the now-unlocked mutex, destroy it, and call `pthread_cond_destroy()`; it ignores the condition destroy result (`semaphore.c:165-185`). `pthread_cond_destroy()` returns `EBUSY` when its waiter list is nonempty, but `sem_destroy()` continues and reports success. `sem_unlink()` then frees the semaphore allocation while the waiter still holds pointers into it. When signaled or otherwise resumed, the waiter continues accessing the freed `sem_t`, including decrementing `waiters_count` and unlocking the destroyed mutex. Even without active waiters, any caller retaining a pointer from `sem_open()` can use freed storage after another caller unlinks the name.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** clients using the selected pthread named-semaphore implementation; one caller invokes `sem_unlink(name)` while another caller still holds the pointer returned by `sem_open()`, especially while a thread is blocked in `sem_wait()`/`sem_timedwait()`. **Confidence:** high for immediate free, absent handle refcounting, ignored `pthread_cond_destroy()` result, and retained pointers; exact waiter interleaving is conditional. Separate name removal from object destruction and defer freeing until the last `sem_close()`; reject destruction while waiters remain. No semaphore operation or concurrent unlink was run; source-only.

<a id="ek608"></a>
### EK608 — `pthread_join()` does not respond to deferred cancellation while waiting (conditional cancellation-point failure; high source confidence).

`pthread_join()` calls `pthread_testcancel()` once before registering itself as the target's waiter, then waits in a loop using only `Wait(SIGF_PARENT)` while the target is unfinished; after the wait it reads the return value and clears the thread slot without testing cancellation again (`compiler/pthread/pthread_join.c:34-58`). Deferred `pthread_cancel()` marks the target joiner canceled and sends `SIGBREAKF_CTRL_C` (`pthread_cancel.c:26-50`), but that bit is not in the join wait mask. Exec `Wait()` only waits for one of the requested signal bits (`rom/exec/wait.c:48-104`), so cancellation alone cannot release a blocked join. If the joined worker later exits, its completion path signals the joiner's `SIGF_PARENT` (`pthread_create.c:208`), releasing the wait, but `pthread_join()` then returns success without calling `pthread_testcancel()`; the deferred cancellation remains unacted upon. Thus a joiner may remain blocked after cancellation while the worker is still running, or return normally after the worker exits instead of acting on the pending cancellation. This is distinct from cancellation behavior in condition/timed waits.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** selected AROS pthread library with deferred cancellation enabled; a thread is blocked in `pthread_join()` when another thread calls `pthread_cancel()` on it. **Confidence:** high for the signal-mask mismatch and absence of a post-wait test; observed outcome depends on whether/when the joined worker exits. Include the cancellation signal in an interruptible wait and run cancellation cleanup before completing the join. No join/cancel interleaving was run; source-only.

<a id="ek609"></a>
### EK609 — A failed concurrent `pthread_create()` can overwrite or falsely publish a reused thread slot (conditional slot corruption; high source confidence).

`pthread_create()` selects an empty slot and initializes its `ThreadInfo` while holding `thread_sem`, but calls `ReleaseSemaphore(&thread_sem)` immediately after `CreateNewProcTags()` returns and only then checks `inf->task` (`compiler/pthread/pthread_create.c:234-286`). On task-creation failure, `inf->task` remains NULL and the slot still satisfies `GetThreadId(NULL)`'s empty-slot test (`pthread.c:80-96`). The failing caller sets `inf->parent = NULL` outside the semaphore.

A second concurrent creator can therefore reuse and populate that same slot during the gap. If it has not yet returned from `CreateNewProcTags()` when the first caller executes its failed-path store, the first caller clears the second creator's newly written `parent`; the second creator may still publish a task and return success, but later `GetThreadInfo()`/join/cancel paths treat the slot as nonexistent. If the second creator has already stored its task pointer, the first caller instead sees non-NULL `inf->task`, assumes its own creation succeeded, signals the second creator's worker, and returns success with the reused thread ID. The worker's `StarterFunc()` waits on `SIGF_SINGLE`, so this signal releases the second creator's worker; it does not restore the first call's start routine or argument, which were overwritten when the slot was reused (`pthread_create.c:119-146,255-286`).

**Affected configuration and trigger:** selected AROS pthread library; one `CreateNewProcTags()` call fails while another `pthread_create()` concurrently claims the newly empty slot before the failed caller processes the result. **Confidence:** high for the unlocked failure cleanup, slot predicate, and both data-flow outcomes; occurrence depends on allocation failure plus scheduling interleaving. Keep the slot reserved until failure cleanup completes, or perform failure-state publication under `thread_sem` with generation-safe ownership. No process creation failure or concurrent create was induced; source-only.

<a id="ek613"></a>
### EK613 — OpenSBI Zicbom maintenance skips cache blocks when the CPU block size is below 64 bytes (conditional DMA coherency failure; high source confidence).

Both `cbo_clean_range()` and `cbo_flush_range()` round the start down to a 64-byte boundary and advance by `CBO_BLOCK`, fixed at 64 (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/exec/cpu_init.c:77-101`). The selected CPU feature check only searches the flattened device tree for the `zicbom` string and does not read its `riscv,cbom-block-size` property (`cpu_init.c:152-193`); when the substring is found, it installs these routines as Exec's `CachePreDMA` and `CachePostDMA` vectors (`:210-218`). RISC-V CMO block size is implementation-specific; with 32-byte blocks, each instruction affects only the addressed 32-byte block, while the 64-byte loop stride skips every other block. The affected interval is passed through the clean path for `DMA_ReadFromRAM`, the flush path for device reads, and the post-DMA flush path for device writes (`:104-143`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an OpenSBI RISC-V64 CPU advertises Zicbom but has a cache-maintenance block size smaller than 64 bytes, and a non-coherent DMA client requests maintenance over a span covering the skipped blocks. The helpers leave alternating blocks unmaintained; dirty CPU data can then be absent from device reads, or device-written data can remain hidden by stale CPU cache lines. The repository review did not establish a checked-in non-coherent device configuration that triggers this consequence: the selected in-tree DMA clients use these hooks, but the reviewed PCIDT contract describes its bus-master controllers as cache coherent. The finding therefore remains conditional at the Exec cache-vector/API boundary and does not claim a default in-tree DMA failure.

**Affected configuration:** OpenSBI `riscv64` builds with Zicbom enabled and a sub-64-byte `riscv,cbom-block-size`, combined with a non-coherent DMA client. Derive the stride from the reported block size or provide a supported block-size-specific implementation. **Confidence:** high that the fixed 64-byte arithmetic skips blocks on a smaller-block implementation; actual coherency impact requires such hardware plus a non-coherent DMA consumer, neither established for a checked-in configuration. No firmware, DMA request, cache operation or build was run; source-only. See the [Zicbom block-size and selected-client review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7960).

<a id="ek626"></a>
### EK626 — CloseAsync reports success when the underlying DOS Close fails (conditional lost close status; high source confidence).

`CloseAsync()` stores the result from `AS_WaitPacket()` and may replace it with the result of its final buffered `Write()`, but when `af_CloseFH` is set it calls DOS `Close()` without assigning or checking that return value; it then frees the `AsyncFile` and returns the earlier result (`workbench/libs/asyncio/src/CloseAsync.c:39-71`). The public AsyncIO documentation promises a negative result when closing fails and directs callers to `IoErr()` for more information (`workbench/libs/asyncio/asyncio.doc:20-40`). DOS `Close()` returns the `ACTION_END` packet result, but frees its DOS filehandle regardless of that result (`rom/dos/close.c:68-79`). Several checked-in handlers can reject `ACTION_END`: RAM `CmdEnd()` returns `ERROR_DISK_WRITE_PROTECTED` for a changed file closed while the volume is locked and leaves its `Opening` and lock allocated (`rom/filesys/ram/commands.c:510-545`; dispatch at `rom/filesys/ram/handler.c:169-173`); FAT returns the `TestLock()` error before freeing the lock (`rom/filesys/fat/packet.c:375-392`, `rom/filesys/fat/lock.c:55-70`); PFS3 can return false when its close-time `CheckVolume()` fails, before removing the file entry (`rom/filesys/pfs3/fs/dd_funcs.c:767-789`); and CDVDFS rejects a handle whose volume no longer matches (`rom/filesys/CDVDFS/src/device.c:701-722`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an AsyncIO caller closes a write-mode file with `af_CloseFH` set after the pending packet/final write succeeds, but the DOS handler rejects `Close()` (for example, the RAM handler sees a changed file and a write-protected volume). `CloseAsync()` discards the failed close result and returns the prior nonnegative wait/write result, falsely reporting success and hiding the close failure from its caller; this review does not establish what `IoErr()` contains on the caller task. The RAM handler's rejected `ACTION_END` also retains its private opening/lock even though DOS `Close()` frees the public filehandle; that backend cleanup effect is specific to this demonstrated RAM-handler path. The finding does not claim that every handler rejects close or that every AsyncIO caller observes the status.

**Affected configuration:** the AsyncIO library's `CloseAsync()` entry and callers that use it to close the DOS handle (`workbench/libs/asyncio/src/mmakefile.src:1-7`; `asyncio.conf:16`). RAM, FAT, PFS3 and CDVDFS source paths establish conditional reject-close cases; other handler behavior still depends on its `ACTION_END` contract. The maintained direct C callers are AHIRecord (`workbench/tools/AHIRecord/AHIRecord.c:3055,3086`) and `testasync.c:27`; those callers ignore `CloseAsync()` and do not establish a user-visible reaction. **Confidence:** high that `CloseAsync()` discards the DOS close result and violates its documented result contract; the triggering close failure is conditional on the handler. No file, volume, write-protection state, close failure or build was exercised; source-only. See the [CloseAsync caller and handler-contract review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L2418).

<a id="ek629"></a>
### EK629 — ExecSMP interrupt-server traversal can race removal and free of an active server node on PC VBlank and Raspberry Pi AArch64 SMP (conditional list use-after-free; high source confidence).

The generic `IntServer()` walks `intList` with `ForeachNode()` and invokes each node's callback without acquiring `IntrList` read protection; the loop reads the current node's `ln_Succ` after the callback returns (`rom/exec/intservers.c:29-45`; `compiler/include/exec/lists.h:195-200`). `AddIntServer()` and `RemIntServer()` take `IntrList`'s write lock and disable interrupts only on the calling CPU while changing the list (`rom/exec/addintserver.c:64-75`; `rom/exec/remintserver.c:53-63`; `rom/exec/exec_locks.h:32-68`). Those writer operations do not exclude an already running VBlank walk on another CPU.

The race is reachable through selected SMP VBlank routes. On PC, the packaged all-PC timer enables `USE_VBLANK_EMU`; its IRQ0 `TimerInt()` processes the MICROHZ queue, and expiry of the permanent VBlank request calls the `INTB_VERTB` vector, which chains through `VBlankServer()` into `IntServer()` (`arch/all-pc/timer/make.opts:1-2`; `arch/all-pc/timer/timer_init.c:34-56,163-167`; `rom/timer/lowlevel.c:284-305`; `arch/all-pc/exec/intserver_vblank.c:20-72`). The PC board-support packages include this timer, and their `smp` target defines `__AROSEXEC_SMP__` (`arch/i386-pc/boot/mmakefile.src:70-78`; `arch/x86_64-pc/boot/mmakefile.src:64-75`; `configure.in:1669-1670,2197-2199`). On Raspberry Pi AArch64 SMP, BCM2711 routes VBlank dispatch to CPU 0 while other CPUs can continue running tasks (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/platform_bcm2711.c:184-194`); its Exec uses the generic VBlank wrapper (`arch/aarch64-native/exec/mmakefile.src:20-27`; `rom/exec/mmakefile.src:39`).

**Trigger and consequence:** while CPU0 is walking the VBlank server list, another CPU removes a server and its owner frees the containing object before the walk has finished. `realtime.library` is a selected concrete owner: its VBlank node is embedded in the library base; expunge calls `RemIntServer()` and then returns, and generated expunge frees the base without waiting for an in-flight VBlank callback (`workbench/libs/realtime/realtime_timer.c:65-83`; `realtime_init.c:52-61`; `tools/genmodule/writestart.c:1558-1587`). If the callback is active, `rtVBlank()` dereferences its base to signal the Pulse task; if it has returned but the walker has not advanced, `ForeachNode()` reads `ln_Succ` from the freed node. Either interleaving can access freed memory during interrupt traversal. This is distinct from EK9051's Pulse worker continuing to use the base after its stop signal.

**Affected configuration:** ExecSMP builds using PC VBlank emulation or Raspberry Pi BCM2711 VBlank routing, with concurrent removal/free of a VBlank server; realtime.library supplies a selected concrete owner path. **Confidence:** high that the reader is unprotected, writers do not synchronize with that reader, and the selected owner can free its embedded node after removal; exact overlap is conditional. Other architecture VBlank delivery paths and owner lifetimes remain open. No IRQ, callback, library expunge or concurrent interleaving was run; source-only. See the [interrupt-server traversal and teardown review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8227).

<a id="ek647"></a>
### EK647 — Efika publishes a partial OpenFirmware tree, then treats the missing-node list sentinel as a real device.

`ofw_get_properties()` can return `-1` when a property allocation fails, and `ofw_build_tree()` can return `-1` when a child allocation fails; the parent ignores the property result and `ofw_scan_tree()` ignores the recursive builder result, returning the root with whatever nodes were built (`arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/of1275.c:568-600,603-673`). The selected bootstrap publishes that root in `KRN_OpenFirmwareTree` without checking whether construction completed (`arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/bootstrap.c:201-209`). Efika kernel startup copies the tree and searches its children for `builtin`, then the node's properties for `reg` (`arch/ppc-chrp/efika/kernel/kernel_init.c:234-238,302-328`). Both searches use `ForeachNode()` and then test the loop variable as a Boolean; the list macro leaves it pointing at the non-NULL tail sentinel on a no-match exit (`compiler/include/exec/lists.h:195-200`). The code therefore enters the matched-node/property path with a list sentinel interpreted as an `OFWNode` or `OFWProperty`.

**Trigger and consequence:** the Efika OpenFirmware tree is incomplete and omits the expected direct `builtin` node or its `reg` property; a child/property allocation failure during tree construction provides a checked-in source path to a partial tree. The no-match loop leaves a non-NULL sentinel, which startup treats as a real node/property and reads fields at the wrong layout offsets. It can traverse invalid list pointers or use an invalid MBAR value for interrupt-controller setup and MMU mapping. This is conditional on the missing entry and does not claim that ordinary firmware omits it.

**Affected configuration:** the explicit CHRP PPC Efika OpenFirmware bootstrap/kernel package; its aggregate build and boot ISO edges are commented in `arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/mmakefile.src:4-17`, so default-image inclusion is not claimed. **Confidence:** high for ignored tree-build errors, sentinel truthiness and unchecked field use; manifestation requires an incomplete tree. Propagate tree-build failures and compare list iterators to the list tail/successfully matched node before dereferencing. No firmware response, allocation failure or boot was induced; source-only. See the [Efika OpenFirmware tree and consumer review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8229).

<a id="ek648"></a>
### EK648 — Efika uses an unchecked OpenFirmware `reg` read as the MBAR address.

`ofw_get_properties()` obtains the property length, allocates storage for that declared length, records it in `op_length`, calls `ofw_get_prop()`, and ignores the returned byte count/status (`arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/of1275.c:568-600`). `ofw_get_prop()` returns the firmware's signed result (`:147-170`). After locating the `builtin` node and `reg` property, Efika startup neither checks `op_length` nor validates the copied result before reading the first 32-bit word as `MBAR` (`arch/ppc-chrp/efika/kernel/kernel_init.c:306-328`). It then passes that value to interrupt-controller initialization and uses it for the MBAR MMU mapping (`:334-340`).

**Trigger and consequence:** firmware reports a `reg` property length but its subsequent `getprop` call fails or returns fewer bytes, or supplies a `reg` value shorter than four bytes. The tree retains the declared length and partially filled/uninitialized property storage; startup still reads a 32-bit MBAR from it. The resulting peripheral base can be invalid, causing later interrupt-controller/MMIO setup to fail or use the wrong address. No conforming firmware response or checked-in firmware image demonstrating this short/failing result was established.

**Affected configuration:** the explicit CHRP PPC Efika OpenFirmware bootstrap/kernel package; aggregate build and boot ISO edges are commented (`arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/mmakefile.src:4-17`). **Confidence:** high that the property-read status, returned length and stored extent are not validated before the 32-bit read; actual trigger depends on firmware returning inconsistent/short data. Require a successful read of at least four bytes before publishing/consuming the property. No firmware service, boot, MMIO operation or build was run; source-only. See the [Efika OpenFirmware tree and consumer review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8229).

<a id="ek649"></a>
### EK649 — A missing OpenFirmware child-name property publishes a null name that boot code dereferences.

When a child node's `name` property length is zero or the length query fails, `ofw_build_tree()` sets `child->on_name` to NULL and still links the node into the tree (`arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/of1275.c:621-645`). The selected bootstrap walks top-level children and passes each name to its local `strcasecmp()` while looking for `rtas`; that implementation dereferences both string pointers without a NULL check (`bootstrap.c:362-385`; `support.c:61-65`). If the unnamed node is nested or appears after an RTAS node that terminates this walk, the Efika kernel's recursive `krnCopyOFWTree()` still calls `strlen(orig->on_name)` (`arch/ppc-chrp/efika/kernel/kernel_init.c:440-474`).

**Trigger and consequence:** OpenFirmware exposes a child whose `name` property is absent, has length zero, or returns an error. The bootstrap may dereference NULL in `strcasecmp()` before kernel handoff; a nested or later node can instead reach the kernel copier and fault in `strlen()`. This prevents startup from completing for that tree. The report does not claim that conforming Efika firmware omits the required node name.

**Affected configuration:** the explicitly buildable CHRP PPC Efika OpenFirmware bootstrap/kernel path; its aggregate build and boot ISO edges are commented in `arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/mmakefile.src:4-17`, so default-image inclusion is not claimed. **Confidence:** high that nonpositive name length publishes NULL and both selected consumers dereference it; trigger depends on firmware returning a missing/invalid name property. Reject or skip unnamed child nodes before linking them, and validate names at both consumers. No firmware response or boot was run; source-only. See the [Efika OpenFirmware property/tree review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8229).

<a id="ek650"></a>
### EK650 — OpenFirmware cleanup forwards an uninitialized RTAS size on selected bootstrap failure paths.

`bootstrap()` declares `rtas_size` as an uninitialized local (`arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/bootstrap.c:97-102`). A kickstart/module load failure reaches cleanup at `:298-306` before the later `/rtas` lookup and `rtas-size` read at `:323-326`, but cleanup passes `rtas_size` to both `ofw_release(rtas_base, rtas_size)` and `ofw_release(0x07000000, 0x01000000 - rtas_size)` (`:302-304`). `ofw_release()` forwards the supplied address and size directly to the OpenFirmware `release` service (`arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/of1275.c:459-475`). The later final-return cleanup also uses `rtas_size` when no `/rtas` node is found, or when its size query fails, because the query result is ignored (`bootstrap.c:323-326,419-422`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a selected Efika bootstrap load fails before RTAS discovery, or the tree lacks `/rtas` / its `rtas-size` read fails, and execution reaches one of these cleanup blocks. The firmware release calls receive an indeterminate size; the complement calculation can also produce an incorrect range. Cleanup may therefore fail or release a range different from the allocation actually made. The exact firmware response to those parameters is not established.

**Affected configuration:** the explicit CHRP PPC Efika OpenFirmware bootstrap target. **Confidence:** high that the local is read before initialization on the early load-failure path and that the value is forwarded unvalidated; cleanup consequences depend on firmware `release` behavior. Initialize the size, track the actual RTAS allocation extent, and release only ranges that were successfully claimed. No load failure, firmware release or boot was induced; source-only. See the [Efika OpenFirmware bootstrap cleanup review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8229).

<a id="ek651"></a>
### EK651 — A failed OpenFirmware property-length query becomes a huge copy length in Efika startup.

`ofw_get_prop_len()` initializes its signed result to `-1` and returns that value when the firmware service does not replace it (`arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/of1275.c:123-145`). For each property name returned by `nextprop`, `ofw_get_properties()` uses that signed length in the allocation expression without checking for failure, stores it in the unsigned `op_length`, and passes it to `ofw_get_prop()` whose buffer-size parameter is `uint32_t` (`:568-600,147-170`). On the Efika's 32-bit target, `-1` therefore becomes `UINT32_MAX` at both unsigned interfaces, while the allocation arithmetic reserves one byte less than the header/name-only size. The property-name copy itself uses the full `name_len`, and the subsequent value pointer is passed to firmware with the huge capacity. No checked-in firmware trace demonstrates an enumerated property for which `getproplen` fails and the following `getprop` nevertheless returns data.

**Trigger and consequence:** OpenFirmware enumerates a property with `nextprop`, but its following `getproplen` call returns `-1` and `getprop` then succeeds or writes data. The copier has reserved no valid value extent and advertises a capacity of 4,294,967,295 bytes; the name copy is also one byte beyond the undersized claim. A firmware write of the property value can overrun the allocated record, corrupting the in-memory tree later consumed by bootstrap/kernel startup. If `getprop` also fails without writing, the large capacity alone does not establish a write; this finding is limited to inconsistent service results.

**Affected configuration:** the explicit CHRP PPC Efika OpenFirmware bootstrap/tree builder; the aggregate build and boot ISO edges are commented in `arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/mmakefile.src:4-17`. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked signed-to-unsigned conversion and undersized allocation arithmetic; memory corruption requires an enumerated property plus inconsistent `getproplen`/`getprop` results. Reject negative lengths and validate allocation/read sizes before publishing the property. No firmware service, property copy or boot was run; source-only. See the [Efika OpenFirmware property/tree review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8229).

<a id="ek653"></a>
### EK653 — A trailing `--root` boot argument makes the OpenFirmware bootstrap scan past the end of the string.

The bootstrap obtains `/chosen/bootargs` as a length-terminated string (`arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/bootstrap.c:211-214`; `of1275.c:677-685`). When it sees `--root`, it skips spaces after the option, sets `bootargs` to one byte after the beginning of the root value, and scans until the local `isspace()` reports a delimiter (`bootstrap.c:223-242`). This bootstrap-local `isspace()` recognizes only the six whitespace characters and returns false for NUL (`support.c:31-34`).

**Trigger and consequence:** `/chosen/bootargs` ends with a `--root` value that has no trailing whitespace, or the option has no value after its spaces. The scan starts within or just beyond the terminator, treats NUL as a non-space byte, and continues reading beyond the allocated string until it happens to encounter whitespace. It then writes a NUL at that out-of-bounds location. The boot may fault or corrupt adjacent bootstrap data before handoff. A trailing delimiter after a nonempty value stops the scan normally; this finding is limited to the unterminated final-token case.

**Affected configuration:** the OpenFirmware CHRP PPC bootstrap, explicitly buildable through `ub2lb-chrp-ppc-efika` (`arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/mmakefile.src:14-21`); the Efika aggregate/boot ISO edges are commented in `arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/mmakefile.src:4-17`, and no default-image inclusion is claimed. **Confidence:** high that the custom whitespace predicate does not stop at NUL and the parser scans/writes beyond the allocated string under the stated input. Bound the token scan by the string terminator and reject a missing root value. No bootargs string or boot was exercised; source-only. See the [OpenFirmware `--root` parser review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8230).

<a id="ek679"></a>
### EK679 — `C:Mount` scans an uninitialized error buffer when `VSNPrintf()` cannot allocate scratch space (conditional invalid read; high source confidence).

`ShowFault()` declares an uninitialized stack buffer, calls `VSNPrintf(buf, ...)`, then immediately passes `buf` to `strlen()` without checking whether formatting wrote anything (`workbench/c/Mount.c:1979-1990`). The selected `VSNPrintf()` implementation first computes the required size, then allocates a temporary buffer; if `AllocMem()` fails, it skips formatting/copying but still returns the required size, leaving the caller's buffer untouched (`rom/utility/vsnprintf.c:66-80`). `ShowFault()` therefore scans indeterminate stack bytes for a NUL. It can read beyond the local buffer if no terminator occurs in its bounds, and subsequent formatting uses the resulting invalid length. The selected `Mount` source has five direct call sites (`Mount.c:430,439,503,535,1128`), covering directory-name/AddPart failures, CLI startup errors, and invalid mountfile parsing; each enters the same reporter. This is conditional on low memory during the utility formatter's temporary allocation, not merely on a Mount operation failing.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** builds that include `workbench/c/Mount.c`; one of its five `ShowFault()` paths is reached while `VSNPrintf()`'s scratch allocation fails. **Confidence:** high that the failure path leaves `buf` untouched and `strlen()` reads it; exact out-of-bounds extent depends on stack contents. Initialize the destination before formatting and check the formatting result or change `VSNPrintf()` to guarantee termination on allocation failure. No allocation failure or Mount operation was induced; source-only.

<a id="ek683"></a>
### EK683 — `C:Mount` can spin forever when a source file reaches EOF before its measured size is read (conditional no-progress loop; high source confidence).

`readfile()` seeks to end and records the file size, seeks back to the beginning, allocates for that size, then loops while `rest` is nonzero (`workbench/c/Mount.c:1228-1277`). Each iteration calls DOS `Read()` with `rest` bytes; it breaks only on `-1`, otherwise subtracts the returned count and advances the buffer pointer. DOS documents `Read()` returning zero at EOF (`rom/dos/read.c:24-45`). If the file is truncated after the initial size query and a later `Read()` reaches EOF before `rest` reaches zero, `sub` remains zero, so neither `rest` nor `buf` changes and the loop repeats forever. The error cleanup and `Close()` are after the loop, so they are never reached. Both `readmountlist()` and `readmountfile()` call this shared helper before parsing their respective mount sources (`Mount.c:1013-1018,1115-1120`); a file changed by another task between sizing and reading can therefore hang the Mount operation.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** builds including `workbench/c/Mount.c`; a mountlist or mountfile is truncated after `Seek(OFFSET_END)` reports a positive size and before the helper reads that many bytes. **Confidence:** high for the no-progress loop on zero-byte `Read()` and its documented EOF return; concurrent truncation timing is conditional. Treat zero as premature EOF/error and break through the existing cleanup path. No file was modified or read through Mount; source-only.

<a id="ek684"></a>
### EK684 — `C:Mount` double-frees the handler string and leaks its node when DOS rejects an entry (conditional cleanup fault; high source confidence).

`mount()` builds a `DeviceNode` with `MyMakeDosNode()`, then for the load-handler path stores the global `HandlerString` pointer in `dn_Handler` (`workbench/c/Mount.c:1846-1880`). If `AddDosEntry()` rejects the node, the failure branch frees `HandlerString` but does not set the global to NULL and does not free `dn` (`Mount.c:1891-1921`). The normal callers subsequently invoke `FreeStuff()`, which frees any non-NULL global `HandlerString` and clears it (`Mount.c:680-702`; `readmountlist()`/`readmountfile()` cleanup at `:1013-1046,1115-1218`). This frees the same allocation a second time. The unregistered node is also abandoned: `MyMakeDosNode()` separately allocates the `DeviceNode`, its name/handler string block, and, for device-style entries, `FileSysStartupMsg` and `DosEnvec`, returning the owning node only after all construction succeeds (`Mount.c:1463-1599`). The AddDosEntry failure branch releases none of that node-owned storage. DOS `AddDosEntry()` can reject a non-volume entry when an existing device/handler has the same name (`rom/dos/adddosentry.c:85-115`), so this is reachable on duplicate-name input; the DOS routine itself leaves rejected nodes with the caller.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** builds including `workbench/c/Mount.c`; a load-handler entry is constructed with non-NULL `HandlerString` and `AddDosEntry()` fails, such as for an existing same-name non-volume node. **Confidence:** high for the duplicate free and unreleased node allocations on this path; occurrence depends on the rejection condition and subsequent caller cleanup. Clear `HandlerString` when freeing it and dispose the complete unregistered node on AddDosEntry failure. No duplicate mount or allocation cleanup was exercised; source-only.

<a id="ek8957"></a>
### EK8957 — Concurrent `C:Mount` shutdown requests can strand the second synchronous packet (conditional hang; high source confidence).

`ShutdownDevice()` reads `dn_Task` while holding the DOS-list read lock, releases the lock, then sends a synchronous `DoPkt(port, ACTION_DIE, ...)` (`workbench/c/Mount.c:561-590`). Two Mount tasks can therefore both snapshot the same running handler port before either sends or completes its shutdown packet. In the selected console handler, `ACTION_DIE` replies success when `usecount` is zero, sets the current packet pointer to NULL, and immediately jumps out of the packet loop (`rom/filesys/console_handler/con_handler.c:1202-1211`). If both callers have queued packets before the first is handled, the handler replies only to the first and exits without receiving or replying to the second; that caller remains blocked in `DoPkt()` waiting for its packet (`rom/dos/dopkt.c:119-141`). If the first handler receives ACTION_DIE while `usecount` is positive, it replies `ERROR_OBJECT_IN_USE` and continues, so the stranded-packet outcome requires a successful shutdown request.

The selected default `DOSDrivers/AUX` is generated to use `aux-handler`; `workbench-fs-aux` is a dependency of the complete filesystem target, and the AUX handler hands the stream to the console handler (`workbench/devs/mmakefile.src:63-83`; `workbench/fs/aux_handler/mmakefile.src:4-15`; coverage-traced handoff). The report is scoped to this selected console-handler shutdown behavior, not every third-party handler that may implement ACTION_DIE differently. On handler exit, the console handler clears `dn_Task` only later under the DOS-list write lock, after the successful packet reply, leaving the window for the concurrent snapshot/queue sequence (`con_handler.c:1229-1245`).

**Affected configuration and trigger:** `C:Mount` REMOVE processing on builds with the generated default AUX/console-handler path; two callers target the same device while its handler has no open handles, and both synchronous packets reach its message port before the first shutdown is serviced. **Confidence:** high for the port snapshot, reply-then-exit path and synchronous reply wait; the overlap/queue timing is conditional. Serialize shutdown per device or reject/complete queued shutdown requests before exiting. No mount command, packet, or task interleaving was run; source-only.

<a id="ek8925"></a>
### EK8925 — FileSystem.resource duplicate checks and insertions race across ExecSMP CPUs (conditional duplicate/corrupt registrations; high source confidence).

The partition library's `AddFS()` checks for an existing DOS type/version under `Forbid()`, loads the filesystem outside that section, then repeats the lookup and inserts the new `FileSysEntry` with `AddHead()` under another `Forbid()` section (`rom/partition/fsloader.c:35-111`). The repeated lookup is intended to suppress duplicate loads, but Exec documents that `Forbid()` only prevents task switches on the local processor on ExecSMP; it does not serialize another CPU (`rom/exec/forbid.c:42-64`). Two CPUs can therefore both observe no matching node in the second check and concurrently insert same-type entries, or interleave the list pointer updates and corrupt the shared resource list.

A selected in-tree producer has the same issue: PFS3 handler initialization calls `AddToFSResource()` for its DOS type (`rom/filesys/pfs3/fs/init.c:305-311`; selected `kernel-fs-pfs3` module in `rom/filesys/pfs3/fs/mmakefile.src:78-83`). The function scans for the DOS type and adds an entry while protected only by `Forbid()` (`rom/filesys/pfs3/fs/fsresource.c:26-72`). Concurrent PFS3 initializations for the same type, or overlap with partition `AddFS()`, can therefore publish duplicates or corrupt the list on ExecSMP. The checked-in direct `AddBootFileSystem()` caller found in DOSBoot is a sequential boot scan (`rom/dosboot/bootscan.c:242`); no concurrent direct caller was established, so the general AddFS API race remains conditional on external or concurrent callers. The PFS3 initialization path is the maintained in-tree producer. `AddBootFileSystem()` releases its own `bootSem` before calling `AddFS()` (`rom/partition/addbootfilesystem.c:56-64`), so that semaphore does not provide cross-producer serialization.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** ExecSMP builds using PFS3 with concurrent initialization for the same DOS type, or any concurrent `AddFS()` producers that pass the same type/version checks; also applies to PFS3/partition cross-producer overlap. **Confidence:** high that the shared list scan/insertion is not cross-CPU protected and can admit duplicates; pointer corruption depends on concurrent update interleaving. Protect lookup plus insertion with a shared cross-CPU lock. No registration, handler initialization, build, or interleaving was run; source-only.

<a id="ek8921"></a>
### EK8921 — `C:Mount` leaks a constructed `DeviceNode` when no handler or filesystem entry matches (conditional allocation leak; high source confidence).

For filesystem entries with no explicit handler, `mount()` calls `PatchDosNode()`, which asks `GetFileSysEntry()` for a matching DOS type and leaves the node unchanged when no entry is found (`workbench/c/Mount.c:1379-1449,1859-1863`). The constructed node has initially cleared `dn_SegList` and `dn_Handler` fields (`Mount.c:1463-1514`). The later branch assigns `dn_Handler` from `HandlerString`, but when that global is NULL and no filesystem entry supplied a segment list, both fields remain zero. The `if (dn->dn_SegList || dn->dn_Handler)` guard then skips `AddDosEntry()` and returns `ERROR_OBJECT_NOT_FOUND` without freeing `dn` or its owned allocations (`Mount.c:1865-1928`). `MyMakeDosNode()` allocated the DeviceNode and its string block, and for device-style entries also allocates startup-message and environment objects (`:1463-1599`). Both `readmountlist()` and `readmountfile()` call `FreeStuff()` after `mount()` returns, but that helper frees only the global parsed strings; it does not know about the local `dn` (`:680-702,1013-1046,1115-1218`). Each such failed mount attempt therefore leaks the constructed node and its separately allocated storage. This is separate from EK684, where a populated handler node reaches `AddDosEntry()` and the insertion failure branch mishandles ownership.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** builds including `workbench/c/Mount.c`; a filesystem mount with no explicit handler and no matching FileSystem.resource entry for its DOS type. **Confidence:** high for the no-match state, skipped insertion, and missing node cleanup; trigger depends on the filesystem not being registered. Dispose the unregistered node and all owned fields before returning the error. No mount or resource lookup was run; source-only.

<a id="ek672"></a>
### EK672 — MinGW host timer delivery coalesces elapsed periods while AROS interrupts are disabled (conditional time/VBlank undercount; high source confidence).

The host creates the two system waitable timers as auto-reset objects (`arch/all-mingw32/kernel/host_intr.c:286-296`) and `TaskSwitcher()` waits for their signals. Each delivered signal stores only `1` in `PendingInts[obj]`; if AROS interrupts are disabled or the host context is unsafe, the switcher resumes the main thread without dispatching/clearing pending IRQs. Further expirations of the same timer overwrite the same byte with `1`, not an elapsed count. Once delivery is safe, the IRQ vector runs once for that pending bit and the array is cleared (`host_intr.c:147-190`). `KrnCli()` sets the shared interrupt state disabled and `KrnSti()` reenables it outside supervisor mode (`arch/all-mingw32/kernel/cli.c:9-16`; `sti.c:9-22`).

Timer 1's selected callback advances current and elapsed EClock values by exactly one configured interval and increments the tick count once (`arch/all-mingw32/timer/timer_init.c:36-43`); lost timer-1 expirations therefore make those software time counters lag elapsed host time and delay timer.device clients that depend on them. Timer 0 is the kernel VBlank source: after the pending byte is dispatched, `kernel_intr.c` calls `core_Cause(INTB_VERTB, ...)` only once (`arch/all-mingw32/kernel/kernel_intr.c:88-94`), and Graphics.library increments its VBlank counter per dispatched VBlank (`rom/graphics/graphics_init.c:160-202`). Thus a long masked interval can undercount VBlank events as well. One VBlank waiter still receives a wake when the pending IRQ is dispatched; no extra post-resumption stall is claimed. This is distinct from EK674's separate integer period conversion in `StartClock()`.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** Windows-hosted MinGW32 AROS; AROS interrupt delivery is disabled or deferred across multiple expirations of timer 0 or timer 1. **Confidence:** high that repeated host events are represented by a Boolean slot and each resumed dispatch accounts one interval/event; actual lost count depends on the masked duration and host timer delivery. Preserve elapsed expiration counts or derive timer ticks from monotonic elapsed time. No Windows host, timer, masked interval or graphics VBlank was run; source-only.

<a id="ek715"></a>
### EK715 — i386 alert formatting can overrun its stack padding array on long instructions (conditional stack corruption; high source confidence).

When disassembly is enabled, `FormatAlertExtra()` allocates `insPad[(__WORDSIZE/2)+1]`, computes the hex string length as an unsigned `ULONG`, then loops while `x < ((__WORDSIZE/2) - inslen)` and writes spaces to `insPad[x]` (`rom/exec/alertextra.c:57-73,103-137`). On i386, `__WORDSIZE` is 32, so the array has 17 bytes and the target hex width is 16 characters. The selected i386 debug initializer enables `DBFF_DISASSEMBLE` (`arch/i386-all/debug/debug_platform.c:54-59`), and its platform backend uses udis86 (`arch/i386-all/debug/disassemble.c:121-154`; `arch/i386-all/debug/make.opts`). udis86's decoder permits 15-byte instructions (`arch/all-pc/udis86/libudis86/decode.h:33`), and `ud_insn_hex()` emits two characters per instruction byte (`udis86.c:162-181`), so a valid instruction longer than eight bytes yields a string longer than 16 characters. Subtracting that length from the unsigned width wraps to a huge value; the loop then writes past the 17-byte local array, corrupting stack memory or faulting while formatting an alert. The alert path is conditional on a valid instruction at the saved PC and disassembly being enabled.

**Affected configuration and trigger:** i386 builds using the selected x86 debug backend with `DBFF_DISASSEMBLE`; an alert PC points at a decodable instruction of at least nine bytes. **Confidence:** high for the unsigned-underflow and out-of-bounds writes; exact outcome depends on stack layout and bytes overwritten. Bound the padding to the array capacity and skip it when the instruction text meets/exceeds the target width. No alert or disassembly was run; source-only.

<a id="ek728"></a>
### EK728 — OpenSBI DBCN output discards short-write completion counts (conditional lost console output; high source confidence).

The shared `sbi_debug_console_write()` helper invokes DBCN WRITE and returns only `ret.error`, discarding the SBI return value containing the completed-byte count (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_sbi.h:92-99`). `krnSBIPutStr()` sends the entire string in a single call and ignores the helper result; it does not retry any unwritten suffix (`kernel_console.c:48-65`). `krnSBIPutC()` similarly issues a one-byte write and ignores the result (`:14-24`); only systems where DBCN is unavailable use the legacy putchar fallback. Thus if the firmware reports a successful partial write, the remaining text is silently dropped; a zero-byte completion also loses the single character. If DBCN returns an error, these void output paths likewise provide no retry/fallback. The selected kernel debug wrapper suppresses only the intentional 0x03 marker and forwards other characters through this one-byte path (`kernel_debug.c:15-23`); generic `KrnPutChar` and `_bug` are maintained callers (`rom/kernel/putchar.c:17-53`; `_bug.c:17-27`).

**Affected configuration and trigger:** OpenSBI RISC-V64 builds where SBI BASE probing selects DBCN, and firmware completes a requested console write with fewer bytes than requested or an error. **Confidence:** high that completion counts/errors are discarded and no retry is attempted; visible truncation depends on firmware returning a short count/error. Preserve the returned count and loop until the buffer is complete or report the failure; do not silently fall back after partial output without accounting for already written bytes. No SBI firmware call or console output was run; source-only.

<a id="ek745"></a>
### EK745 — Generated library reference counts lose concurrent updates on ExecSMP.

The ordinary generated library `OpenLib` vector runs its `OPENLIB` hooks and then updates `lib_OpenCnt` with an ordinary `++`; it also clears `LIBF_DELEXP` with a separate ordinary read/modify/write (`tools/genmodule/writestart.c:1295-1305`). The ordinary `CloseLib` vector decrements `lib_OpenCnt`, runs `CLOSELIB` hooks, then tests the count and delayed-expunge flag to decide whether to call `ExpungeLib` (`:1463-1468,1506-1518`). Neither path takes `Library.lib_SpinLock` or uses an atomic operation. On ExecSMP, two CPUs can both read the same count and store the same incremented/decremented value: simultaneous successful opens can leave fewer references recorded than clients actually hold, while simultaneous closes can leave a phantom reference after all clients have closed. The separate delayed-expunge flag updates and tests are likewise not serialized with the count.

The public `Library` layout explicitly documents `lib_SpinLock` as protecting `lib_OpenCnt`, `lib_Flags`, and vectors on ExecSMP (`compiler/include/exec/libraries.h:52-59`); the selected `SetFunction()` and `SumLibrary()` paths take that lock (`rom/exec/setfunction.c:81-112`; `sumlibrary.c:56-96`). `OpenLibrary()` releases the `LibList` read lock before calling the Open vector and retains only `Forbid()` until return (`rom/exec/openlibrary.c:73-107`). `CloseLibrary()` and `RemLibrary()` also wrap their generated vectors only in `Forbid()` (`rom/exec/closelibrary.c:64-82`; `remlibrary.c:64-88`); Exec documents that this prevents task switches only on the local processor under ExecSMP (`rom/exec/forbid.c:52-61`). These wrappers therefore do not serialize count changes across CPUs.

The selected `asl.library` target uses genmodule's ordinary library vectors (`workbench/libs/asl/mmakefile.src:49-53`; `workbench/libs/asl/asl.conf` has no `noexpunge` or `dupbase` option). A successful open clears delayed-expunge state, so the early-expunge consequence requires a later direct expunge request while references remain open: after a lost open increment, one close can make the recorded count zero and run the pending expunge while another client still holds the library base. Conversely, lost close decrements can leave a nonzero count and prevent pending expunge after every client has closed. A source search found no in-tree direct `RemLibrary(asl.library)` caller, so these expunge consequences are conditional on an API client requesting delayed expunge; the lost count itself is independent of that request. Other libraries using ordinary generated vectors share the count race when built for ExecSMP; custom vectors, `dupbase` paths, and `noexpunge` paths are not asserted to be affected by this generated-code finding.

**Trigger and consequence:** two CPUs successfully open or close the same ordinary generated library concurrently. The stored reference count can diverge from the number of live clients; with delayed expunge requested, an undercount can free a still-referenced base, while an overcount can retain an otherwise unused library. **Affected configuration:** ExecSMP with an ordinary genmodule library; `asl.library` is a checked-in selected example. Single-CPU builds are excluded by local `Forbid()` serialization. **Confidence:** high for the unprotected generated read/modify/write operations, the SMP lock contract, and the selected ASL vector path; occurrence requires overlapping operations. No cross-CPU schedule, library open/close, or expunge was run; source-only.

<a id="ek752"></a>
### EK752 — `AllocAbs` accepts a wrapped endpoint outside a standard MemHeader (conditional 32-bit free-list corruption; high source confidence).

`nommu_AllocAbs()` forms `endlocation` as `location + byteSize` before validating the range (`rom/exec/memory_nommu.c:88-93`). For an ordinary, non-managed MemHeader it accepts the header when `mh_Lower <= location && mh_Upper >= endlocation` (`:132-136`). There is no overflow check and no separate requirement that `location <= mh_Upper`. On a 32-bit build, a start near `UINT32_MAX` and a size that wraps the endpoint into a low address can therefore pass this test against an unrelated low-address standard header.

For example, with a standard header spanning `0x1000..0x3000` and a free chunk beginning at `0x1000`, a request at `location=0xfffffff0` for `byteSize=0x1010` wraps the computed endpoint to `0x1000`. The header test passes (`0x1000 <= 0xfffffff0` and `0x3000 >= 0x1000`). After alignment, `p3` remains `0xfffffff0` and `p4` becomes `0x1000`; the ordinary free-chunk fit test accepts the chunk because its end is above `p4` and its start is below `p3` (`:154-205`). The carve then writes the new tail header at `p4`, links it after `p2`, and rewrites `p2->mc_Bytes` as the distance from the low chunk to the high requested start (`:205-220`). In this example `p4` aliases the original chunk node, so linking it back to itself creates a free-list cycle; the returned allocation address is also outside the selected header. A subsequent allocator traversal can loop on the cycle or operate on corrupted chunk metadata. Requests whose wrapped endpoint is unmapped may instead fault while the carve writes the tail header; the exact immediate symptom depends on address mapping.

The public `AllocAbs()` documentation does not state an overflow precondition (`rom/exec/allocabs.c:31-63`). It rejects zero size and routes through `InternalAllocAbs()` to this allocator; the distinct MungWall path adjusts the start and size first (`:68-84`). **Trigger and consequence:** on a 32-bit configuration using the standard non-managed MemHeader allocator, a caller requests a range whose end wraps and whose wrapped endpoint passes the header test; the standard allocator can corrupt its free-chunk chain or fault during the carve. The concrete example requires a low free chunk at the wrapped endpoint. **Affected configuration:** 32-bit builds using the standard non-managed MemHeader allocator with MungWall disabled; managed/TLSF headers dispatch through their own bounds/allocation methods and are not generalized here. The i386-PC startup selects the standard allocator when its command line contains `notlsf`, then passes that allocator choice into `mmap_InitMemory()` (`arch/i386-pc/kernel/kernel_startup.c:320-321,346-347`). This establishes a selected configuration for the standard-header path, but not that a normal in-tree caller makes the extreme request. No selected in-tree `AllocAbs()` caller issues such a near-address-space-sized range. **Confidence:** high for wrapped endpoint acceptance and the free-list writes; practical reachability depends on a caller supplying the extreme range and the relevant header/chunk layout. Check addition overflow and reject ranges whose endpoint is below the start before selecting a header. No allocation or free-list traversal was run; source-only.

<a id="ek769"></a>
### EK769 — OpenSBI boot hangs while parsing a zero-width memory tuple (malformed-DTB conditional; high source confidence).

The early parser reads root `#address-cells` and `#size-cells` into unsigned `addr_cells` and `size_cells` values without validating that they are nonzero (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_fdt.c:70-71,138-145`). For a depth-2 node whose name begins with `memory`, its `reg` path computes `pair = (addr_cells + size_cells) * 4` and iterates by `off += pair` while the retained-region cap is not full (`:146-156`). If both cell counts are zero and the `reg` property is present, `pair` is zero. `read_cells()` returns zero for both zero-cell reads, so `size` is zero; the loop's `continue` skips `off += pair` and does not increment `nregions` (`:155-166`). The loop condition therefore remains true and parsing never returns.

`kernel_cstart()` invokes `krnParseFDT()` before either the EFI-provided memory fallback or the fixed `0x80000000`/128-MiB fallback (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_startup.c:515-568`). A valid-magic DTB with explicit zero root address and size cell counts and a `/memory/reg` property therefore hangs the selected boot path before those recovery branches.

**Trigger and consequence:** malformed OpenSBI DTB with both root cell counts zero and a present memory `reg`; early boot loops forever in the first zero-sized tuple. **Affected configuration:** OpenSBI RISC-V64 startup parsing that DTB; ordinary trees with nonzero cell counts and trees without a matching memory node are outside this trigger. **Confidence:** high for the zero increment, zero-size `continue`, and caller ordering; requires the malformed firmware input. Reject zero cell counts and zero tuple width before entering the loop. No DTB was constructed or parsed and no boot was run; source-only.

<a id="ek772"></a>
### EK772 — OpenSBI early FDT cell-count overflow bypasses the memory tuple bound (malformed-DTB conditional out-of-bounds read; high source confidence).

The early parser accepts the root `#address-cells` and `#size-cells` values directly from their properties (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_fdt.c:138-145`), then computes a 32-bit tuple width with `(addr_cells + size_cells) * 4` (`:151`). The `reg` loop checks only that this computed width fits in the property (`:155-156`); it does not bound either cell count by the property length before `read_cells()` consumes the cells (`:157-160`; `read_cells()` itself loops for the full supplied count at `:53-59`).

A concrete malformed root uses `#address-cells = 0x40000001`, `#size-cells = 1`, and an eight-byte memory `reg`. The sum times four wraps modulo 32 bits to eight, so the tuple-width check admits one iteration. `read_cells(c, addr_cells)` then attempts to consume 1,073,741,825 address cells from the eight-byte property, reading beyond its end before the parser can reach the startup fallback. This differs from EK769: here the calculated width is nonzero, and the failure is an unbounded read rather than a zero-progress loop.
