**Trigger and scope:** any target using the shared Exec semaphore core (`rom/exec/mmakefile.src:15-29,40`) and its signed 16-bit `WORD` fields can reach the defect if one semaphore accumulates the stated number of holds or queued requests. For the ordinary 16-bit two’s-complement representation, the precise thresholds are 65,536 successful same-owner obtains/attempts, or 32,769 queued requests behind an exclusive owner. A false-free transition can admit a second owner; the release threshold can leave waiters blocked. These thresholds are derived from source arithmetic; no such workload was run.

**Confidence:** High for counter widths, sentinel transitions, and the branches that corrupt ownership or skip replies. Practical reachability requires unusually large acquisition/waiter counts.

<a id="ek9072"></a>
### EK9072 — Logger can remove a new broadcast while waiting on a timer reply it already dequeued.

**Finding:** The selected Logger task dequeues messages with `GetMsg()`. When the returned message is its timer request, it immediately calls `WaitIO()` on that same request (`workbench/c/Logger.c:531-545`). `GetMsg()` removes the request from the port but leaves its reply type and node links unchanged (`rom/exec/getmsg.c:61-77`). `WaitIO()` sees `NT_REPLYMSG` and calls `Remove()` on the request's node again (`rom/exec/waitio.c:57-77`; `rom/exec/remove.c:51-65`).

If the timer request was the sole message on the port when dequeued, and a log broadcast is appended before `WaitIO()` performs its second removal, the timer node's stale successor still points at the port tail. The repeated `Remove()` rewrites the port head to that tail and detaches the newly queued broadcast. Logger then fails to process that notification; the log entry remains outside this delivery path until another mechanism handles it.

**Trigger and scope:** selected Workbench Logger is running, the timer reply is the only queued message, and a log-resource broadcast arrives between `GetMsg()` and `WaitIO()`. This is a narrow message-list race. The Logger command-line utility in `workbench/network/common/C/logger.c` is unrelated.

**Confidence:** High for the dequeue/type/second-remove sequence; the lost-broadcast outcome requires the stated message timing. No listener or timer interleaving was run.

<a id="ek9073"></a>
### EK9073 — TLSF initialization can zero its control structure past a small managed-memory region.

**Finding:** `krnConvertMemHeaderToTLSF()` accepts a free chunk once its size reaches `ROUNDUP(sizeof(tlsf_t)) + 3 * ROUNDUP(sizeof(bhdr_t))` (`rom/kernel/tlsf.c:1512-1536`). `krnCreateTLSFMemHeader()` places the `MemHeaderExt` at the start of that same chunk and sets `mh_Free` to the full chunk size (`:1444-1500`). In `tlsf_init()`, when the extension is at `mh_Lower`, the TLSF pointer is advanced by `ROUNDUP(sizeof(struct MemHeaderExt))`, but the in-region eligibility check still compares the full `mh_Free` against the control-structure threshold without adding that prefix (`:1244-1262`). A chunk whose size falls between the checked threshold and that threshold plus the rounded extension size is accepted, then `bzero(tlsf, sizeof(tlsf_t))` writes past the chunk end.

The selected PC startup defaults to TLSF and the shared map builder may pass small usable chunks through conversion; the same initializer is also called for additional AArch64 native ranges. No checked-in boot map in the vulnerable size interval was established.

**Trigger and scope:** a selected TLSF-enabled startup passes a free region at or just above the accepted threshold but smaller than the required extension-prefix-plus-control-block extent. The initialization write can corrupt adjacent memory or boot data; the exact target depends on the physical layout.

**Confidence:** High for the threshold omission and out-of-region clear; trigger frequency and adjacent-memory effect depend on supplied firmware memory ranges. No boot or memory map was run.

<a id="ek9074"></a>
### EK9074 — Efika retains and publishes the idle-task pointer when `NewAddTask()` fails.

**Finding:** Efika kernel initialization allocates a `MemList`, task structure, and 4 KiB stack for its idle task, then calls `NewAddTask()` without checking its return value and unconditionally stores the allocated task address in global `idle_task` (`arch/ppc-chrp/efika/kernel/kernel_init.c:652-696`). `NewAddTask()` can return NULL when `InitETask()` fails or `PrepareContext()` fails (`rom/exec/newaddtask.c:268-310`); those failure paths do not release the caller-provided MemList allocations. `Kernel_Init()` nevertheless proceeds and returns success.

The allocation remains unregistered and unreclaimed, and `idle_task` points to a task that was never added to Exec. The selected Efika interrupt accounting compares `SysBase->ThisTask` against this pointer when accounting idle cycles (`arch/ppc-chrp/efika/kernel/intr.c:374-388`), so the failed creation also prevents the intended idle-time accounting from recognizing the actual idle state (there is no successfully registered Efika idle task).

**Trigger and scope:** all three allocations succeed, but `NewAddTask()` fails during ETask or context setup. Affected configuration is the PPC-CHRP Efika kernel.

**Confidence:** High for unchecked failure, retained allocation, and stale/unregistered pointer publication. No allocation failure or Efika boot was run.

<a id="ek9075"></a>
### EK9075 — POSIX `flock()` can obtain a semaphore after its last unlock has removed and freed it.

**Finding:** `flock()` looks up the path-named semaphore with `FindSemaphore()` and retains the returned pointer (`compiler/crt/posixc/flock.c:147-168`). On ExecSMP, `FindSemaphore()` holds `SemListSpinLock` only while traversing the list, releases it, and then returns the unpinned pointer (`rom/exec/findsemaphore.c:53-61`). `flock()` later releases its local `Forbid()` at line 187 before calling `AttemptSemaphore[Shared]()` or `ObtainSemaphore[Shared]()` at lines 191-217.

During that gap, another task can perform the last `LOCK_UN` on the same named semaphore. It releases the lock, removes its per-task flock record, observes an unowned semaphore with no queued waiters, unlinks it with `RemSemaphore()`, and frees both the name and semaphore (`flock.c:170-184`). `RemSemaphore()` protects list unlinking but does not wait for outstanding lookup results (`rom/exec/remsemaphore.c:47-58`). The acquiring task can then pass the freed pointer to the semaphore obtain/attempt routine. Exec documents that `Forbid()` is CPU-local on ExecSMP and cannot pin the pointer against this remote-CPU removal (`rom/exec/forbid.c:58-60`).

**Trigger and scope:** two tasks use POSIX `flock()` on the same path; one has looked up the existing semaphore but has not yet begun its obtain/attempt when the other performs the final unlock and frees it. ExecSMP permits the overlap on separate CPUs because the list lock is released before return and `Forbid()` is CPU-local. On a uniprocessor build, the same window can occur if `Permit()` at line 187 performs a pending task switch before the caller reaches its obtain/attempt; `Permit()` explicitly reschedules when a switch is pending (`rom/exec/permit.c:81-103`). This is distinct from EK588's simultaneous first-publication race. No in-tree call or interleaving was run.

**Confidence:** High for the unpinned lookup, final-unlock free, and later use in the selected source. SMP permits the remote overlap; the UP case requires a pending switch at the Permit boundary.

<a id="ek9076"></a>
### EK9076 — VMM priority arithmetic can wrap the pre-pager above the paging device.

**Finding:** For partition-backed paging, `VM_Manager_Init()` calls `adjust_priority()` after starting the page handler and pre-pager (`workbench/system/VMM/VM_Manager_Init.c:699-730`). If a task named after the paging device exists, the function reads its signed-byte node priority and assigns one less to the page handler and two less to the pre-pager (`:228-238`). `SetTaskPri()` accepts a `LONG`, but writes the requested priority directly into the task node's signed `BYTE ln_Pri` field (`rom/exec/settaskpri.c:24-29,98-103`; `compiler/include/exec/nodes.h:30-37`).

At the documented lower useful priority of -127, the pre-pager request is -129, outside the signed-byte range. On AROS GCC targets where this out-of-range conversion wraps to a signed byte, the stored priority becomes 127, the highest positive priority; the page handler request is -128. This reverses the intended ordering described in `adjust_priority()` and can let pre-pager work outrank the paging device and page handler. The pre-pager normally waits for signals (`workbench/system/VMM/prepager.c:457-478`), so sustained starvation is not claimed; the defect is the incorrect priority assignment when that worker is runnable.

**Trigger and scope:** optional VMM handler explicitly built and started with partition or pseudo-partition paging; a same-named paging-device task exists at priority -127; and the selected compiler narrows -129 to 127. The handler is selected in the Workbench:System aggregate through the VMM MUI target (`workbench/system/VMM/MUI/mmakefile.src:18-21`; `workbench/system/VMM/mmakefile.src:45-52`); reaching this trigger still requires the VMM app and stated paging setup to run. The checked-in AROS VMM startup also has earlier/later limitations tracked separately by EK428 and EK9906; this finding describes the priority setup reached on the explicit handler path before its later memory-registration failure, not a claim that default paging currently operates.

**Confidence:** High for the unsaturated subtraction and signed-byte storage; conditional on the paging-device priority, compiler's out-of-range conversion, and explicit VMM use. No task priority, paging operation, build, or runtime path was exercised.

<a id="ek9077"></a>
### EK9077 — A 2–4 GiB allocation can loop forever in the standard allocator's size-index helper.

**Finding:** `stdAlloc()` rounds the requested size, takes the MemHeader write spinlock on ExecSMP, verifies that the header has enough free bytes, and then calls `mhac_GetBetterPrevMemChunk()` (`rom/exec/memory.c:565-595`). When an allocator context exists, that helper passes the `IPTR` request size to `mhac_CalcIndex(LONG size, ...)` (`:354-367`). On 64-bit builds, a request in `[2^31, 2^32)` fits `IPTR` but is out of range for signed 32-bit `LONG`; on AROS GCC targets that narrow it to a negative value, the helper right-shifts it (`:311-320`). With arithmetic right shift, it eventually becomes -1, and `while (size >>= 1)` remains true forever.

The request reaches this helper only if a plain MemHeader's total `mh_Free` count is at least the rounded request size and `mhac_GetSysCtx()` supplies the index context (`rom/exec/memory_nommu.c:31-43,75-83`). The free bytes need not form one contiguous chunk: the hang occurs in the index calculation before the free-list search can determine whether a suitable chunk exists. The PC x86-64 startup supports explicitly selecting the standard allocator with `notlsf` (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/kernel_startup.c:374-375`); the default PC allocator is TLSF, so that default is excluded. On ExecSMP, the loop retains the MemHeader write spinlock and the caller's shared MemList lock, blocking same-header allocator operations and preventing exclusive MemList changes while the caller spins.

**Trigger and scope:** x86-64 PC using `notlsf` (or another selected 64-bit standard-allocator configuration with the same compiler behavior), a plain MemHeader with a live allocator index context and enough total free space, and a request of at least 2 GiB but less than 4 GiB. The checked-in source does not establish an in-tree caller making such a request; sufficient total free bytes in one MemHeader and an external/future caller are required. The size conversion and negative right-shift behavior are implementation-defined C operations, so the infinite loop is scoped to targets whose compiler performs the described signed narrowing and arithmetic shift.

**Confidence:** High for the nonterminating loop under those compiler and input conditions; practical reachability is conditional on the large request and a MemHeader with sufficient total free bytes. No large allocation or build was run.

<a id="ek9078"></a>
### EK9078 — DOS handler startup dereferences a failed process creation result.

**Finding:** `RunHandler()` calls `CreateNewProcTags()` but does not test the returned `process` pointer before it allocates a reply port and startup packet (`rom/dos/runhandler.c:131-153`). If process creation fails but those later allocations succeed, the unconditional `PutMsg(&(process->pr_MsgPort), ...)` dereferences NULL (`:163-165`). `CreateNewProc()` has failure paths that return NULL after cleaning up its partial process state (`rom/dos/createnewproc.c:594-669`).

The selected `GetDeviceProc()` caller invokes `RunHandler()` when a DOS device has no task and intends to translate a NULL result to `ERROR_DEVICE_NOT_MOUNTED` (`rom/dos/getdeviceproc.c:288-307`); boot-time `CliInit` also checks its return and removes the DOS entry on failure (`rom/dos/cliinit.c:401-418`). The unchecked dereference occurs before either caller can handle the failure.

**Trigger and scope:** a selected DOS device handler needs starting, `CreateNewProcTags()` fails, then `CreateMsgPort()` and `AllocDosObject(DOS_STDPKT)` succeed. Failure of either later allocation returns NULL without this dereference. The bug is in the shared DOS `RunHandler()` path; no handler or allocation failure was run.

**Confidence:** High for the missing process check and NULL dereference under the stated allocation ordering. No task creation was attempted.

<a id="ek9079"></a>
### EK9079 — DOS leaves a started handler process waiting when startup-message setup fails.

**Finding:** After `CreateNewProcTags()` starts the handler process, `RunHandler()` can fail to allocate its reply port or startup packet (`rom/dos/runhandler.c:131-153`). Both branches free the local path buffer (and the packet-allocation branch deletes the reply port) and return NULL, but neither stops or signals the already-started process. Since no startup packet has been sent (`:155-165`), the child remains at its initial wait.

This wait is present in the selected RAM handler (`rom/filesys/ram/handler.c:82-92`), FAT handler (`rom/filesys/fat/main.c:128-145`), AUX handler (`workbench/fs/aux_handler/aux_handler.c:85-103`), and hosted `emul-handler` (`arch/all-hosted/filesys/emul_handler/emul_handler.c:1394-1400`). For emul-handler, the module manifest selects this body and the Unix bootstrap config requests `@arch@/L/emul-handler`; its parent boot aggregate dependency is commented, so the module is an explicit/packaged configuration rather than a claim about the default build (`arch/all-hosted/filesys/emul_handler/mmakefile.src:12-24`; `arch/all-unix/filesys/emul_handler/mmakefile.src:21-22`; `arch/all-unix/boot/AROSBootstrap.conf:8-13`; `arch/all-unix/boot/mmakefile.src:45`). The startup path has one DOS startup packet posted to the process port, which the handler consumes after `WaitPort()`; no competing reader or independent null-result issue was found. `GetDeviceProc()` reports the failed startup as `ERROR_DEVICE_NOT_MOUNTED` (`rom/dos/getdeviceproc.c:302-307`); boot-time `CliInit` removes the device-list entry after a NULL result (`rom/dos/cliinit.c:410-418`). Those callers do not recover or terminate the child process, which retains its process/task resources while waiting indefinitely.

**Trigger and scope:** handler process creation succeeds, then either `CreateMsgPort()` or `AllocDosObject(DOS_STDPKT)` fails before the startup packet is sent. The stranded-wait consequence is confirmed for the selected RAM, FAT, and AUX handlers; other handler entry points require their own startup-wait check. No allocation failure or handler was run.

**Confidence:** High for the two unhandled post-spawn returns and the selected handlers' initial waits. Resource retention follows from the live process waiting without a startup message; no task lifetime was exercised.

<a id="ek9080"></a>
### EK9080 — withdrawn: TLSF realloc shrink sentinel failure was not established.

The earlier coverage note claimed that shrinking by exactly one rounded header makes `INSERT_FREE_BLOCK()` reject a remainder located at the area sentinel and enter the corruption handler. Rechecking `GET_NEXT_BHDR()`, the sentinel construction, `tlsf_block_in_area()`, `tlsf_validate_insert()`, and `INSERT_FREE_BLOCK()` does not support that failure path (`rom/kernel/tlsf.c:242-250,304-329,427-485,904-924,1155-1170`). The zero-sized remainder header is immediately before the sentinel, so its address passes the area's strict `< area->end` test; bucket zero is valid and the insertion validator does not reject a zero size. Its free-list links overlap the sentinel header, but the selected code does not establish a caller-visible failure from that transient metadata state: positive allocations do not search the zero-size bucket, and freeing or growing the preceding block merges the zero-size remainder and rewrites the sentinel links. The original corruption-alert consequence is therefore withdrawn. Exact caller sizes, resident-name duplicates and terminal-block placement remain conditional; no replacement defect is credited without a demonstrated consequence.

<a id="ek9081"></a>
### EK9081 — TLSF frees can leave Exec's managed-memory size prefilter stale.

**Finding:** TLSF's successful allocation path snapshots its private `tlsf->free_size` into the public `MemHeader.mh_Free` (`rom/kernel/tlsf.c:598-600`). Its free path increases only the private count (`:832-838`), and the in-place realloc shrink path also increases only that count (`:900-914`). The installed `mhe_Free` and `mhe_FreeVec` callbacks route to these functions (`:1472-1479`); `memory_nommu.c` serializes them under the MemHeader write spinlock on ExecSMP but does not refresh `mh_Free` afterward (`rom/exec/memory_nommu.c:269-284`).

Before invoking a managed allocator, `nommu_AllocMem()` skips any header whose `mh_Free` is below the request (`:31-43`). Therefore, after a free or shrink raises TLSF's private count above the last snapshot, an allocation request larger than stale `mh_Free` but no larger than a suitable TLSF free block is rejected before TLSF can try it. The failure persists until a smaller successful allocation reaches `tlsf_malloc()` and refreshes the snapshot. `AvailMem()` can meanwhile report the private count through `mhe_Avail` (`memory_nommu.c:361-375`; `tlsf.c:1318-1352`), so an availability query can say sufficient memory exists immediately before such an allocation fails.

**Trigger and scope:** a TLSF managed header is selected (including default i386/x86-64 PC startup unless `notlsf` is selected); a free or in-place shrink increases private available memory without a later successful allocation refreshing `mh_Free`; and a request is greater than stale `mh_Free` but fits within the largest suitable TLSF block, with no other matching MemHeader able to satisfy it. If another header succeeds, the specific failed-allocation consequence does not occur. The checked-in source establishes the accounting and prefilter paths; the exact request/caller ordering is conditional. No allocation or free was run.

**Confidence:** High for the stale snapshot and prefilter skip. Caller-visible allocation failure requires the stated range and absence of a suitable alternative header.

<a id="ek9082"></a>
### EK9082 — Native AArch64 `CacheClearE()` truncates pointer-sized lengths to 32 bits.

**Finding:** The public `CacheClearE()` vector accepts an `IPTR length` and documents it as the memory range size (`rom/exec/cachecleare.c:19-22,40-45`; vector declaration `rom/exec/exec.conf:182`). The selected native AArch64 override instead declares the argument as `ULONG` and forwards that 32-bit value in x1 (`arch/aarch64-native/exec/cachecleare.c:18-30`). The SVC receiver reads x1 into a 64-bit `uint64_t` and passes it to the cache walker (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/syscall.c:280-288`), so it cannot recover the discarded high bits.

For a valid range whose length is at least 4 GiB, the wrapper therefore forwards only `length mod 2^32`. A length of exactly 4 GiB becomes zero; with a cache-line-aligned address this makes the kernel's rounded start and end equal, so it performs no line maintenance (`syscall.c:109-110,120-158`). A length of 4 GiB plus a cache line causes only the first cache line to be maintained. The requested tail remains stale in the data and/or instruction cache, contrary to the public API's cache-coherency purpose.

**Trigger and scope:** native AArch64 Exec, selected by the Raspberry Pi AArch64 target (`arch/aarch64-native/exec/mmakefile.src:12-14,28-30`), and a caller passes a valid non-wrapping range longer than `ULONG_MAX` to `CacheClearE()`. The checked in-tree caller review found no selected ordinary range exceeding 4 GiB; the defect is currently an external/public API and future large-buffer candidate. Other architectures have their own `CacheClearE()` implementations and are not covered by this finding.

**Confidence:** High for the API-width mismatch and truncation. The stale-cache consequence requires a caller to request a range above 4 GiB; no cache operation, DMA, or such caller was run.

<a id="ek9083"></a>
### EK9083 — PC SMP CPU load uses mismatched sample and idle intervals.

**Finding:** The PC SMP heartbeat waits until the elapsed TSC interval exceeds one `cpu_TSCFreq` unit, then computes the actual interval as `timeCur = now - cpu_LastCPULoadTime` (`arch/all-pc/kernel/apic_heartbeat.c:58-61`). It calculates `cpu_Load` using the fixed one-second baseline minus `cpu_SleepTime`, divided by that possibly longer interval (`:122-127`). `cpu_SleepTime` accumulates the full TSC duration of each ACPI HLT sleep (`arch/all-pc/kernel/acpi_pm.c:96-112`), and both fields are UQUAD values (`arch/all-pc/kernel/apic.h:35,44-46`). When the sample interval exceeds one second and accumulated idle duration exceeds one second, the unsigned subtraction underflows before the Q32 division. For example, at a 2 GHz TSC, a two-second fully idle sample has 4 billion sleep ticks: subtracting that from the 2-billion-tick baseline wraps to a large unsigned value and produces a nonzero load instead of zero. Even without underflow, using a fixed one-second numerator against a longer denominator makes utilization too low when the interval is extended but sleep is below one second.

The result is consumed by the PC CPU-frequency governor (`arch/all-pc/kernel/cpu_freq.c:80-99`) and exposed through the PC CPU-load attribute (`arch/all-pc/kernel/getcpuattr.c:64-70` and `getsystemattr.c:56-76`). A sampling delay can therefore cause false load readings and an inappropriate governor decision.

**Trigger and scope:** selected `arch/all-pc` PC SMP builds (the accounting is guarded by `__AROSEXEC_SMP__`); a heartbeat sample spans longer than one second and accumulated ACPI HLT time exceeds the one-second TSC baseline, or the interval is extended enough to skew the fixed-baseline ratio. UP accounting is a separate branch. The heartbeat and ACPI power-management sources are selected in `arch/all-pc/kernel/mmakefile.src:54-63`.

**Confidence:** High for the arithmetic mismatch and unsigned underflow. The frequency of delayed samples and resulting hardware governor behavior were not measured; no timer, HLT, load attribute, or frequency transition was run.

<a id="ek9084"></a>
### EK9084 — PC SMP per-task CPU-usage fixed-point conversion overflows on long samples.

**Finding:** The x86-64 PC task-switch path accumulates each task's runtime as TSC ticks in the 64-bit `iet_private2` field (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/kernel_cpu.c:323-327`; field declaration `rom/exec/etask.h:52-53`). At the PC SMP heartbeat, ready, waiting and spinning tasks are converted to a Q32 usage fraction with `(iet_private2 << 32) / timeCur` (`arch/all-pc/kernel/apic_heartbeat.c:58-61,64-86,110-118`). The left shift is performed in the 64-bit type and discards high bits before division. Thus a task sample of at least `2^32` TSC ticks cannot be represented by the intermediate: exactly `2^32` ticks shifts to zero, and values above it wrap to a different numerator. A task that ran for almost an entire long interval can consequently be reported with near-zero or otherwise incorrect CPU usage. The running-task branch uses the same shift when `time < timeCur`, so it has the same overflow; its saturation branch only covers `time >= timeCur` (`:97-105`). `TaskTag_CPUUsage` exposes the stored ULONG result (`rom/task/QueryTaskTagList.c:163-169`).

**Trigger and scope:** the selected x86-64 PC SMP accounting path, when a heartbeat sample interval and an individual task's accumulated runtime exceed `UINT32_MAX` TSC ticks. At a 2 GHz TSC, the threshold is about 2.15 seconds of task runtime in one sample; a delayed heartbeat or long scheduling/interrupt pause can extend the sample. The APIC heartbeat itself gates sampling at more than one TSC second (`apic_heartbeat.c:58`), so ordinary near-one-second samples stay below this per-task threshold. This finding concerns task-use fractions, not the separate aggregate `cpu_Load` calculation in EK9083.

**Confidence:** High for the width/shift overflow and its incorrect stored fraction. Long-sample occurrence and consumer-visible effects were not measured; no task scheduling, heartbeat or runtime query was run.

<a id="ek9085"></a>
### EK9085 — ARM/AArch64 CPU-load sampling loses elapsed time after a 32-bit counter wrap.

**Finding:** The ARM and AArch64 `KrnGetSystemAttr(KATTR_CPULoad + cpu)` readers obtain a full-width microsecond timestamp, but narrow it to `ULONG` before calculating the sample window. They likewise narrow the idle task's cumulative busy-time counter before taking the idle delta (`arch/arm-native/kernel/getsystemattr.c:46-49,61-76`; `arch/aarch64-native/kernel/getsystemattr.c:46-48,56-71`). Unsigned subtraction correctly handles a single 32-bit wrap when the real interval is less than `2^32` microseconds. It cannot represent elapsed time across a full 32-bit period: after an exact `2^32`-microsecond gap, `window` is zero, the calculation is skipped, and the function stores/returns `retval == 0` as the new load (`arm-native:64-76`; `aarch64-native:59-71`). For a longer gap, the reported window and idle delta omit one or more full periods, so their ratio need not represent the actual CPU load across the gap.

The underlying platform timer is a 64-bit 1 MHz counter (`arch/arm-native/kernel/kernel_arm.h:23`; `platform_bcm2708.c:192-204`; AArch64 declaration `kernel_arm.h:25`, implementation `arch/aarch64-native/kernel/platform_bcm27xx.c:466-478`), so this is loss in the load-reader arithmetic rather than a wrap in the source timer. The result is exposed by the public kernel system-attribute API. The selected ARM `processor.resource` maps `GCIT_ProcessorLoad` to this attribute (`arch/arm-native/processor/getcpuinfo.c:141-145`); the selected ARM SMP getter is only reached when the caller requests the load tag.

**Trigger and scope:** ARM-native and AArch64-native SMP builds when the same core's load attribute is not sampled for at least `2^32` microseconds (about 71.6 minutes), or when sampling resumes after a longer gap. Regular queries with shorter intervals use valid modulo deltas. UP builds do not compile this SMP load reader. This finding concerns the aggregate per-core load attribute, not the per-task CPU-usage sweep.

**Confidence:** High for the timestamp narrowing, lost-wrap arithmetic, and exact-wrap zero result. Whether a selected user interface leaves a core unqueried for this long depends on caller behavior; no 71-minute gap or processor-load query was run.

<a id="ek9086"></a>
### EK9086 — OpenSBI RISC-V ACPI MADT parser reads recognized entries past the table end.

**Finding:** `krnACPIPLICInfo()` sets `end` from the MADT's declared length and verifies that at least an entry header remains (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_acpi.c:329-339`). It stops entries whose declared length is smaller than the common header, and recognized RINTC/PLIC entries must declare at least the full known structure size (`:341-344,359-362`). However, it never checks that `p + e->length <= end` before casting and reading the recognized entry. A final entry can therefore declare a full RINTC or PLIC structure while extending beyond the MADT's declared extent; the parser reads `flags`/`ext_intc_id` or controller `base`, `size` and source count from bytes outside that table (`:344-356,362-376`). The subsequent `p += e->length` happens after those reads (`:379`).

The result can be an out-of-table read or, if adjacent memory is readable, acceptance of unrelated bytes as interrupt-controller configuration. Startup calls this ACPI fallback when no PLIC base was supplied by the device tree, then passes the resulting information to `krnPLICInit()` (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_startup.c:661-668`). This can leave external-interrupt initialization misconfigured or unavailable. The separate `dump_madt()` diagnostic loop has a similar missing entry-end check (`kernel_acpi.c:195-205,207-231`); the live PLIC configuration parser is the operational path described above.

**Trigger and scope:** OpenSBI RISC-V boot using ACPI to describe the PLIC because the device tree supplied no PLIC, with a malformed MADT whose recognized final entry length extends beyond `header.length`. This finding concerns the MADT's internal declared extent; validation of ACPI table addresses and complete spans against EFI memory regions is separately tracked as EK9088.

**Confidence:** High that the live parser can read beyond the MADT-declared end for such a record. Controller misconfiguration or a fault depends on the bytes/mapping after the table; no malformed firmware, boot, or interrupt-controller initialization was run.

<a id="ek9087"></a>
### EK9087 — OpenSBI reads the revision-2+ XSDT pointer without checking the RSDP length.

**Finding:** The ACPI RSDP layout places its `length` field before the revision-2 `xsdt_address` (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_acpi.c:19-32`). Both the live `acpi_find()` path and the boot-time ACPI dump select XSDT based on `revision >= 2` and a nonzero `xsdt_address`, without checking that the declared RSDP length includes that field (`:263-276,488-491`). For a malformed revision-2+ RSDP whose declared length ends before the 8-byte XSDT pointer, the code reads beyond the declared object and may use unrelated adjacent bytes as the root-table address. In the live path, the resulting root pointer is dereferenced for its length and entry addresses (`:276-299`); when the ACPI MADT is needed to configure the PLIC, this can lead to invalid table reads or incorrect controller data. The optional diagnostic dump has the same unchecked field read.

The EFI stub records the RSDP pointer from the ACPI 2.0+ configuration-table GUID (or the ACPI 1.0 GUID fallback) without validating its internal declared length (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/efi_stub.c:778-797`).

**Trigger and scope:** OpenSBI RISC-V boot via UEFI with a revision-2-or-later RSDP whose `length` does not cover `xsdt_address`; the live configuration effect matters when the ACPI path is used (for example, no PLIC base was supplied by the device tree). Valid RSDP lengths do not trigger this. This is distinct from EK9088, which concerns bounds of the root and child tables relative to retained EFI regions.

**Confidence:** High that the field is read without validating the RSDP length. Resulting table faults or PLIC misconfiguration depend on adjacent contents and address mapping; no malformed RSDP or boot was used.

<a id="ek9088"></a>
### EK9088 — OpenSBI trusts ACPI root and child table extents outside retained EFI regions.

**Finding:** The EFI stub records up to a bounded set of firmware memory regions, retaining EFI runtime and ACPI reclaim/NVS descriptors (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/efi_stub.c:522-556`). After MMU setup, only those saved regions are explicitly mapped for firmware reads (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_mmu.c:424-446`). The ACPI parser does not use this region map to validate table addresses or spans before dereferencing them. `acpi_find()` takes the RSDT/XSDT pointer from the RSDP, reads its header, and derives the entry count from the root's own `length` (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_acpi.c:263-280`). It reads each root entry, follows the child address, and dereferences the child signature without first confirming that the root header, full root span, or child header lies in a retained firmware region (`:281-299`). The live PLIC parser then uses the child MADT's self-reported `length` to form its end pointer and walk subtables (`:320-335,379`), without validating the complete MADT span against the mapped ACPI regions. `krnDumpACPI()` likewise follows the root and its entries (`:445-523`).

Malformed or inconsistent ACPI pointers/lengths can therefore make the parser read unmapped addresses or continue beyond a mapped firmware region, causing an early boot fault; when the reads land in mapped adjacent data, unrelated bytes can be interpreted as table entries and influence PLIC setup. This is the broader root/child table containment issue. The unchecked RSDP XSDT field is separately tracked as EK9087, and a MADT subtable that exceeds an otherwise reachable table's declared end is separately tracked as EK9086.

**Trigger and scope:** OpenSBI RISC-V UEFI boot with an ACPI RSDP/root/child pointer or declared table length that refers outside the retained EFI runtime/ACPI regions. The live PLIC configuration consequence applies when device-tree PLIC data is absent and startup invokes the ACPI fallback (`kernel_startup.c:661-668`); the optional ACPI dump also follows these pointers. EFI-region collection capacity and skipped descriptors are separately covered by EK8863.

**Confidence:** High that the ACPI walkers trust firmware addresses and self-declared extents without checking them against the regions deliberately mapped for ACPI access. A fault or controller misconfiguration depends on the malformed values and page mapping; no malformed table or boot was used.

<a id="ek9090"></a>
### EK9090 — Sashimi recovery can inspect past a MemHeader's upper bound.

**Finding:** With the `RECOVER` option, Sashimi scans each memory header's `[mh_Lower, mh_Upper)` range (`developer/debug/sashimi/sashimi.c:668-694`; the option calls `Recover()` at `:780`). `mh_Upper` is exclusive: `AddMemList()` sets it to `base + size` (`rom/exec/addmemlist.c:84-89`), and Exec validates chunks against that end (`rom/exec/memory.c:482-495`). The recovery loop uses a `do` body and only checks `++start != end` after the body. At the last in-range word, if it equals the Sashimi cookie, the body reads `start[1]` to check the backlink; if that also matches, it reads `start[2]` for the creation time (`sashimi.c:676-690`). Those reads are one and two `IPTR`s beyond the region. A cookie at the penultimate word can also make the creation-time read land exactly at `end`.

This is a conditional out-of-range read during memory scanning. If the adjacent address is not readable, recovery can fault while its memory-list exclusion/Forbid is active; if readable, adjacent contents are treated as marker metadata and can affect which candidate is selected. A complete valid Sashimi resource should fit within its allocation, so the boundary condition requires stale, partial or coincidental marker data rather than an intact resource at that location.

**Trigger and scope:** only the developer/debug Sashimi command's `RECOVER` path, with a MemHeader whose last one or two words match enough of the cookie/backlink sequence to take the guarded reads. The issue is more directly relevant to an incomplete/stale buffer than a valid live Sashimi resource. No claim is made for ordinary Sashimi capture/save operation.

**Confidence:** High that the loop can read beyond the exclusive bound under the stated marker condition; low that a real system will contain a matching boundary marker. No recovery scan or memory fault was run.

<a id="ek9091"></a>
### EK9091 — Negative Sashimi buffer size can underallocate the FIFO on 32-bit builds.

**Finding:** The `BUFFERSIZE/N` option is parsed through `ReadArgs()`'s `/N` conversion to `LONG` (`developer/debug/sashimi/sashimi.c:99-114,848-853`; `rom/dos/readargs.c:875-889`). `StrToLong()` explicitly accepts `-1` and returns it as a `LONG` (`rom/dos/strtolong.c:28-35,55-77`). Sashimi casts that value to `ULONG`; the minimum-size test does not clamp `0xffffffff` (`sashimi.c:848-853`). On a 32-bit build, `AddSashimiResource()` then calculates `sizeof(MemChunk) + sizeof(*sr) + bufferSize - 1` in 32-bit size arithmetic, which wraps to approximately `sizeof(MemChunk) + sizeof(*sr) - 2` instead of allocating the requested FIFO (`:426-463`). The source defines `NO_ALLOCABS` as 1, so the selected implementation keeps this single undersized `AllocMem()` result rather than replacing it with the alternative `AllocAbs()` allocation (`:53,441-449`). It stores the unbounded `0xffffffff` value in `sr_FIFOTotalSize` (`:451-463`).

When Sashimi's raw-output patch receives bytes, `StoreFIFOChar()` writes at `sr_FIFO[sr_FIFOWriteIndex]` and advances the index modulo that oversized recorded total (`:266-280,293-319`). After the small allocation's limited trailing space is consumed, captured output writes beyond the allocated FIFO. This is conditional on the wrapped allocation succeeding and later raw output reaching Sashimi; it is not a claim about normal-sized buffers.

**Trigger and scope:** optional developer/debug Sashimi on a 32-bit target, invoked with `BUFFERSIZE=-1`, with the wrapped small allocation succeeding and subsequent non-NUL raw output captured. Sashimi is selected by the workbench-complete graph, but must be run with this option to reach the path. On 64-bit targets the allocation-size expression is pointer-width and does not wrap in this way; other extreme numeric inputs are outside this concrete trace.

**Confidence:** High for `/N` acceptance, 32-bit size wrap, stored FIFO size and unchecked indexed writes. The actual allocation result and subsequent neighboring-memory effects were not exercised; no Sashimi run or raw output was performed.

<a id="ek9092"></a>
### EK9092 — Unix `KrnMayGetChar()` can block when called before input acquisition.

**Finding:** The generic `KrnMayGetChar()` contract says the call never waits and returns `-1` when no character is available (`rom/kernel/maygetchar.c:24-36`). The Unix override directly reads one byte from `STDERR_FILENO` and returns `-1` only when the read result is not exactly one (`arch/all-unix/kernel/maygetchar.c:17-23`). On a blocking stderr descriptor, that `read()` waits for input rather than reporting no available character. Unix `KrnObtainInput()` is what makes the descriptor nonblocking by adding `O_NONBLOCK` (`arch/all-unix/kernel/obtaininput.c:30-38`); `KrnMayGetChar()` does not check whether that setup was performed.

The normal SAD path calls `KrnObtainInput()` before entering `RawMayGetChar()` polling and releases input on the quit command (`rom/exec/debug_internal.c:37-46,413-417`), so that selected caller meets the setup requirement. However, the public `RawMayGetChar()` wrapper and debug.library `KMayGetChar()` simply forward to the kernel poll without acquiring input (`rom/exec/rawmaygetchar.c:41-45`; `rom/debug/kmaygetchar.c:10-13`). A direct caller using those documented nonblocking APIs while stderr remains blocking can stall indefinitely when there is no pending character.

**Trigger and scope:** Unix-hosted builds, a blocking `STDERR_FILENO`, and a direct `KrnMayGetChar()`/`RawMayGetChar()`/`KMayGetChar()` call without a preceding successful `KrnObtainInput()`. The selected built-in SAD caller obtains input first; no other maintained in-tree caller was found that reaches this condition. External callers and other uses of the public poll API remain possible.

**Confidence:** High that a blocking descriptor makes the Unix override wait and that its nonblocking behavior depends on separate acquisition. No selected direct in-tree trigger was identified outside the paired SAD path; no host read or blocking call was run.

<a id="ek9093"></a>
### EK9093 — `GetPlayerAttrsA()` counts unsupported tags as successfully filled.

**Finding:** The function documents its return value as the number of tag items “successfully filled in” (`workbench/libs/realtime/getplayerattrsa.c:30-47`). It writes outputs only for tags handled by the switch (`:79-137`), but increments `nAttrs` after the switch for every item returned by `NextTagItem()` (`:77-78,137-143`). An unsupported or unimplemented tag therefore leaves its output storage unchanged while increasing the returned success count. A caller that uses the count to determine whether all requested outputs were filled can accept stale/uninitialized values as valid. `PLAYER_ErrorCode` is present in the shared tag enum but is not a player getter case (`compiler/include/libraries/realtime.h:137-152`; `getplayerattrsa.c:79-137`); arbitrary unknown tags have the same count behavior.

**Trigger and scope:** `realtime.library` `GetPlayerAttrsA()` with a non-NULL player and a tag list containing at least one unhandled tag. NULL player returns zero; supported attributes are stored normally. The only selected direct in-tree caller uses supported `PLAYER_Ready` (`workbench/libs/realtime/setconductorstate.c:137-155`), so no current internal caller impact was established. The defect is in the reported API result for external/future callers.

**Confidence:** High that unsupported items are counted without writing their outputs and that this conflicts with the documented return count. Caller-visible stale-value use depends on a caller supplying an unsupported tag and trusting the count; no player or tag query was run.

<a id="ek9094"></a>
### EK9094 — Console paste can send through a freed ConClip port during shutdown.

**Finding:** The console handler's `do_paste()` obtains the public ConClip port with `FindPort()` (`rom/filesys/console_handler/support.c:752-763`), then initializes a private reply port and `SGWork`, allocates a paste buffer, and only afterward calls `PutMsg()` (`:765-792`). It does not protect the lookup-to-send interval. `FindPort()` documents that callers must protect port-list arbitration with `Forbid()`/`Permit()` (`rom/exec/findport.c:25-28`); its ExecSMP spinlock only protects the list traversal and is released before the borrowed pointer is returned (`:53-61`).

ConClip's `OFF` path signals its task, which can leave `handleall()` on the control-C signal and proceed to cleanup; cleanup unhooks the editor and calls `DeletePort()` (`workbench/c/ConClip.c:154-165,388-425,115-120`). `DeletePort()` removes the port and frees its storage (`compiler/alib/deleteport.c:42-46`; `rom/exec/deletemsgport.c:48-56`). If this shutdown runs after `FindPort()` returns but before `PutMsg()`, the console handler passes a stale pointer to `PutMsg()`, which adds to the port's message list and uses its signal target (`rom/exec/putmsg.c:71-105`). The paste path then waits on its private reply port (`support.c:790-792`), which the terminated ConClip task cannot service. This is distinct from EK9529, where a message is queued before shutdown but omitted by the worker's final signal-snapshot drain.

**Trigger and scope:** selected console.handler paste request concurrent with ConClip shutdown via its `OFF`/Ctrl-C path. On a uniprocessor the sender can be task-switched after lookup; on ExecSMP the port-list lock does not pin the returned object against remote removal/free. ConClip is optional, and the race requires the ConClip task to shut down in the lookup-to-send interval. The result can be an invalid send through freed port storage and a paste request that never receives a reply.

**Confidence:** High for the unprotected borrowed-pointer interval, port deletion, and subsequent send/wait behavior. The shutdown interleaving was not induced; no paste or port operation was run.

<a id="ek9095"></a>
### EK9095 — x86-64 PC advertises RAM beyond its 512-GiB identity map.

**Finding:** x86-64 startup asks the bootloader memory map for the highest RAM endpoint and passes that value to `core_SetupMMU()` (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/kernel_startup.c:433-454`; `mmap_LargestAddress()` includes every RAM record in `arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_mmap.c:323-348`). The MMU builder clamps its 2 MiB page count to 262,144 entries, a 512 GiB window, and `core_InitMMU()` maps only `PML4[0]` (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/mmu.c:29-43,66-83,147-158`). The memory map is processed afterward by `mmap_InitMemory()` (`kernel_startup.c:515-520`). Its x86-64 `PC_Memory` table defines high memory from 2 GiB to `-1` (`kernel_startup.c:59-71`), and the map walker intersects bootloader RAM records with that region and adds the resulting chunks without clipping them to the MMU window (`kernel_mmap.c:120-185,213-239`). Thus a RAM chunk extending above 512 GiB can be represented in a MemHeader even though its upper part has no identity mapping.

If a separate usable chunk starts above the mapped boundary, constructing its MemHeader/chunk touches an unmapped address during startup. If the above-limit portion is part of a larger chunk starting below the boundary, later allocation/initialization that reaches that portion can fault. The default allocator selection can further make high-memory headers attractive, but the precise failure point depends on the bootloader's RAM map and allocation order.

**Trigger and scope:** x86-64 PC bootloader map reports usable RAM above 512 GiB, and the selected startup path includes that range in the all-address high-memory region. Systems whose RAM ends within the 512 GiB identity window are unaffected by this mismatch. This finding concerns RAM usability; the separate early-GOP framebuffer bound is tracked as EK8941.

**Confidence:** High that the selected MMU mapping is capped while the memory-list builder accepts the larger RAM ranges. Whether startup faults immediately or a later allocation reaches the unmapped portion depends on physical-map fragmentation and allocation use; no high-RAM boot or allocation was run.

<a id="ek9096"></a>
### EK9096 — x86-64 PC `KrnMapGlobal()` ignores `MAP_Supervisor`.

**Finding:** The public kernel mapping flags include `MAP_Supervisor` (`compiler/include/aros/kernel.h:28-39`). In the selected x86-64 PC implementation, `set_pde_2m()` unconditionally sets the leaf PDE user/supervisor bit to 1 instead of deriving it from `flags` (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/mapglobal.c:69-85`). The parent PML4E and PDPE created by this path also set their user bits to 1 (`:42-67`), so the leaf remains user-accessible. A caller requesting `MAP_Supervisor` therefore receives a mapping accessible from user mode, subject to the requested readable/writable/executable leaf permissions. This contrasts with the same target's `KrnSetProtection()`, which clears the user bit when `MAP_Supervisor` is set (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/setprotection.c:31-35`), and with the m68k `KrnMapGlobal()` implementation, which derives its `supervisor` value from that flag (`arch/m68k-all/kernel/mapglobal.c:24-29`).

**Trigger and scope:** x86-64 PC callers invoke `KrnMapGlobal()` with `MAP_Supervisor` set. The maintained direct-caller census found no selected in-tree caller using this flag (`arch/x86_64-pc/kernel/mapglobal.c:69-145`; selected PCIPC caller uses only readable, writable and cache-inhibit flags at `arch/all-pc/hidds/pcipc/pcipc_driverclass.c:246-247`). The defect is therefore an external/public API and future-caller condition in the checked tree.

**Confidence:** High that the flag is ignored and the resulting x86-64 leaf mapping has the user bit set. Practical impact depends on a caller relying on supervisor-only protection; no mapping or user-mode access was performed.

<a id="ek9097"></a>
### EK9097 — RISC-V OpenSBI maps and reserves only the first 2 MiB of the device tree.

**Finding:** The early parser records the firmware blob's declared `totalsize` in `fdtinfo`, but the later explicit mapping uses the constant `2 << 20` (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_fdt.c:91-98`; `arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_startup.c:687-688`). The full DTB pointer is published through `KRN_FlattenedDeviceTree`, and the selected RISC-V FDT library walks the structure and strings in place using the blob's offsets and `size_dt_struct` (`kernel_startup.c:379-410`; `arch/riscv-all/linklibs/fdt/fdt.c:50-58,119-146,165-195`). If a valid DTB is larger than 2 MiB and lies outside all RAM and firmware ranges already mapped by `krnInitMMU()`, accesses into its tail after MMU setup can fault because only the first 2 MiB receives an explicit mapping.

The same constant limits the later MemHeader exclusion (`kernel_startup.c:965-968`). In the separately enumerated RAM regions, bytes beyond the first 2 MiB can therefore be added to Exec as allocatable memory even when they remain part of the DTB. The scalar bootstrap bank has an additional cutoff at the DTB's starting page (`:780-789`), so this allocator-overlap case concerns later region headers, not that initial bank. Selected in-tree FDT consumers are initialized before those later headers are published (`arch/riscv64-all/processor/processor_init.c:432-457`; `arch/riscv64-opensbi/hidd/pcidt/pcidt_driverclass.c:1055-1068`; `arch/riscv64-opensbi/hidd/dwi2c/dwi2c_init.c:285-307`; `arch/riscv64-opensbi/hidd/dwuart/dwuart_init.c:187-205`); overwrite is therefore retained only for later clients using the public boot-info pointer, not claimed for those startup readers. If the DTB lies within a RAM or firmware range already mapped in full, the fixed mapping does not itself leave its tail unmapped.

**Trigger and scope:** a DTB larger than 2 MiB is supplied, and either its tail is outside ranges mapped by `krnInitMMU()` and a later reader accesses it, or it overlaps a separately added RAM region and a later allocation reuses bytes past the fixed exclusion. The checked-in source does not establish a deployed DTB above this size or a selected post-publication in-tree reader. **Affected configuration:** RISC-V OpenSBI startup with such firmware placement and a later tail access/reuse. **Confidence:** high that the declared extent is discarded for these two later operations and that the stated conditional behaviors follow from their source paths; low that current firmware reaches either trigger. Use the recorded DTB extent for both mapping and reservation. Source-only; no DTB, allocation, or boot was used.

<a id="ek9098"></a>
### EK9098 — AArch64 Raspberry Pi boot tags can exceed the fixed tag buffer.

**Finding:** The selected Raspberry Pi AArch64 bootstrap reserves `BOOT_TAGS_SIZE = 64 * 16` bytes for tags, matching the 1,024-byte `bm_boottags` member in `struct bcm2708bootmem`; on this 64-bit target that holds 64 `TagItem`s (`arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/include/boot.h:13-17`; `include/bcm2708_boot.h:28-42`). `boot()` starts `boottag` at that array (`boot.c:416-421`). `query_memory()` emits two entries for every nonzero tuple in `/memory/reg` and has no check against the tag-area capacity (`boot.c:274-321`). The later mandatory path emits at least 12 more entries for a valid DTB/kernel boot: DebugUartBase, Platform, PeripheralBase, BootLoader, the two protection-area tags, FlattenedDeviceTree, three kernel-bound tags, OpenFirmwareTree, and TAG_DONE (`:582-610,707-709,761-767,928-940,958-968,1044-1053,1070-1071`). Thus 27 nonzero memory tuples produce at least 66 entries, writing the final two `TagItem`s past the 64-entry array and into the adjacent bootstrap stack area. Optional VideoCore-memory, framebuffer, and command-line tags can lower the tuple count needed to overflow.

**Trigger and consequence:** firmware supplies a valid memory `reg` property with at least 27 nonzero ranges (or fewer ranges plus enough optional tags). The unchecked tag writes then extend into the neighboring reserved stack storage; this can corrupt stack contents used by the continuing bootstrap. The tag list is subsequently passed to the kernel (`boot.c:1088`). The checked-in code establishes no normal Pi firmware DTB with this many memory ranges, and this review did not establish the exact live stack overlap or a resulting boot failure. **Affected configuration:** AArch64 Raspberry Pi bootstrap with sufficiently many nonzero firmware memory tuples. **Confidence:** high for the fixed capacity, unbounded per-range writes, and arithmetic overflow threshold; low for deployed-firmware reachability and the concrete runtime consequence. Bound the tag emission or size the area from the actual maximum range count. Source-only; no DTB, boot, or stack was used.

<a id="ek9100"></a>
### EK9100 — ExecSMP exception dispatch silently drops handlers after the eighth on a vector

`krnAddExceptionHandler()` validates only that the exception number is in range, allocates a node, and inserts it at the head of that exception's list; it imposes no per-vector handler limit (`rom/kernel/addexceptionhandler.c:97-127`). In ExecSMP, `krnRunExceptionHandlers()` snapshots callbacks into a fixed eight-entry array. Once full, it logs and skips each remaining matching handler, then invokes only the copied callbacks (`addexceptionhandler.c:157-185`). Registration has already returned a non-NULL handle, so the registering client is not told that its callback will be omitted. The non-SMP path walks the full list (`:187-194`).

**Trigger and consequence:** in an ExecSMP build, more than eight non-NULL handlers are registered for one exception vector and that exception is dispatched. Because insertion is at the list head, the newest eight are called and older handlers are skipped; any skipped callback's exception handling or required side effect is absent on every dispatch while the chain remains over the cap. The handler API is documented as preliminary/private (`addexceptionhandler.c:38-61`). A repository-wide scan found no maintained selected registration combination that reaches nine handlers on one vector: the PC/APIC handlers use distinct vectors, optional x86-64 trap-debug installs one each on its listed vectors, and Hyper-V/VMM add only the separately documented second handlers at vectors 2 and 14. **Affected configuration:** ExecSMP only, with an external kernel module or future integration registering a ninth handler for a vector. **Confidence:** high that the cap silently drops callbacks after successful registration; low that any current in-tree configuration triggers it. Enforce the same limit during registration and return failure, or use a dynamically sized snapshot. Source-only; no exception was dispatched.

<a id="ek9101"></a>
### EK9101 — OpenSBI FDT parser uses a two-cell size default when root `#size-cells` is absent

`krnParseFDT()` initializes both root cell counts to two (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_fdt.c:70`). It overwrites them only when the corresponding depth-one properties are present (`:138-145`). For each depth-two `memory...` node's `reg` property, it computes each tuple width from those values and parses only complete tuples (`:146-166`). DTSpec §2.3.5 says a boot program should supply both properties on nodes with children, but says a client should assume a default of one for `#size-cells` when absent ([Devicetree Specification](https://devicetree-specification.readthedocs.io/en/stable/devicetree-basics.html#address-cells-and-size-cells)). With the parser's correct two-cell address default but incorrect two-cell size default, an ordinary 12-byte tuple containing a two-cell address and one-cell size is skipped because the parser expects 16 bytes. With no other accepted memory tuple, `mem_size` stays zero and `krnParseFDT()` returns failure (`kernel_fdt.c:257-261`).

**Trigger and consequence:** the RISC-V OpenSBI target receives an FDT whose root omits `#size-cells`, while its `/memory/reg` uses the specification's one-cell missing-property default. `kernel_cstart()` then uses the EFI scalar range if available, otherwise installs a fixed 128 MiB fallback (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_startup.c:515-568`). A later nonempty EFI region list replaces the parsed region list and may update the scalar bounds (`:575-596`), so this is not a claim that every UEFI boot loses its memory map. Without that later map, the system sees only the fallback range: memory outside it is unavailable, and a boot package outside the fallback range may not be loadable. **Affected configuration:** RISC-V OpenSBI startup on firmware that omits the root property; DTSpec-compliant boot programs are required to provide it, so this is a defensive interoperability case rather than a normal-compliant-firmware failure. No matching in-tree firmware DTB was found. **Confidence:** high for the default mismatch and parse/fallback path; low for current deployment likelihood. Use the specified default of one for missing `#size-cells`, independently of the address-cell default. Source-only; no DTB or boot was used.

<a id="ek9102"></a>
### EK9102 — AArch64 Raspberry Pi bootstrap waits forever on a full VideoCore mailbox transmit FIFO

`vcmb_write()` validates the message/channel, then spins while `VCMB_STATUS_WRITEREADY` remains set, with no timeout, yield, or failure return before writing to `VCMB_WRITE` (`arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/vc_mb.c:67-82`; bit definition in `arch/arm-native/soc/broadcom/2708/include/hardware/videocore.h:21-27`). The sibling mailbox resource bounds its transmit-full poll in `MBoxCall()` and reports failure when the budget expires (`arch/arm-native/soc/broadcom/2708/mbox/mbox_init.c:51-65`). The AArch64 read helper has a separate timeout and returns NULL, but that is reached only after the write succeeds (`vc_mb.c:24-64`).

The selected AArch64 boot manifest includes `vc_mb.c` (`arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/mmakefile.src:6-8`). There are eight `vcmb_write()` call sites outside `vc_mb.c`: the early serial clock query (`serialdebug.c:102-112`), framebuffer queries (`vc_fb.c:54,117,179`), VideoCore memory query (`boot.c:73-93`), and ARM clock queries/setting (`boot.c:131-180`). The helper's `vcmb_firmware_present()` function adds a ninth `vcmb_write()` call site (`vc_mb.c:87-100`), and the bootstrap calls that wrapper once (`boot.c:711-713`). In particular, `serInit()` calls the write before the bootstrap emits its first console message on BCM2836/37/2711-class boards (`boot.c:578-587`; `serialdebug.c:80-117`); BCM2712 skips that query but still reaches the later firmware-presence probe (`boot.c:711-718`).

**Trigger and consequence:** an AArch64 Raspberry Pi bootstrap call reaches `vcmb_write()` while the mailbox transmit-full status bit remains asserted. The busy loop never reaches a later read timeout or caller fallback, so bootstrap stops at that query. **Affected configuration:** the selected `arch/aarch64-raspi` boot image on Raspberry Pi 2/3/4/5 mailbox paths; the exact blocked call depends on SoC and startup stage. **Confidence:** high that the source has no bound or escape while the full bit stays asserted; hardware frequency and duration of that condition are unverified. Bound the poll and return failure so each caller can use its existing fallback or stop setup cleanly. Source-only; no mailbox hardware or boot was exercised.

<a id="ek9103"></a>
### EK9103 — The CHRP OpenFirmware bootstrap can write outside its stack buffer while reading `load-base`.

When the `/options` node is present, bootstrap calls `ofw_get_prop()` with a 20-byte local `str` buffer, then independently calls `ofw_get_prop_len()` and writes a terminator at `str[length]` without checking the result or the buffer bound (`arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/bootstrap.c:152-169`). The length query returns signed `-1` when the OpenFirmware service does not provide a result (`arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/of1275.c:123-145`); it may also report lengths larger than the 20-byte destination, while the preceding `getprop` is capped at 20 bytes (`of1275.c:147-170`).

**Trigger and consequence:** the CHRP OpenFirmware tree contains `/options`, and its `load-base` property is absent/failed or has a reported length of 20 bytes or more. The terminator assignment writes before or beyond the local stack array. A long property can overrun by more than one byte; the missing-property case writes at `str[-1]`. This can corrupt bootstrap stack data or fault before the loader proceeds.

**Affected configuration:** the explicitly buildable CHRP PPC Efika OpenFirmware bootstrap (`arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/mmakefile.src:4-15`; loader link and source selection in `arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/mmakefile.src:3-21`). The aggregate/boot ISO edges are commented, so default-image inclusion is not claimed. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked signed length and out-of-range index; occurrence depends on `/options/load-base` contents. Check the length is nonnegative and less than `sizeof(str)` before terminating or parsing. No firmware property or boot was exercised; source-only. See the [OpenFirmware `load-base` caller review](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L6579).

<a id="ek9104"></a>
### EK9104 — The CHRP OpenFirmware bootstrap dereferences the claim-failure sentinel in its small-allocation pool.

The __claim() allocator initializes its global small-allocation pool by assigning the result of ofw_claim(0, 4096, 4096) to mempool. The firmware wrapper initializes the result to (void *)-1 and returns that sentinel when the claim service does not supply a base address. Although the initializer skips writing pool metadata for that sentinel, it leaves mempool non-NULL. For requests smaller than 4096 - sizeof(pool_t), control then enters the pool branch and immediately reads p->free through p = mempool without checking the sentinel (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/of1275.c:375-407,434-456).

**Trigger and consequence:** the initial 4-KiB pool claim fails and a later small __claim() request is made. The selected bootstrap makes its first such request for debug_info and passes the result to new_list() (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/bootstrap.c:154-155). The sentinel dereference can fault or otherwise prevent the boot loader from continuing. This is distinct from EK9411, which covers unchecked direct claims used by the boot-tag list and command-line buffer.

**Affected configuration:** the explicitly buildable CHRP PPC Efika OpenFirmware bootstrap (arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/mmakefile.src:4-15; loader link in arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/mmakefile.src:14-21). Its aggregate and boot-ISO edges are commented, so default-image inclusion is not claimed. **Confidence:** high for the sentinel publication and subsequent unchecked dereference; occurrence depends on the firmware claim failing. A fix should leave the pool uninitialized on claim failure and return NULL before entering the pool branch. No claim failure or boot was induced; source-only. See the [allocator and bootstrap trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L1600).

<a id="ek9105"></a>
### EK9105 — An Efika boot menu with more than 1,024 nonempty lines overwrites the parser's line-pointer table.

The parser stores pointers to the start of every nonempty line in a fixed global array, menu_lines[1024]. While scanning the loaded menu bytes, it appends each line pointer with menu_lines[menu_lines_cnt++] and has no capacity check (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/menu.c:28-31,161-185). load_menu() determines the byte count from the NUL-terminated image loaded at the fixed menu staging address, copies that many bytes, and returns success for a successfully claimed menu buffer (menu.c:90-131). Bootstrap calls parse_menu() on that success path (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/bootstrap.c:253-259).

**Trigger and consequence:** a successfully loaded menu contains at least 1,025 nonempty lines. The 1,025th pointer is written one element past menu_lines, corrupting adjacent bootstrap state before the parser processes the collected lines. Blank lines do not consume slots. The exact adjacent object and resulting boot symptom depend on link layout; no more specific consequence is claimed.

**Affected configuration:** the explicitly buildable CHRP PPC Efika OpenFirmware loader, which links menu.c (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/mmakefile.src:3-21; target declaration arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/mmakefile.src:4-15). The aggregate and boot-ISO edges are commented, so default-image inclusion is not claimed. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked 1,025th pointer write; whether a supplied menu reaches that line count is input-dependent. Bound the append by the array capacity or reject excess lines. No menu file or boot was used; source-only. See the [menu parser boundary trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L4299).

<a id="ek9106"></a>
### EK9106 — Efika bootstrap can call the kernel entry without successfully loading an image.

The bootstrap initializes kernel_phys_entry to the fixed KERNEL_PHYS_BASE address (0x07800000). The selected menu branch loads and relocates the kernel image only when execute_menu() returns a selection with kernel/module content. However, execute_menu() returns NULL when the user enters an invalid key for a multi-entry menu, and load_menu() can also return an error after both firmware load attempts fail. Both conditions bypass the guarded selection/load block; neither causes bootstrap() to return before it later constructs tags and calls kernel_phys_entry unconditionally (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/bootstrap.c:108,253-321,388-415; menu.c:41-87,90-131).

**Trigger and consequence:** either the menu file cannot be loaded, or a multi-entry menu receives input outside the accepted range. No selected kernel is loaded into the fixed kernel image region on these paths, but bootstrap still transfers control to 0x07800000 with boot tags. The target can therefore execute stale/uninitialized contents as the kernel entry and fail before a valid kernel starts. The claim is limited to those no-image paths; selected-image load failures with a non-NULL selection take the explicit error return at bootstrap.c:298-306.

**Affected configuration:** the explicitly buildable CHRP PPC Efika OpenFirmware loader (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/mmakefile.src:3-21; target declaration arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/mmakefile.src:4-15). The aggregate and boot-ISO edges are commented, so default-image inclusion is not claimed. **Confidence:** high that both paths reach the unconditional fixed-address call without a menu-selected image; the eventual machine symptom depends on the memory contents at that address. Return on menu-load or selection failure before the handoff. No menu input or boot was used; source-only. See the [no-image handoff trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L4302).

<a id="ek9107"></a>
### EK9107 — The Efika menu's parsed `default` entry is never selected automatically.

parse_menu() reads the default directive into default_option, and execute_menu() initializes selected from that value. But when multiple entries exist, execute_menu() always waits for a key; a valid key overwrites selected with the user choice, while an invalid key returns NULL. A single-entry menu bypasses the default and selects its only entry directly (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/menu.c:41-87,208-213).

**Trigger and consequence:** a multi-entry menu contains a default directive, as does the checked-in Efika menu (arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/menu.lst:3-4,6-12). The parsed default never selects an entry: boot still requires explicit valid input, and invalid input follows EK9106 no-image handoff. This is a menu behavior defect; the source does not establish whether the value is intended to be zero-based or one-based, so no indexing-convention claim is made.

**Affected configuration:** explicitly buildable CHRP PPC Efika OpenFirmware loader (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/mmakefile.src:3-21; arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/mmakefile.src:4-15). **Confidence:** high that the directive has no effect on multi-entry selection; the desired default-index convention is undocumented in-tree. Use the configured default when no key is supplied or a timeout expires. No menu input or boot was used; source-only. See the [directive and selection trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L4307).

<a id="ek9108"></a>
### EK9108 — The Efika menu's parsed `timeout` setting does not time out the boot prompt.

parse_menu() stores the timeout directive in timeout_option, and the checked-in Efika menu sets it to five (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/menu.c:200-205; arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/menu.lst:3). Source-wide search finds no read of timeout_option after parsing. For multiple entries, execute_menu() polls ofw_read() and issues a fixed 10-ms OpenFirmware delay only when the read returns an error; it has no elapsed-time check or timeout exit (menu.c:49-65). The wrapper returns the firmware read result or -1 on service-call failure (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/of1275.c:289-313).

**Trigger and consequence:** a multi-entry menu is displayed and no valid key is received. The configured timeout does not select the default or continue boot; the prompt remains in its read/retry path until input arrives, and invalid input returns NULL as covered by EK9106. The source establishes the missing timeout behavior but not the intended policy after expiry.

**Affected configuration:** explicitly buildable CHRP PPC Efika OpenFirmware loader; the checked-in Efika menu exercises the directive (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/mmakefile.src:3-21; arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/mmakefile.src:4-15; menu.lst:3). **Confidence:** high that timeout_option is unused and no deadline is implemented; firmware read timing is external. Apply the configured deadline and defined expiry behavior in the prompt loop. No timer, input or boot was run; source-only. See the [directive and prompt trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L4307).

<a id="ek9109"></a>
### EK9109 — Efika menu parsing dereferences the firmware claim-failure sentinel for a new entry.

For each parsed title, parse_menu() stores the result of ofw_claim(NULL, sizeof(menu_entry_t), 4) into menu_entries while incrementing menu_entries_cnt, then immediately writes the entry fields without checking the claim result (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/menu.c:215-227). The selected ofw_claim() wrapper initializes and returns (void *)-1 when firmware does not provide a claimed address (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/of1275.c:434-456).

**Trigger and consequence:** a successfully loaded menu contains a title directive and the corresponding OpenFirmware claim fails. The first field initialization dereferences the failure sentinel, preventing normal menu parsing and boot; the count has already advanced to include the invalid entry.

**Affected configuration:** the explicitly buildable CHRP PPC Efika OpenFirmware loader, which links menu.c (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/mmakefile.src:3-21; arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/mmakefile.src:4-15). **Confidence:** high for the unchecked sentinel dereference; occurrence depends on firmware claim failure. Check the result before publishing/incrementing the menu entry. No claim failure or menu was exercised; source-only. See the [menu entry allocation trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L4307).

<a id="ek9111"></a>
### EK9111 — Efika ELF debug-symbol registration dereferences failed metadata allocations.

After all loadable sections and relocations are processed, load_elf_file() allocates a module record and checks that allocation and the module-name allocation. It does not check the separate __claim() results for the copied symbol string table or individual symbol_t records (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/elf.c:295-326,348-364). __claim() can return NULL when a direct claim fails or when a pool extension fails (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/of1275.c:391-431). The string-table path immediately passes the unchecked result to memcpy; the executable-symbol path immediately stores through the unchecked symbol pointer.

**Trigger and consequence:** a successfully loaded ELF image has a non-section-name string table, or executable symbols to register, and the corresponding metadata allocation fails. The string-table case reaches memcpy with a NULL destination; the symbol-node case dereferences NULL while initializing the node. In either case symbol registration can fault after the image's loadable sections have already been written. If the checked module record or module-name allocation fails instead, those paths are skipped and this finding does not apply.

**Affected configuration:** the explicitly buildable CHRP PPC Efika OpenFirmware loader; its selected menu loads ELF kernels and modules through load_elf_file() (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/mmakefile.src:3-21; arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/bootstrap.c:269-286; target declaration arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/mmakefile.src:4-15). **Confidence:** high for both unchecked allocation uses; occurrence requires a symbol-bearing image and the relevant allocation failure. Check each allocation and either stop registration cleanly or omit the affected metadata. No image or allocation failure was exercised; source-only. See the [ELF symbol metadata trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L4314).

<a id="ek9112"></a>
### EK9112 — Efika ELF section placement has no boundary check against the claimed 16-MiB image area.

The Efika bootstrap claims the 16-MiB kernel area at 0x07000000-0x07ffffff, while the ELF loader initializes both placement cursors at KERNEL_PHYS_BASE (0x07800000), the midpoint (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/bootstrap.c:194-199; arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/elf.c:25-26; support.h:100-103). For every nonempty SHF_ALLOC section, load_hunk() aligns and advances ptr_ro upward for read-only sections or moves ptr_rw downward for writable sections, then copies or zeroes section->size bytes through the resulting address. Neither path checks the cursor against the claimed region (elf.c:82-119). These static cursors persist as load_elf_file() is called for the kernel and subsequent modules (bootstrap.c:269-286).

**Trigger and consequence:** the cumulative selected ELF sections require more than the available 8 MiB above the midpoint for read-only sections, or more than 8 MiB below it for writable sections, including alignment padding. The corresponding cursor crosses the 16-MiB claim boundary, but the loader still copies/zeros at that address and continues relocating. This can overwrite memory outside the reserved image area or fault; no particular neighboring object or eventual boot symptom is asserted.

**Affected configuration:** the explicitly buildable CHRP PPC Efika OpenFirmware loader and its selected ELF kernel/module path (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/mmakefile.src:3-21; bootstrap.c:269-286; arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/mmakefile.src:4-15). **Confidence:** high that the placement cursors are unchecked against the claimed region; occurrence depends on aggregate section sizes/alignment in the loaded ELF set. Reject a placement that exceeds the reservation before copying or zeroing. No oversized image or boot was used; source-only. See the [ELF section placement trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L4317).

<a id="ek9113"></a>
### EK9113 — The Efika ELF loader trusts section-table offsets and sizes without validating them against the loaded image.

The loader accepts an ELF input after checking only the four magic bytes, ET_REL type, and EM_PPC machine value; load_elf_file() receives a file pointer but no file length (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/elf.c:59-76,231-248). It forms the section-header pointer from eh->shoff and loops eh->shnum entries without validating the table extent. Section offsets and sizes are then trusted when SHF_ALLOC data is copied by read_block(), and symbol/string/relocation tables are addressed from their supplied offsets and sizes without checking that they lie inside the loaded image (elf.c:51-54,82-119,248-291). The selected direct kernel and module/package callers pass the staging pointer without a byte count (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/bootstrap.c:48-86,269-286).

**Trigger and consequence:** a selected firmware-loaded ELF has a valid minimal header but a truncated or inconsistent section table, section extent, or relocation metadata. The loader can read beyond the loaded file/staging contents and may copy those bytes into kernel memory or use malformed table indexes during relocation. The exact read/write extent and resulting failure depend on the ELF fields and adjacent memory; no specific crash or corruption target is asserted.

**Affected configuration:** the explicitly buildable CHRP PPC Efika OpenFirmware loader and its ELF kernel/module path (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/mmakefile.src:3-21; arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/bootstrap.c:48-86,269-286; arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/mmakefile.src:4-15). **Confidence:** high that input length and table/section extents are not checked; occurrence requires malformed or truncated selected ELF data. Pass the actual loaded byte count into the loader and validate all table arithmetic and extents before dereferencing or copying. Package container length parsing is tracked separately as EK9115. No image or boot was used; source-only. See the [ELF input extent trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L4320).

<a id="ek9114"></a>
### EK9114 — Unbounded Efika boot strings overrun fixed command buffers.

The selected OpenFirmware support sprintf() writes every literal, character, and formatted string to dest without a capacity parameter or bound check, then appends a terminator (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/support.c:143-196). Bootstrap uses it to assemble firmware load commands in a 1,024-byte stack buffer from bootpath and menu kernel/module paths (arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/bootstrap.c:263-285). Neither source string has a corresponding length cap. It also concatenates a selected menu command-line remainder and bootargs into a 10,240-byte buffer allocated for KRN_CmdLine (bootstrap.c:203,309-317; menu parser: arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/menu.c:245-277). The menu parser retains that remainder without a per-line length limit.

**Trigger and consequence:** either a load command's bootpath plus selected kernel/module path exceeds the 1,024-byte destination, or a selected command-line remainder plus bootargs exceeds the successfully allocated 10,240-byte command-line buffer. The custom formatter writes past the destination in either case. The stack case can corrupt bootstrap locals; the command-line case can overwrite memory after the claimed buffer before the pointer is passed to the kernel. Exact adjacent state and resulting boot symptom are not established. If the 10,240-byte allocation itself fails, that separate unchecked-claim path is EK9411.

**Affected configuration:** the explicitly buildable CHRP PPC Efika OpenFirmware loader (`arch/ppc-chrp/boot/openfirmware/src/mmakefile.src:3-21`; `arch/ppc-chrp/efika/boot/mmakefile.src:4-15`). **Confidence:** high that formatting is unbounded and both destinations are fixed-size; occurrence depends on selected path/command-line lengths. Use bounded formatting and reject values that do not fit. No long path, menu line or boot was used; source-only. See the [formatted boot-command bounds trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L4323).

<a id="ek9115"></a>
