In the matching-signature branch, `my_iteration()` assigns `malloc(e->len)` directly to `d->entry` and unconditionally copies into it (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/cdrom.c:244-249`). If that allocation fails, `memcpy()` receives a NULL destination. `get_entry()` uses this callback for initial root `RR` detection and directory-name `NM` searches (`:254-270,332-337,562-568`), so the failure is reachable during optional CD boot setup and path lookup. The existing `e->len` source-extent issue is separately tracked as EK9223.

**Trigger and consequence:** in the explicitly built Parthenope Sam440 CD backend, a matching SUSP entry is found while its copy allocation fails. The immediate copy through a NULL destination can stop setup or the current lookup. **Affected configuration:** explicit optional `parthenope-sam440`; the active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` rule depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`), selecting this path when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked allocation and subsequent copy; occurrence depends on allocation failure for a matching entry. Check the allocation and return a distinct scan error before copying. No allocation failure, CD, or boot was exercised; source-only. See the [Parthenope SUSP entry-copy trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5049).

<a id="ek9225"></a>
### EK9225 — CD path lookup dereferences unchecked allocations on memory pressure.

`fs_cdrom_find_file()` allocates a copy of the requested path and immediately copies into it without checking the result (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/cdrom.c:291-292`). During directory iteration, the non-Rock-Ridge fallback similarly allocates `dirent.namelen + 1` bytes and passes the pointer to `cdrom_read()` before checking allocation success (`:372-380`). Thus allocation failure can cause a NULL destination in `memcpy()` for every lookup, or a NULL read destination when a directory entry needs its on-disc name. The function is called by the CD file loader (`:446-456`), which supplies kernel, menu, module and initrd filenames from the selected boot flow (`parthenope.c:131,186,290,373`; `menu.c:590-596`).

**Trigger and consequence:** explicitly built Parthenope Sam440 performs CD path lookup and one of these allocations fails. The unchecked use can fault during lookup, disrupting the current boot file/menu operation. **Affected configuration:** explicit optional `parthenope-sam440`; the active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` rule depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`), selecting this path when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the missing checks and pointer use; occurrence depends on memory pressure. Check both allocation results and return a lookup error while releasing already-owned temporary storage. No low-memory condition, CD, or boot was exercised; source-only. See the [Parthenope CD lookup allocation trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L4994).

<a id="ek9226"></a>
### EK9226 — Concurrent `InternalFlush` calls can both pass the flag check and write the same buffered bytes.

`InternalFlush()` waits while `FHF_FLUSHING` is set and then sets the bit in a separate, explicitly noted non-atomic operation (`rom/dos/internalflush.c:25-38`). Two tasks flushing the same write-mode `FileHandle` can therefore both observe the bit clear before either sets it, snapshot the same positive `fh_Pos`, and submit the same buffered bytes through `Write()` (`:40-55`). If one flush resets `fh_Pos` to zero before the other reaches its cleanup, the latter takes the concurrent-data branch and subtracts its older positive snapshot from the now-zero position (`:57-78`). In the 32-bit layout this can produce a negative position; in the 64-bit layout arithmetic can wrap. Subsequent buffered `FWriteChars()` uses `fh_Pos` as a buffer index (`rom/dos/fwrite.c:150-164`; `compiler/include/dos/dosextens.h:293-335`).

**Trigger and consequence:** two tasks share a buffered write-mode handle and enter flush while the flag is clear, with an interleaving that lets both pass the check. The handler may receive duplicate bytes; after the competing cleanup, later buffered writes may use a corrupted position. The selected animation datatype passes `Output()` to two asynchronous children (`workbench/classes/datatypes/animation/animationclass.c:210,231`), but this review has not established that those children overlap flushes on a shared handle, so it is not cited as a demonstrated trigger. **Affected configuration:** DOS clients sharing one write handle; occurrence requires concurrent callers and a suitable scheduling interleaving. **Confidence:** high that the check/set is not serialized and that competing cleanup can corrupt `fh_Pos`; handler-visible duplication depends on the concurrent call sequence. Protect the check, flag transition, position snapshot and buffer accounting with per-handle serialization. No shared handle, concurrent task, or handler write was exercised; source-only. See the [InternalFlush caller and interleaving trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5053).

<a id="ek9227"></a>
### EK9227 — Parthenope accepts short multi-block CD reads as complete file data.

`block_dev_desc_t.block_read` is a count-returning U-Boot callback (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/uboot.h:49-51`), not a Boolean success result. U-Boot's block API defines the result as the number of blocks read and permits fewer blocks than requested ([U-Boot block API](https://docs.u-boot.org/en/stable/api/part.html); legacy driver callback description in [U-Boot `systemace.c`](https://nest-open-source.googlesource.com/manifest_repos/u-boot/+/5e15fb1fe70ac2857e056ad5d238ad8e3373fdb5/drivers/block/systemace.c)). In `cdrom_read()`, the whole-block branch requests `length / 2048` blocks but checks only whether the result is zero (`cdrom.c:147-152`). Any positive short count is treated as if every requested block had been filled: the function accounts for and advances over the requested count (`:154-157`) and returns success (`:177`). The local `transferred` variable is not used to report the actual number copied.

The selected file loader further discards `cdrom_read()`'s return and returns the ISO directory's advertised file size (`cdrom.c:446-456`). Selected Parthenope consumers reject only negative results and then parse/load the destination using that advertised size: the module path calls `load_elf_file()` (`parthenope.c:184-192`), while menu loading passes the full positive count to its parser (`menu.c:589-596`). Thus a positive short multi-block completion can leave the remainder of the destination without bytes from the requested file while downstream code treats it as complete. This is distinct from EK536's zero/failed-read result handling.

**Trigger and consequence:** the explicitly built Parthenope Sam440 target uses a CD block callback that returns a positive count smaller than a multi-block request. The local checkout does not contain the selected U-Boot callback implementation, so this trigger is permitted by the callback's count contract but not confirmed for a particular Sam440 CD driver. Affected consumers can parse incomplete/stale destination contents as the complete menu, module, or image. **Affected configuration:** explicit `parthenope-sam440`; the active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` rule depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`), selecting this path when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked count and propagation; medium for occurrence of a positive short count from a selected firmware driver. Require the returned block count to equal the request, and propagate read failure/actual byte count from `fs_cdrom_load_file()`. No media, firmware callback, short read, or boot was exercised; source-only. See the [CD reader caller and callback trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L12071).

<a id="ek9228"></a>
### EK9228 — Parthenope reads ISO directory names and System Use Areas without validating the record length.

`fs_cdrom_find_file()` enters its directory loop whenever `offset < size`, then reads a full `struct iso9660_dir` without checking that the remaining directory extent contains that fixed header (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/cdrom.c:303-317`). For a nonzero record, it derives `nameoffset`, `sua_off`, and `sua_size` from the fixed structure and untrusted `dirent.namelen`/`dirent.len`, without requiring the name, alignment byte, and SUA to fit within the declared record or directory extent (`:319-327`). It reads `namelen` bytes at `offset + sizeof(dirent)` and later advances by `dirent.len` (`:372-380,414`); neither operation validates the record boundary. With Rock Ridge enabled, the derived SUA range is passed to `get_entry()` and its iterator (`:332-337`; `:254-270`; `:180-235`), also without checking that it lies within the containing directory record.

A malformed/truncated directory can therefore make the parser consume bytes belonging to a following record or beyond the declared directory extent as an identifier or SUSP data. A short `dirent.len` can also make the computed SUA length negative before it is converted to the iterator's unsigned `size` parameter. These reads and calculations are separate from EK9222's non-progressing SUSP-entry cases, EK9223's unchecked copy from a matching entry, and EK532's fixed destination-buffer capacity issue.

**Trigger and consequence:** the explicitly built Parthenope Sam440 CD backend scans a directory containing a truncated or internally inconsistent ISO directory record. Lookup can compare a name or Rock Ridge name derived from bytes outside the record and can accept an incorrect next-component block/size, causing later file lookup or loading to use the wrong extent. **Affected configuration:** explicit `parthenope-sam440`; the active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` rule depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`), selecting this path when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the absent extent/record checks and cross-boundary reads; the particular incorrect lookup outcome depends on malformed media bytes. Validate fixed-header availability and require record length, identifier/padding, SUA offset/size, and directory remaining length to be mutually consistent before reading or advancing. No image or boot was used; source-only. See the [CD parser source and caller ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L12074).

<a id="ek9229"></a>
### EK9229 — The m68k Hunk loader reports success when the input ends before all Hunk records are parsed.

`M68KEmu_LoadHunksFromMemory()` reads the declared hunk count and sizes, allocates their guest ranges, and parses records while at least one type word remains (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_memory.c:293-323`). `HUNK_END` increments the current hunk index, but reaching EOF simply exits the loop; there is no final check that all declared hunks received an end marker (`:368-384`). The common success tail records and returns the first hunk address even when the record stream ended early. Its `fail` cleanup is only taken by explicit parse/allocation checks.

The selected `RunFile()` caller passes the whole file to this parser and treats any nonzero entry as a successfully loaded program, then invokes `setup_and_execute()` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_run.c:207-232`). A truncated but otherwise accepted Hunk header/size table and first hunk can therefore cause an incomplete image to be started instead of rejected. The separate runtime disk-library caller also uses this parser, but subsequent resident-tag validation may reject some truncated libraries; the concrete demonstrated caller path here is `RunFile()`.

**Trigger and consequence:** an explicitly built/loaded m68kemu receives a Hunk file whose header and hunk-size table are accepted but whose record stream reaches EOF before all declared hunks have ended. `RunFile()` treats the first allocated hunk address as success and enters guest execution with missing or partial hunk contents, so the program can fail during startup or execute incomplete data. **Affected configuration:** optional `m68kemu.library` on supported hosted targets, through its `RunFile()` API; no default-image inclusion is claimed. **Confidence:** high for parser success after premature EOF and the selected nonzero-result caller; the resulting guest behavior depends on the missing records and hunk contents. Reject EOF until the parser has consumed all declared hunk records and their required `HUNK_END`s. No Hunk file or guest program was loaded; source-only. See the [Hunk parser caller reconciliation](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5069).

<a id="ek9230"></a>
### EK9230 — WITHDRAWN: resident-name length overflow does not stall the m68k Hunk loader.

The earlier candidate treated `p += n * 4` as the only progress in the resident-name loop. Re-reading the exact order shows that `rd32(&p)` advances `p` by four bytes before the multiplication and skip (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_memory.c:285-291`). For `n == 0x40000000`, the 32-bit product wraps to zero, but the next loop iteration reads the following word and advances another four bytes; the parser does not reread the same length field indefinitely. The loop is bounded by `p + 4 <= end`. A wrapped skip can desynchronize interpretation of malformed header words, but this review did not establish a separate concrete caller-visible consequence. Withdraw the non-progress/hang claim; do not count EK9230 as an active finding. Source-only; no malformed file was loaded.

<a id="ek9231"></a>
### EK9231 — An overflowing argument length can turn a small guest allocation into a huge native copy.

`setup_and_execute()` passes `argSize + 1` to the guest allocator but, on a nonzero result, copies the original `argSize` bytes (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_run.c:64-70`). The guest allocator rounds with `(size + 3) & ~3` and then adds its header without overflow checks (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_memory.c:62-103`). With 32-bit `ULONG`, `argSize == 0xfffffffc` makes the call argument `0xfffffffd`; the allocator's `+3` wraps to zero, so `needed` becomes only the small allocation header and can be satisfied from the initially available guest heap. The following `CopyMem()` still uses `0xfffffffc` and writes that many bytes starting at the small guest allocation inside the fixed 32 MiB context arena (`m68kemu_memory.c:19-27`; `m68kemu_intern.h:108-113`).

Both public runner entry points reach this helper: `RunHunk()` (`m68kemu_run.c:138-178`) and `RunFile()` (`:191-229`). Their selected DOS callers derive lengths from command/process argument buffers, and the existing caller census found no near-`ULONG_MAX` in-tree length; this is therefore not claimed as a normal command-line trigger.

**Trigger and consequence:** an optional m68kemu client calls `RunHunk()` or `RunFile()` with a caller-valid argument buffer and a length near the 32-bit maximum that wraps the allocator rounding as above. The small guest allocation is followed by a copy much larger than the 32 MiB guest-memory region, so the copy can write beyond the emulator's allocated context memory and corrupt adjacent native memory or fault. **Affected configuration:** explicitly built `m68kemu.library` on supported hosted targets; its parent aggregate edges are commented out. **Confidence:** high for the arithmetic and oversized copy; low practical reachability because no checked-in caller supplies such a buffer/length and a caller-valid buffer must span the requested range. Reject lengths that overflow the allocation arithmetic and require the allocation to cover the exact copy before copying. No runner, large buffer, copy, or build was used; source-only. See the [argument-size and selected-caller recheck](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L6448).

<a id="ek9232"></a>
### EK9232 — WITHDRAWN: duplicate of EK9473.

This ID initially recorded the `m68k_read32()` high-address wrap and a selected tag-conversion caller. The later full accessor pass verified that the same unchecked `addr + width - 1` arithmetic also affects the inline 16/32-bit helpers and the selected Moira word callbacks; those shared causes and caller paths are consolidated under [EK9473](#ek9473). EK9232 adds no independent trigger or consequence and is withdrawn to avoid duplicate active findings. The 2026-10-28 accessor recheck is recorded in the [coverage ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L8591). Source-only; no guest access was run.

<a id="ek9233"></a>
### EK9233 — Parthenope's ELF loader trusts section-table and section-data extents beyond the loaded file.

`load_elf_file()` accepts an `ET_REL`/`EM_PPC` header but is not given the loaded file length (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/elf.c:53-64,220-235`; declaration in `elf.h:32`). It forms the section-table pointer directly from `eh->shoff` and iterates `eh->shnum` fixed `struct sheader` entries without validating the table extent or the declared entry size (`elf.c:237-260`). For each allocated section, `load_hunk()` copies `sh->size` bytes from `file + sh->offset` unless the type is `SHT_NOBITS`, with no check that the source range lies inside the loaded file (`:45-48,69-107`). String and symbol table section addresses are likewise set to `file + sh->offset` and later consumed by relocation/debug-symbol code (`:242-244,263-273,296-340`) without a file-extent check.

Both in-tree callers use this unchecked entry point. The AROS boot path calls it first for the kernel and then for each module (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/parthenope.c:168-194`). The boot-device interface returns a loaded length, but the caller discards it before invoking the ELF loader (`device.h:26-29`; `parthenope.c:372-379,184-190`). The backing kernel/module buffers have fixed capacities, but this finding concerns section metadata extending past the actual bytes loaded, independently of EK532's oversized-file-to-destination-capacity path and EK9234/EK9260's placement limits.

**Trigger and consequence:** the explicitly built Parthenope Sam440 path passes an `ET_REL`/`EM_PPC` file whose section table or referenced non-NOBITS section/string/symbol extent exceeds the bytes actually loaded. The parser reads beyond the file image; depending on offsets and backing allocation, it can consume unrelated/stale memory, fault, or copy unintended bytes into the loaded section before relocation and handoff. **Affected configuration:** explicit `parthenope-sam440`; the active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` target depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`), selecting this path when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the absent input-length propagation and unchecked extents; exact failure depends on malformed file metadata and memory layout. Pass the loaded length into `load_elf_file()` and validate the ELF header, complete section table, and every referenced file extent with overflow-safe range checks before pointer formation or copy. No ELF file, boot, or build was used; source-only. See the [Parthenope ELF caller and bounds ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L12089).

<a id="ek9234"></a>
### EK9234 — Parthenope's ELF placement can run past the Sam440's fixed 16 MiB low-memory window.

The Parthenope ELF loader initializes its persistent read-only section cursor at `KERNEL_PHYS_BASE` (`0x00800000`) and advances it by each aligned allocated read-only section's size without an upper-bound check (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/elf.c:26,83-90`; constant in `support.h:105`). After loading the kernel and modules, the AROS handoff publishes that cursor as `KRN_KernelHighest` (`parthenope.c:163-203`). Sam440 startup rounds the tag value to 64 KiB and passes `0x01000000 - memLowest` as the initial RAM header size (`arch/ppc-sam440/kernel/kernel_startup.c:180-189`). If the cursor exceeds 16 MiB, this subtraction wraps as an unsigned address-sized value; the bootloader has already placed sections beyond the intended low-memory interval, and startup may construct a bogus overlapping memory range. Exact downstream behavior depends on the resulting value and platform memory layout.

At exactly `0x01000000`, startup supplies a zero-size first RAM header; above it, the `0x01000000 - memLowest` arithmetic wraps in `IPTR` (`kernel_startup.c:184-189`). `krnCreateMemHeader()` nevertheless writes the header and first `MemChunk`, subtracting `MEMHEADER_TOTAL` from that size (`rom/kernel/kernel_memory.c:51-69`), before the resident scanner and Exec-base setup consume it (`rom/kernel/prepareexecbase.c:17-41`). Startup later adds the post-16-MiB Fast RAM range at `0x01000000` (`kernel_startup.c:209-216`), so the malformed first header can also overlap the range subsequently advertised as Fast RAM.

**Trigger and consequence:** the explicitly built Parthenope Sam440 AROS boot path loads enough aligned read-only kernel/module sections for the cursor to reach or pass `0x01000000`. Starting from `0x00800000`, this means at least 8 MiB of aggregate read-only placement, plus any per-section alignment. No checked-in production artifact establishes that the selected image reaches this threshold, so default-image reachability remains unverified. **Affected configuration:** explicit optional `parthenope-sam440`; the active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` target depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`), selecting this path when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked cursor, zero/wrapped size and unconditional header writes; image-size reachability and subsequent manifestation are conditional. Bound each placement to the available low-memory interval and reject images that exceed it before publishing tags. EK9233 covers malformed ELF file extents; EK9260 has been consolidated here because it described this same read-only 16 MiB cursor and size-wrap chain, not a separate writable-cursor issue. No image or boot was used; source-only. See the [Parthenope placement and MemHeader trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5284).

<a id="ek9235"></a>
### EK9235 — Parthenope passes an uninitialized or incomplete initrd to U-Boot after load failure.

When a Linux-format menu entry specifies an initrd, `testboot_linux()` allocates an 18 MiB buffer, calls the selected device's `load_file()` and ignores its result. It then sets `argc` to 3, formats that buffer's address as `argv[2]`, and invokes `bootm()` unconditionally (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/parthenope.c:100-138`, especially `:129-137`). The menu parser supplies `entry->initrd` from the configured `initrd` field (`menu.c:420-422,515-524`). The common `boot_dev_t.load_file` contract returns an `int` (`device.h:26-29`); checked local backends can report missing/read-failed data, and the CD backend has the separate positive-size-on-read-failure case recorded under EK536.

**Trigger and consequence:** the explicitly built Parthenope Linux boot path selects an entry with an initrd and its file load fails or returns incomplete data. The code still asks U-Boot to boot with the allocated destination as the initrd, so startup may fail or consume an incomplete image. **Affected configuration:** explicit optional `parthenope-sam440`, Linux-format menu entry with an initrd; actual backend and failure behavior determine reachability. The active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` rule depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`), selecting this path when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high that the load status is ignored and the initrd argument is always passed; exact U-Boot response is not established. Check the load result and only pass a fully loaded initrd. No initrd, device failure, U-Boot boot, or image was exercised; source-only. See the [Parthenope Linux initrd caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5084).

<a id="ek9236"></a>
### EK9236 — PC bootstrap GNU archive-name references are not bounded by the long-name table.

For a GNU ar member whose name field contains `/offset`, `ar_name()` parses the decimal offset, adds it to the `//` long-name table payload, then scans until slash or newline without knowing the table's declared size or the containing module end (`arch/all-pc/bootstrap/bootstrap.c:254-271`). `ar_data()` verifies only the archive magic and skips a BSD extended name; it does not return or validate a payload extent (`:211-224`). The archive scan calls this resolver for every member (`:422-437`), then uses the returned string to prepare and name ELF modules (`:439-444`).

**Trigger and consequence:** a boot archive contains a GNU long-name reference whose offset is outside its `//` table, or a referenced name lacks a terminating slash/newline within the table. The resolver reads beyond the name table and copies the scanned span into a new string; this can consume bytes from following archive data or beyond the module extent and produce an invalid module name. **Affected configuration:** selected i386/x86-64 PC bootstrap when bootloader-provided modules include an ar archive; the bootstrap source is selected by `arch/all-pc/bootstrap/mmakefile.src`. **Confidence:** high for missing table/module extent checks; malformed archive required. Validate the offset against the `//` payload length and bound the delimiter scan to the remaining table bytes and module extent. EK9031 separately covers archive member/header extents. No archive or boot was parsed; source-only. See the [PC bootstrap archive-name trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5087).

<a id="ek9237"></a>
### EK9237 — The 32-bit Raspberry Pi boot maps the high kernel image to the wrong physical offset when the firmware memory end is not 1 MiB aligned.

The boot code rounds the firmware-reported RAM upper address down to 4 KiB, then rounds total read-only and writable image reservations up to 1 MiB before subtracting them from that endpoint (`arch/arm-raspi/boot/boot.c:483-499,552-557`). Thus `kernel_phys` can remain only 4 KiB aligned. The loader clears and fills the image at that address, then unmaps the covering sections and calls `mmu_map_section()` for the high virtual kernel mapping (`:556-559,583-590`). That mapper aligns the virtual start to 1 MiB and encodes the physical base after `phys >>= 20`, discarding its lower 20 bits (`arch/arm-raspi/boot/mmu.c:80-105`). The `/memory/reg` setup accepts a 4 KiB-aligned endpoint without rounding it to a 1 MiB boundary (`boot.c:354-362`).

**Trigger and consequence:** ARM32 Raspberry Pi firmware supplies a usable memory endpoint that is 4 KiB aligned but not 1 MiB aligned, and boot proceeds through the high-kernel remap. The kernel image is loaded at an offset within a physical 1 MiB section, while the descriptor maps the virtual image base to the beginning of that section; the entry address can therefore fetch different bytes than those loaded as the kernel. **Affected configuration:** 32-bit `arm-raspi` boot path. **Confidence:** high for the alignment mismatch in the selected code; the firmware endpoint and resulting boot behavior were not observed. Align or otherwise preserve the physical low bits when constructing section mappings, or reject incompatible placement. No firmware, device tree or boot was used; source-only. See the [Raspberry Pi boot mapping trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5132).

<a id="ek9238"></a>
### EK9238 — RISC-V OpenSBI can consume an ordinary `ebreak` as an unsupported scheduler syscall.

The OpenSBI trap classifier treats every breakpoint with `SysBase` present and saved `a7 <= 0x100` as a scheduler syscall, advances `sepc` over the instruction, and returns `TRAP_SYSCALL` (`arch/riscv64-opensbi/kernel/kernel_traps.c:224-235`). The outer trap handler then passes that same `a7` value to `core_SysCall()` (`:155-178`). The shared syscall IDs include `SC_CLI == 4`, but the selected generic `core_SysCall()` switch handles only IDs 0 through 3 (`rom/kernel/kernel_syscall.h:15-30`; `rom/kernel/kernel_intr.c:61-81`). Thus a breakpoint with `a7 == SC_CLI` is advanced past and receives no ordinary breakpoint/exception handling. The RISC-V privileged ISA specifies that EBREAK raises a breakpoint exception; `a7` is not part of that instruction's meaning ([RISC-V privileged architecture specification](https://docs.riscv.org/reference/isa/priv/machine.html)). The task context's `a7` is available as a register value; this review found no ordinary in-tree `ebreak` producer, so the particular application path is not demonstrated by a maintained caller.

**Trigger and consequence:** on the RISC-V OpenSBI target after SysBase initialization, task code executes `ebreak` with `a7` holding an admitted but unsupported scheduler code (for example `SC_CLI`). The trap is silently consumed and execution resumes after the breakpoint instead of reaching the normal breakpoint exception path. Other admitted IDs may invoke scheduler cases, depending on value. **Affected configuration:** RISC-V OpenSBI kernel. **Confidence:** high for classifier/dispatcher mismatch; no in-tree ordinary breakpoint caller or runtime occurrence was established. Classify scheduler traps by the exact supported instruction/register convention or validate the syscall ID before stepping over the breakpoint; route other breakpoints through exception dispatch. No trap was executed; source-only. See the [OpenSBI syscall-ID trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5135).

<a id="ek9244"></a>
### EK9244 — `ftruncate()` returns success after RAMFS changes the current file position.

Both POSIXC `ftruncate()` and `ftruncate64()` save the shared FCB position, resize the file, then try to restore the saved offset; the restore result is ignored and success is returned (`compiler/crt/posixc/ftruncate.c:78-86,110-114`; identical logic in `ftruncate64.c`). RAMFS `ChangeFileSize()` clamps each open's position to the new file length when shrinking below it (`rom/filesys/ram/filesystem.c:741-756`). Its seek handler rejects attempts to seek beyond EOF (`rom/filesys/ram/commands.c:725-739`). Thus truncating a 100-byte RAMFS file while positioned at byte 80 to 50 bytes leaves the descriptor at byte 50: the saved offset cannot be restored, and the wrapper still returns 0.

**Trigger and consequence:** POSIXC `ftruncate()` or `ftruncate64()` is called on a RAMFS file with current offset greater than the new, smaller length. The file is truncated, but the descriptor offset changes to EOF despite the wrapper's explicit attempt to preserve it; callers that continue I/O observe a different position while receiving success. **Affected configuration:** POSIXC linked against the selected RAMFS handler; both truncate variants share the behavior. **Confidence:** high for the two source paths and RAMFS position clamp/seek rejection. Preserve offsets past EOF if the filesystem/API supports it, or report a restoration failure rather than silently returning success. No file operation was run; source-only. See the [POSIXC/RAMFS truncate trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5164).

<a id="ek9245"></a>
### EK9245 — AArch64 Raspberry Pi boot can leave the upper part of a contiguous RAM range unmapped when it crosses 4 GiB.

`query_memory()` parses each `/memory/reg` tuple, publishes its full `[lower, upper)` range as `KRN_MEMLower`/`KRN_MEMUpper`, and passes the same range to `mmu_map_section()` (`arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/boot.c:277-321`). The mapper chooses its low-address PMD path based on the starting virtual address; `mmu_slot()` returns NULL for addresses at or above 4 GiB, and the low-path loop silently skips those entries (`arch/aarch64-raspi/boot/mmu.c:128-133,226-245,277-318`). A single tuple beginning below 4 GiB and extending above it therefore has only its low part mapped, while the kernel receives the full range. AArch64 startup passes that range to TLSF (`arch/aarch64-native/kernel/kernel_startup.c:331-359`), and `tlsf_add_memory()` registers the supplied byte extent (`rom/kernel/tlsf.c:1175-1225`), so allocations in the unmapped upper portion can fail when accessed.

**Trigger and consequence:** Raspberry Pi firmware supplies one contiguous `/memory/reg` tuple crossing 4 GiB and the boot proceeds. The unrepresented upper RAM is still advertised to the kernel allocator, creating the possibility that allocations land in unmapped addresses and fault. **Affected configuration:** AArch64 Raspberry Pi boot with such a firmware memory tuple. **Confidence:** high for the split behavior and full-range publication; no checked-in device tree establishes that firmware uses this tuple shape. The comments say Pi 4 firmware emits separate entries beyond its first GiB, but Pi 5/other supplied firmware remains unverified. Split crossing tuples at 4 GiB or map their upper portion through the high-address PUD path before publishing them. No FDT or boot was used; source-only. See the [AArch64 Raspberry Pi range trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5169).

<a id="ek9250"></a>
### EK9250 — Shell drops the final argument character when expanding an alias inside backticks.

`convertBackTicks()` copies the bytes between the opening and closing backticks into `embedIn` and passes that buffer to `checkLine()` without appending a newline (`workbench/c/Shell/convertBackTicks.c:36-49,88-92`). In `convertLine.c`, `readCommandR()` parses the command token; after recognizing an unquoted alias with `[]` substitution, it copies the remaining input using `in->len - in->cur - 1`, assuming the final byte is a newline (`:131-139,149-165,182-215`). The embedded buffer has no such trailing newline. `convertLine()` appends one only after alias expansion (`:321-332`). For example, an alias with `[]` invoked inside backticks as `say hello` splices `hell` rather than `hello` into the alias command.

**Trigger and consequence:** selected Shell processes an embedded backtick command that names an unquoted local alias containing `[]` and supplies a final argument; the final argument byte is omitted from the expanded command. **Affected configuration:** targets selecting the maintained Shell implementation; requires a configured alias and backtick command. **Confidence:** high for the no-newline input and unconditional one-byte subtraction; consequence depends on alias argument substitution in embedded commands. Normalize embedded input before alias expansion or subtract a byte only when the source actually ends in newline. No alias or command was run; source-only. See the [Shell alias/backtick trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5213).

<a id="ek9251"></a>
### EK9251 — Shell initialization reports success when resident segment creation or registration fails.

The Shell library initializer calls `CreateSegList(ShellStart)` but only enters command registration when it returns nonzero; either way it closes DOS and returns `TRUE` (`workbench/c/Shell/shell_init.c:58-83`). `CreateSegList()` documents and implements `BNULL` on allocation failure (`compiler/arossupport/createseglist.c:32-41,78-85`). When a segment is created, both `AddSegment()` results are ignored (`shell_init.c:71-78`); `AddSegment()` can return `FALSE` for a duplicate resident name or allocation failure (`rom/dos/addsegment.c:64-81`). The library can therefore complete initialization without registering `shell`, `CLI`, or either; if a segment is created but no registration succeeds, this initializer does not release it. On m68k, the two registrations use different segment lists; other targets pass the same list to both (`shell_init.c:73-78`).

**Trigger and consequence:** Shell library initialization encounters a failed segment allocation, or one/both resident registrations fail. Init still reports success, so callers may believe the Shell command names are available when they are absent; an allocated but unregistered segment can also remain unreleased. **Affected configuration:** targets selecting the maintained Shell library; m68k has a distinct `CLI` segment-registration path. **Confidence:** high for ignored failure results and unconditional success; occurrence depends on allocation/registration failure or a duplicate name. Propagate init failure and remove/free any segment whose registration fails, while accounting for whether another registration retained it. No allocation failure or resident-list operation was induced; source-only. See the [Shell resident initialization trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5993).

<a id="ek9252"></a>
### EK9252 — Deleting an unready player can leave a LOCATE transition waiting forever.

`SetConductorState(CONDSTATE_LOCATE)` stores its task in `cdt_Barrier`, then iterates the conductor's players and waits on `SIGF_SINGLE` until each player's `PLAYER_Ready` query reports true (`workbench/libs/realtime/setconductorstate.c:126-155`). `SetPlayerAttrsA(PLAYER_Ready=TRUE)` signals that barrier task (`setplayerattrsa.c:169-186`), but `DeletePlayer()` removes and frees the player without signaling the barrier or changing the readiness condition (`deleteplayer.c:63-88`). If the LOCATE caller is waiting for an unready player that is deleted, no corresponding ready signal is sent and the loop has no deletion/cancellation condition; it can remain blocked. The concurrent removal also means the waiting code may retain a pointer to the deleted player.

**Trigger and consequence:** an application calls `SetConductorState(..., CONDSTATE_LOCATE, ...)` while a player is not ready, and that player is deleted before being marked ready. The LOCATE call can wait indefinitely; if it wakes for an unrelated signal, it may query the removed player pointer. **Affected configuration:** callers of the optional Realtime library API using LOCATE barriers; no maintained in-tree caller of `CONDSTATE_LOCATE` was found, so application reachability is external. **Confidence:** high that deletion neither wakes nor removes the barrier participant and that the wait loop has no cancellation path; runtime scheduling/lifetime effects were not exercised. Coordinate player removal with the barrier, remove/cancel participants safely, and wake the waiter to re-evaluate the list. No player, conductor or wait was created; source-only. See the [Realtime LOCATE barrier trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5222).

<a id="ek9253"></a>
### EK9253 — CD path lookup leaks its path and entry-name buffers when a directory read fails.

`fs_cdrom_find_file()` allocates `local_filename` before scanning the directory (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/cdrom.c:291-295`). If reading a directory record fails, it returns immediately without freeing that copy (`:309-312`). In the non-Rock-Ridge name path it also allocates `name`; if that read fails, it returns without freeing either buffer (`:372-378`). The normal path frees `local_filename` and `name` at the end of the lookup (`:407-412,425`), confirming these error exits bypass cleanup. `fs_cdrom_load_file()` maps lookup failure to zero (`:446-456`); the selected menu loader may then try alternate paths (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/menu.c:584-598`), allowing subsequent failed lookups to allocate and leak again.

**Trigger and consequence:** the explicitly built Parthenope CD backend encounters a firmware read error while scanning directory records or reading an entry name. The current lookup leaks one or two temporary buffers; repeated failed lookups can consume boot memory. **Affected configuration:** explicit optional `parthenope-sam440` CD backend; default-image inclusion is not claimed. **Confidence:** high for the leaked allocations and return paths; repeated exhaustion is not established on the selected boot path. Funnel read errors through cleanup that frees the active entry-name buffer and path copy. No media error, repeated lookup or boot was exercised; source-only. See the [Parthenope CD lookup cleanup trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5227).

<a id="ek9254"></a>
### EK9254 — A failed AOS module read leaks the boot path's module staging allocations.

`testboot_aos()` allocates a module list, a 16 MiB staging buffer, and an initial `struct module` before iterating the configured AOS modules (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/parthenope.c:268-288`). If any `boot->load_file()` call returns a negative result, the function returns immediately (`:290-292`) without freeing the staging buffer, list, or already-created module records and payload buffers. The initial `module` allocation is also overwritten by the per-entry allocation at `:286,293`, so a nonempty module list abandons that allocation before the failure path. The dispatcher calls this function last among its format probes and then frees only the kernel buffer and destroys the boot device (`:372-383`); it has no handle to reclaim these local allocations.

**Trigger and consequence:** the explicitly built Parthenope AOS-format path has one or more modules and a module load returns a negative status. The attempt leaks the staging buffer and accumulated module staging/list allocations until the boot environment is reset; no later cleanup in the dispatcher reclaims them. **Affected configuration:** explicit optional `parthenope-sam440` when loading an AOS-format entry with modules. The parent target is commented out of the default Sam440 boot manifest. **Confidence:** high for the early return and lost ownership; the amount leaked depends on which module fails, and memory exhaustion on this single attempt is not claimed. Use a shared cleanup path for the staging buffer, list and every accumulated module/payload. No load failure or boot was induced; source-only. See the [Parthenope AOS module cleanup trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5230).

<a id="ek9255"></a>
### EK9255 — Parthenope's `strdup()` dereferences its allocation result on memory pressure.

The bootloader-local `strdup()` allocates `strlen(s) + 1` bytes and unconditionally passes the result to `strcpy()` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/support.c:153-159`). The selected menu parser calls it for entry labels, kernel paths, append strings, module names, alternate-format paths and initrd names (`menu.c:35-41,218,267,271,391,446,450,511,522`); `strtrim()` also calls it before copying back (`menu.c:151-154`). If any duplication allocation fails, `strcpy()` writes through NULL before the caller can handle a parse error.

**Trigger and consequence:** explicitly built Parthenope parses a menu line or trims a string while this `strdup()` allocation fails. The bootloader can fault during menu parsing/setup instead of rejecting the entry. **Affected configuration:** explicit optional `parthenope-sam440`; the active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` rule depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`), selecting this path when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked allocation and immediate copy; occurrence requires allocation failure. Check the allocation and propagate an error through menu parsing. No allocation failure or boot was induced; source-only. See the [Parthenope string/list allocation caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5233).

<a id="ek9256"></a>
### EK9256 — Parthenope's `list_new()` writes through a failed list allocation.

`list_new()` allocates a `list_t` and immediately initializes its head, tail and tail predecessor without checking the pointer (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/support.c:171-182`). The selected AROS bootstrap calls it for `debug_info` before boot-device/menu processing (`parthenope.c:311-323`); later ELF symbol loading adds modules to that list (`elf.c:348`). The AOS loader also calls it for its module list (`parthenope.c:268-276`). Allocation failure therefore faults inside the helper before either caller can handle a missing list.

**Trigger and consequence:** explicit Parthenope startup or AOS loading reaches `list_new()` while its allocation fails. Initialization writes through NULL and the boot attempt cannot continue normally. **Affected configuration:** explicit optional `parthenope-sam440`; the active `bootiso-sam440-ppc` rule depends on `parthenope-sam440` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/mmakefile.src:11-14`), selecting this path when that boot-ISO target is built. **Confidence:** high for the unchecked allocation and immediate field writes; occurrence requires allocation failure. Return NULL on failure and check the list at each caller. No allocation failure or boot was induced; source-only. See the [Parthenope string/list allocation caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5233).

<a id="ek9257"></a>
### EK9257 — Parthenope reads the fixed continuation fields of a SUSP CE entry without checking that the entry fits in the remaining area.

The packed CE structure consists of the four-byte SUSP header plus six 32-bit fields, for 28 bytes total (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/cdrom.c:84-102`). In `iterate_entries()`, a `CE` signature is cast to that structure and its block, offset and length fields are read without checking either `e->len` or the bytes remaining in the current SUA allocation (`:195-215`). The iterator can therefore read across the end of a truncated SUA buffer; when the declared CE entry itself is shorter than 28 bytes but more bytes remain, the continuation values instead consume following record data. The selected root RR and per-directory NM queries reach this iterator (`:332-337,562-568`).

**Trigger and consequence:** explicitly built Parthenope scans malformed Rock Ridge data containing a truncated CE entry or a CE entry at the end of an SUA with fewer than 28 bytes remaining. The parser reads beyond the allocated buffer or interprets adjacent SUSP bytes as continuation coordinates, which can make metadata lookup fail or follow an unintended continuation. **Affected configuration:** explicit optional `parthenope-sam440`; parent boot-manifest inclusion is disabled. **Confidence:** high for the missing length/extent validation; malformed media required, and downstream effects depend on adjacent bytes and continuation values. Validate the complete CE record against both its declared entry length and the current buffer extent before reading fields. EK9222 covers non-progress, EK9223 the matching-entry copy overread, and EK9228 parent directory-record bounds. No image or media was parsed; source-only. See the [Parthenope SUSP continuation trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5235).

<a id="ek9258"></a>
### EK9258 — The 64-bit MinGW kernel ignores the hosted bootstrap’s second RAM region [medium impact, high confidence; x86-64 MinGW]

The shared hosted bootstrap splits memory above 512 MiB into two `mb_mmap` entries on 64-bit builds (`arch/all-hosted/bootstrap/bootstrap.c:70-91,306-321`). It allocates the upper region in `MemoryMap[1]` when the requested memory exceeds `LOWMEMSIZE`, increments the published `KRN_MMAPLength`, then limits `MemoryMap[0]` to 512 MiB. The selected 64-bit MinGW kernel startup reads `KRN_MMAPAddress` but ignores `KRN_MMAPLength`; it creates the ordinary RAM `MemHeader` only from `mmap[0]` (`arch/all-mingw32/kernel/kernel_startup.c:39-43,49-73,113-139`). The hosted Unix startup checks the map length and registers the second entry as another RAM header (`arch/all-unix/kernel/kernel_startup.c:229-247`).

**Trigger:** run the supported x86-64 MinGW hosted target with a valid memory setting above 512 MiB (for example `-m 1024`), with both bootstrap allocations succeeding. **Consequence:** AROS’s Exec memory lists expose only the first 512 MiB; the separately allocated upper region is not represented by a `MemHeader` and cannot satisfy ordinary AROS allocations. The capacity loss is the requested amount above 512 MiB. This is a source-derived configuration finding, not a runtime reproduction.

**Scope and confidence:** high source confidence for the allocation/consumer mismatch, limited to 64-bit MinGW hosted startup above the split threshold. It does not affect the 32-bit MinGW path, requests at or below 512 MiB, or the checked Unix consumer. Host allocation and boot behavior were not exercised.

<a id="ek9259"></a>
### EK9259 — Parthenope's ELF section allocator maps a zero-alignment section to address zero.

For nonempty allocated sections, `load_hunk()` computes both writable and read-only placement with bit-mask alignment formulas using `sh_addralign` (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/elf.c:69-90`). When the field is zero, `addralign - 1` becomes all ones and the complemented mask becomes zero; either formula therefore produces address zero. The loader then copies file-backed section bytes to that address or clears a `SHT_NOBITS` section there (`:92-105`). `check_header()` checks ELF magic, type and machine but not section alignment (`:53-64`); selected kernel and module callers pass images to this loader (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/parthenope.c:163-193`).

**Trigger and consequence:** explicitly built Parthenope loads an ELF image with a nonempty `SHF_ALLOC` section whose `sh_addralign` is zero. The section copy or clear targets physical address zero, so loading can fault or overwrite low-memory state. **Affected configuration:** explicit optional `parthenope-sam440` AROS kernel/module ELF path; default-image inclusion is not claimed. **Confidence:** high for the arithmetic and unchecked field; malformed or unsupported input required. Treat zero alignment as no alignment (or reject it consistently) rather than applying the current mask formula. No ELF image or boot was used; source-only. See the [Parthenope ELF alignment trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5246).

<a id="ek9260"></a>
### EK9260 — Parthenope's downward ELF section allocator can overwrite the bootloader image.

Parthenope initializes `ptr_rw` to `KERNEL_PHYS_BASE` (`0x00800000`) and allocates each nonempty `SHF_WRITE` section by subtracting its size/alignment and moving the cursor downward, with no lower-bound or overlap check (`arch/ppc-sam440/boot/parthenope/src/elf.c:26-27,69-82`; base in `support.h:105`). The bootloader itself is linked at `0x00200000` and extends through its text, data and BSS to `_end` (`src/ldscript.lds:1-48`). The selected AROS path loads the kernel and each configured module through this same persistent cursor (`parthenope.c:163-193`). If cumulative writable-section placement crosses the live bootloader image, `load_hunk()` writes or clears section contents over code/data still needed by the loader.

**Trigger and consequence:** explicitly built Parthenope AROS boot loads enough writable ELF section data for the downward cursor to overlap the linked bootloader extent. This depends on aggregate image section sizes and exact linked `_end`; neither is established for the checked-in default boot image. **Affected configuration:** explicit optional `parthenope-sam440` AROS kernel/module path; default-image inclusion and threshold reachability are unverified. **Confidence:** high for cursor direction, absent bound and linker start; overlap is conditional. Reject placement below the bootloader's reserved end (and keep the read-only and writable regions disjoint). EK9234 is the separate upward 16 MiB bound; EK9259 is the zero-alignment formula. No build, ELF image or boot was used; source-only. See the [Parthenope ELF placement trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5249).

<a id="ek9261"></a>
### EK9261 — TimeDelay cleanup passes signal number 255 to FreeSignal instead of disabling signal release.

`TimeDelay()` obtains a MsgPort whose signal bit is stored in the public `UBYTE mp_SigBit` field, frees that allocated bit, then changes the field to `SIGB_SINGLE` for the timer request (`compiler/alib/timedelay.c:61-73`; `compiler/include/exec/ports.h:25-31`). Before calling `DeleteMsgPort()`, it assigns `-1` to that unsigned-byte field intending to suppress signal release (`timedelay.c:87-88`). The value is therefore 255, not -1. `DeleteMsgPort()` passes the stored value to `FreeSignal()` (`rom/exec/deletemsgport.c:48-55`), whose `1 << signalNum` expression is executed for every value other than signed -1 (`rom/exec/freesignal.c:48-56`). The resulting shift count exceeds the width of `int` and has undefined C behavior; it does not reliably act as the intended sentinel.

**Trigger and consequence:** any `TimeDelay()` call that successfully creates its message port reaches this cleanup. The invalid shift can fail to preserve the reserved `SIGF_SINGLE` allocation or affect the wrong signal-allocation bit, depending on generated target code; the precise manifestation is not established. **Affected configuration:** targets selecting the maintained `compiler/alib` implementation. **Confidence:** high for the unsigned-field conversion and out-of-range shift; exact effect depends on compiler/target behavior. Avoid the sentinel through `mp_SigBit`; add a deletion path that does not free a signal or otherwise preserve the reserved bit safely. No port, timer request or signal was created; source-only. See the [TimeDelay signal cleanup trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5255).

<a id="ek9262"></a>
### EK9262 — TimeDelay reports success when setup fails and reports an error after a successful wait.

`TimeDelay()` initializes `error` to zero, returns that value when `CreateMsgPort()` fails or `OpenDevice()` does not succeed, and sets it to one after `DoIO(TR_ADDREQUEST)` and `CloseDevice()` (`compiler/alib/timedelay.c:59-90`). The function's own documentation says zero means success and nonzero means a problem (`:24-35`). It also never checks `DoIO()`'s result (`:77-85`). Thus the ordinary successful wait is reported as an error, while setup failures are reported as success; a failed timer request is indistinguishable from the successful-request result. The two selected Intuition menu callers ignore the return value (`rom/intuition/menutask.c:1254,1412`), but other callers of the public helper receive the inverted status.

**Trigger and consequence:** any caller uses `TimeDelay()` and relies on its documented return value. A successful wait returns 1; port creation or device-open failure returns 0, and timer I/O failure is not distinguished. **Affected configuration:** targets selecting `compiler/alib/timedelay.c`; direct in-tree callers are Intuition menu delays and ignore the value, so impact for maintained callers is limited to wasted/error-status information. **Confidence:** high for the return-value inversion and ignored I/O result. Return zero only after successful `DoIO()` and a nonzero error status for each failed setup/I/O path. No timer request or failure path was run; source-only. See the [TimeDelay result/caller trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5255).

<a id="ek9263"></a>
### EK9263 — PC IRQ removal does not synchronize with its architecture-specific handler-list traversal.

The selected PC `krnRunIRQHandlers()` walks the IRQ list with `ForeachNodeSafe()` and invokes callbacks without taking `kb_IntrSpinLock` (`arch/all-pc/kernel/addirqhandler.c:115-139`). On PC, the loop cursor is also `pdata->kb_LastIntr`, one shared field in the machine-wide `PlatformData`, rather than a per-dispatch local (`arch/all-pc/kernel/kernel_arch.h:48-82`). Two CPUs dispatching IRQs concurrently can overwrite that cursor while each walk is active. Generic `KrnRemIRQHandler()` acquires the spinlock on ExecSMP, unlinks the node and then frees it (`rom/kernel/remirqhandler.c:52-75`), but the PC dispatcher does not participate in the same lock protocol; the PC-specific `KrnAddIRQHandler()` likewise publishes with local `Disable()` and no shared chain lock (`arch/all-pc/kernel/addirqhandler.c:79-110`). A different CPU can therefore mutate the chain while the IRQ traversal uses its saved-next pointer. The PC-specific add source is selected by `arch/all-pc/kernel/mmakefile.src`; the interrupt entry reaches this walker through `cpu_intr.c:500-518`.

**Trigger and consequence:** an ExecSMP PC target dispatches a hardware IRQ while another CPU adds or removes a handler on the same IRQ list, or while two CPUs dispatch IRQs concurrently. The list walk can be corrupted by concurrent insertion/removal or by the shared cursor being overwritten, causing callbacks to be skipped or dispatched from the wrong chain; removal can also free a node still used by the walk. Selected i8042 keyboard/mouse teardown removes handlers outside its own IRQ callback (`workbench/devs/USB/classes/HID/i8042/i8042_kbdclass.c:335-345`; mouse callers are tracked in the ledger), providing a concrete removal class. Nouveau display adds another selected producer-quiescence case: `nvkm_device_del()` removes its top-level IRQ handler before reverse subdevice destruction (`workbench/hidds/nouveau/drm/nouveau/nvkm/engine/device/base.c:3080-3098`; `core/intr.c:367-379`), then the display destructor flushes and stops the supervisor workqueue before freeing display/head state (`engine/disp/base.c:169-215`; `drm-compat/linux_workqueue.c:139-147`). NV50/GF119/GV100 IRQ callbacks can queue the embedded supervisor work item (`engine/disp/nv50.c:1501`; `gf119.c:1130`; `gv100.c:944`); if an already-running callback queues after the flush sees an empty queue, its worker can access display state being destroyed. **Affected configuration:** ExecSMP PC kernel targets using the all-PC IRQ override, with overlapping IRQ dispatch and handler changes or teardown; single-CPU/local interrupt exclusion does not establish this cross-CPU race. **Confidence:** high for the missing shared lock protocol, shared cursor, and source ordering; the overlap and resulting manifestation were not exercised. Use a per-dispatch local cursor and one handler-chain synchronization protocol in add, dispatch and remove; quiesce active IRQ producers before destroying state they can queue work against. No interrupt, handler mutation, workqueue, teardown, build or runtime operation was performed; source-only. See the [PC IRQ list synchronization trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L7503) and the [Nouveau display queue teardown trace](AROS-other-drivers-coverage.md#L37294).

<a id="ek9264"></a>
### EK9264 — PC APIC calibration enables the periodic timer after heartbeat-handler allocation fails (conditional boot-time unhandled exception and system halt; high source confidence).

During BSP calibration, `core_APIC_Calibrate()` stores the nullable result of `KrnAddExceptionHandler(APIC_EXCEPT_HEARTBEAT, APICHeartbeatServer, ...)` but does not check it; it still sets `APF_TIMER` and the platform heartbeat flag (`arch/all-pc/kernel/apic_ia32.c:915-929`). It then programs the local APIC timer vector without the mask bit (`:931-957`). The exception-registration helper can return NULL when its handler-node allocation fails (`rom/kernel/addexceptionhandler.c:97-127`). On the resulting heartbeat, `cpu_Trap()` finds no handler; the heartbeat vector is outside the Amiga-trap forwarding table and unhandled non-spurious exceptions enter the selected system halt path (`arch/all-pc/kernel/cpu_traps.c:71-78,90-115`; heartbeat index in `apic_ia32.h:26`).

**Trigger and consequence:** selected PC APIC BSP calibration cannot allocate the initial heartbeat exception-handler node but continues to unmask/program the periodic heartbeat timer. The first heartbeat becomes an unhandled exception and halts the system during boot. **Affected configuration:** PC APIC targets selecting `arch/all-pc/kernel/apic_ia32.c`; allocation failure is required. **Confidence:** high for the ignored nullable result, enabled periodic vector and unhandled-exception halt path; no allocation failure or APIC event was induced. Keep the timer masked and fail calibration/startup if handler registration fails. Reset-time heartbeat replacement is separately tracked under EK563. No boot, allocation failure or APIC interrupt was run; source-only. See the [APIC heartbeat registration trace](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5278).

<a id="ek9265"></a>
### EK9265 — WITHDRAWN: duplicate consequence consolidated into EK9234.

EK9265 described the same Parthenope `ptr_ro` read-only placement reaching the 16 MiB boundary, `KRN_KernelHighest` publication, and Sam440 `0x01000000 - memLowest` zero/wrap as EK9234. Its downstream first-MemChunk and later Fast RAM range consequences have been added to [EK9234](#ek9234); no independent trigger or root cause remains. EK9265 is withdrawn to avoid duplicate active findings. The source and threshold trace remain in the [coverage ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L5284). No image or boot was used; source-only.

<a id="ek9266"></a>
### EK9266 — WITHDRAWN: late reply is confined to the helper's expired stack frame.

`_obtain_sema_timed()` dequeues at most two messages, then calls `Vacate()` when one was the timer reply. If the semaphore request is still queued, `Vacate()` removes it and calls `ReplyMsg()`; this can append the stack-local semaphore message to the stack-local `msgport` after the helper's final `GetMsg()`. However, neither object nor a pointer to the port escapes `_obtain_sema_timed()`. The list links therefore become unreachable when that call returns; the source trace does not establish a later dereference or list corruption. `ReplyMsg()` may leave the port's signal pending, but `CloseTimerDevice()` frees the allocated signal, and a later `WaitPort()` rechecks its message list after waking. This supports at most a harmless stale wake, not the reported stale-message lifetime defect. EK9266 is withdrawn. The source trace remains in the [coverage ledger](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L2014); no timer, lock or interleaving was run, and no body/path/LOC credit is claimed.

<a id="ek9267"></a>
### EK9267 — The m68k `VNewRawDoFmt` thunk passes a guest argument stream as a native `va_list`.

The generated Exec LVO 822 thunk translates guest A1 only to a host pointer into containment memory, then passes that pointer directly as `DataStream` to native `VNewRawDoFmt()` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2401-2408`; `rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.h:37`; `rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_intern.h:108-122`). Native `InternalRawDoFmt()` interprets a non-NULL `va_list` using the build target's C varargs ABI (`rom/exec/rawdofmt.c:43-74,101-118`); it does not decode the m68k stack stream. On the explicitly supported 64-bit x86_64, AArch64 and RISC-V m68kemu targets, guest 32-bit big-endian argument slots therefore do not represent the native host `va_list` state/layout. A guest call with format conversions can read unrelated values or advance through the wrong arguments, producing incorrect output and potentially reading outside the intended argument stream. The manual `RawDoFmt` thunk separately decodes guest arguments, but it handles LVO 522 and does not override generated LVO 822 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:319-365,699-735`; `rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:7460`; `rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_run.c:40-49`). No maintained in-tree guest caller of this vector was found; scope is external emulated m68k clients that call `VNewRawDoFmt` with conversions. The m68kemu target is optional and its parent edge is commented in this snapshot (`rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:8-18`). High confidence in the ABI mismatch; exact output depends on the guest format and host target. No guest program or formatter was run; source-only.

<a id="ek9268"></a>
### EK9268 — The m68k `VNewRawDoFmt` thunk routes guest callbacks through native function pointers.

The generated LVO 822 thunk passes A2 through `THUNK_PTR`, which maps an ordinary guest code address to its containment-memory address and also translates small nonzero values as addresses (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2401-2408`; `m68kemu_thunks.h:37`; `m68kemu_intern.h:108-122`). Native `InternalRawDoFmt()` compares the resulting pointer with its `RAWFMTFUNC_*` constants; for other values, when the supplied stream is non-NULL, it casts `PutChProc` to a native C callback and calls it directly (`rom/exec/rawdofmt.c:101-118`). The emulator does not dispatch that address back into the guest CPU. Thus a guest custom callback is called using the wrong execution mechanism, and guest sentinel values 1 (`RAWFMTFUNC_SERIAL`) and 2 (`RAWFMTFUNC_COUNT`) are translated to containment addresses and miss the native sentinel checks. A callback or those sentinel modes can therefore fail during formatting instead of producing the requested output. This is distinct from EK9267: a literal-only format is sufficient to reach the output callback without consuming the malformed `va_list`; the wrong callback dispatch remains even if argument decoding is not exercised. Applies to optional m68kemu targets and external guest clients that use non-string output modes. No maintained in-tree guest caller of this vector was found. No guest callback or formatter was run; source-only.

<a id="ek9269"></a>
### EK9269 — The m68k `VNewRawDoFmt` string mode returns a host address to the guest.

For `RAWFMTFUNC_STRING`, guest A2 is zero and A3 is translated to a host pointer in the emulator's containment memory. `InternalRawDoFmt()` advances that native `PutChData` pointer for each output character and returns it (`rom/exec/rawdofmt.c:101-118,316-326`; `compiler/include/exec/rawfmt.h:9-10`). The generated LVO 822 thunk returns that host pointer unchanged (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:2401-2408`), and Moira writes the low 32 bits directly to guest D0 without `host_to_m68k()` conversion (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:258-272`). The guest therefore receives a truncated host address instead of its original guest buffer address advanced by the output length; callers that use the documented final `PutChData` result as a guest pointer cannot safely use it. This is independent of EK9267 because a literal-only format needs no argument fetch, and string sentinel zero is preserved by the pointer translation. Applies to the optional m68kemu targets and external guest clients using string output. No maintained in-tree guest caller of this vector was found. No guest formatter was run; source-only.

<a id="ek9270"></a>
### EK9270 — The m68k Exec `AllocEntry` thunk passes a guest `MemList` as a native structure.

Generated LVO 222 translates guest A0 to a host pointer, then calls native `AllocEntry()` without converting the guest `MemList` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:1899-1904`; `rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.h:37`). Native `NewAllocEntry()` reads `ml_NumEntries`, each `me_Reqs` and `me_Length`, and copies entries using the host `sizeof(struct MemList)`/`sizeof(struct MemEntry)` layout (`rom/exec/allocentry.c:62-78`; `rom/exec/newallocentry.c:78-144`; `compiler/include/exec/memory.h:49-65`). The guest m68k layout has 32-bit pointers and `IPTR`-sized lengths, while the optional emulator targets use 64-bit native pointers/IPTR; the embedded `Node`, count offset, entry stride, and length width therefore differ. Native code reads the wrong count/requirements/lengths from the guest buffer and can allocate the wrong blocks or traverse beyond the guest list. Applies to optional x86_64, AArch64 and RISC-V m68kemu builds when external guest code calls AllocEntry with a MemList. No maintained in-tree guest caller was found. High confidence in the structure mismatch; exact effects depend on input list contents. No allocation or guest call was run; source-only.

<a id="ek9271"></a>
### EK9271 — The m68k Exec `AllocEntry` thunk returns a native `MemList` pointer to guest code.

Native `AllocEntry()` returns the address of its newly allocated host `MemList`; generated LVO 222 returns that `APTR` unchanged (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:1899-1904`). The dispatch code truncates the native `IPTR` result to 32 bits and places it directly in guest D0, without `host_to_m68k()` conversion (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:258-272`). A guest caller therefore receives a host-derived address rather than an address in its 32-bit emulated memory. Passing that result to guest `FreeEntry()` invokes LVO 228, whose thunk interprets A0 as a guest address and translates it back into containment memory (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:1906-1911`; `m68kemu_thunks.h:37`), so the host allocation is not correctly identified or released. This affects optional 64-bit m68kemu builds when external guest code calls AllocEntry; the input-layout mismatch is separately tracked by EK9270. No maintained in-tree guest caller was found. High confidence in the missing return conversion. No guest allocation or free was run; source-only.

<a id="ek9272"></a>
### EK9272 — The m68k Exec `AllocAbs` thunk asks native Exec to allocate inside the already allocated containment block.

Generated LVO 204 translates guest A1 with `THUNK_PTR` and passes the resulting host pointer to native `AllocAbs()` (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:1890-1895`; `m68kemu_thunks.h:37`; `m68kemu_intern.h:108-122`). The emulator's complete guest address space is one host `AllocMem()` block (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_memory.c:17-42`); its guest heap is separately managed inside that block by `M68KEmu_HeapAlloc()` rather than native Exec (`:62-101`). Native `AllocAbs()` searches native MemHeaders for a free chunk covering the translated host interval (`rom/exec/allocabs.c:78-84`; `rom/exec/memory_nommu.c:88-145`). Since the containment block is already allocated as one host block, the mapped guest range is not a free native chunk, so the native absolute allocation cannot reserve that guest interval through the emulator's own heap. Guest clients that require successful absolute allocation in guest memory therefore receive failure even where the requested guest range is otherwise free. This applies to optional m68kemu builds and external guest callers; no maintained in-tree guest caller was found. High confidence in the allocator-domain mismatch; exact call outcomes depend on host MemHeader/allocator implementation. No allocation was run; source-only.

<a id="ek9273"></a>
### EK9273 — m68k Exec list vectors use native 64-bit offsets on guest 32-bit list structures.

The generated `Insert`, `AddHead`, `AddTail`, `Remove`, `RemHead`, `RemTail` and `Enqueue` thunks translate guest addresses to host pointers and call native Exec directly (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:1914-1972,7402-7408`). The list implementations dereference native `struct List` and `struct Node` fields (`rom/exec/addhead.c:53-65`; `addtail.c:49-62`; `insert.c:57-100`; `remove.c:49-61`; `remhead.c:52-66`; `remtail.c:53-67`; `enqueue.c:55-90`). On the supported 64-bit m68kemu targets these layouts use 64-bit pointers and different field offsets/strides from guest m68k's 32-bit `Node` and `List` (`compiler/include/exec/nodes.h:28-48`; `lists.h:28-56`). Passing ordinary guest list/node storage therefore makes native Exec read and write the wrong offsets; pointer-sized writes can also extend past guest fields into adjacent bytes. The guest list operations can corrupt list contents or nearby guest data, or fail while traversing. This affects optional x86_64, AArch64 and RISC-V m68kemu builds when external guest code passes containment-backed lists; no maintained in-tree guest caller of these vectors was found. The source-level layout mismatch is certain; the specific effect depends on operation and list contents. No guest list operation was run; source-only.

<a id="ek9274"></a>
### EK9274 — m68k Exec `RemHead` and `RemTail` return host node addresses to guest code.

Generated LVOs 258 and 264 pass the translated list to native `RemHead()`/`RemTail()` and return the resulting host node pointer unchanged (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:1950-1962,7406-7407`). The emulator dispatch truncates the native `IPTR` to 32 bits and stores it directly in guest D0; it does not translate the node pointer back to a guest address (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_moira.cpp:258-272`). When these calls operate on a shadow-backed/native-layout list or node, the returned value is not a valid guest address and subsequent guest access or re-use as a list node fails. This missing return conversion is separate from EK9273's input structure layout mismatch. Applies to optional 64-bit m68kemu builds and external guest callers using these vectors; no maintained in-tree guest caller was found. No guest list operation was run; source-only.

<a id="ek9275"></a>
### EK9275 — Repeated m68k borrowed-object lookups exhaust the emulator's shadow table.

The m68k emulator has a fixed 256-entry native-to-guest shadow map (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_intern.h:92-94`). Its selected Exec thunks for `FindResident()`, `FindPort()`, `FindSemaphore()`, and `FindTaskByPID()` call the native lookup, then create a fresh guest shadow for each successful result (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:1849-1856,2060-2066,2236-2242,2475-2481`). `FindResident()` returns an entry from the resident-module list (`rom/exec/findresident.c:51-63`). `shadow_register()` appends entries without checking for an existing native pointer and returns failure once all 256 slots are occupied (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:444-455`). The generated thunks do not release these borrowed-result shadows; repeated successful lookups therefore consume both map entries and guest heap space. The same path applies to generated Intuition `ViewPortAddress()`: the thunk accepts a Window shadow (which manual `OpenWindow()` can return), native Intuition returns the screen-owned embedded `Window->WScreen->ViewPort`, and each successful call creates a fresh ViewPort shadow (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:5313-5319`; `rom/intuition/viewportaddress.c:24-33,50`; `rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:477-515,518-523`). It does not reuse the embedded ViewPort shadow registered by `OpenScreen()` or a shadow from a prior call. The separate ViewPort field-layout/synchronization issue is tracked under EK582/EK9180.

The same path applies to the manual `FindName()` thunk for non-Library/non-Device nodes (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks.c:663-677`); native `FindName()` returns a node already owned by its containing list. The generated Hyperlayers `WhichLayer()` thunk likewise creates a fresh `Layer` shadow for each successful result (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:6323-6332`); native `WhichLayer()` returns an existing layer from the supplied LayerInfo chain (`rom/hyperlayers/whichlayer.c:63-74`), with no result-release API. Generated DOS `DeviceProc()` returns a borrowed device-handler MsgPort after freeing its temporary DevProc (`rom/dos/deviceproc.c:61-80`), and the generated thunk wraps each successful result (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:972-979`). `FindCliProc()`, `GetConsoleTask()`, `GetFileSysTask()`, `SetConsoleTask()`, and `SetFileSysTask()` also create shadows for returned Process/MsgPort pointers (`m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:1316-1371`); the native routines return a found process, current process port, or previous port without transferring ownership (`rom/dos/findcliproc.c:51-82`; `getconsoletask.c:57-69`; `getfilesystask.c:55-66`; `setconsoletask.c:58-72`; `setfilesystask.c:58-69`). These wrappers have no matching shadow release. `GetDeviceProc()` is excluded because its owned DevProc result and matching `FreeDeviceProc()` path are covered by EK9891. Manual `FindTask()` is excluded because its additional guest Process/CLI construction and distinct table-full behavior are covered by EK419.

**Trigger and consequence:** an emulated program repeatedly obtains a successful borrowed result through one of these lookup/get/set vectors, or repeatedly calls `ViewPortAddress()` for a live Window or `WhichLayer()` for a hit layer, without reaching table capacity through other live shadows first. Once the table is full, `shadow_create()` frees its just-allocated guest block and returns zero when registration fails (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_shadow.c:80-91`); the wrapper then returns NULL/zero even though the native object was found or returned. The table is shared with other shadowed objects, so unrelated live shadows can make exhaustion occur sooner. The manual `FindTask()` thunk has a different failure behavior and is covered separately under EK419. No stale-pointer consequence is claimed here.

**Affected configuration:** builds that select the optional `kernel-m68kemu` library on supported non-m68k hosts, including the x86-64, AArch64, and RISC-V64 target declarations in `rom/m68kemu/mmakefile.src:14-17`.

**Confidence:** high for the fixed capacity, lack of native-pointer deduplication, unreleased lookup shadows, and zero return after exhaustion; guest-visible occurrence requires repeated successful lookups or other shadow allocations filling the shared table. Reuse a live shadow for an already-mapped native object and release borrowed-result mappings when their guest lifetime ends. No guest lookup, table exhaustion, or build was run; source-only. Coverage: [m68kemu lookup-shadow rows](AROS-exec-kernel-coverage.md#L175).

<a id="ek9277"></a>
### EK9277 — m68kemu passes guest `Task` records to native `AddTask` without field conversion.

The generated `AddTask` and `NewAddTask` thunks resolve A1 to either a registered shadow or the raw host address of guest containment memory, then pass that pointer to native Exec (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_thunks_gen.c:1972-1979,2508-2516`; `m68kemu_intern.h:108-122`). Ordinary guest-allocated `Task` records have no shadow translation. The checked-in x86_64 shadow layout describes a 92-byte m68k Task and maps corresponding fields to native offsets through `tc_UserData` at offset 168 (`rom/m68kemu/m68kemu_shadow_layouts.h:3750-3775,4652`); native `struct Task` is larger and has 64-bit pointer fields (`compiler/include/exec/tasks.h:33-68`). `NewAddTask()` directly reads and writes fields such as `tc_Node.ln_Name`, `tc_MemEntry`, and signal/state fields using native offsets (`rom/exec/newaddtask.c:187-245`). The thunk does not create/synchronize a Task shadow or marshal those fields. A valid guest Task can consequently have the wrong name/list/signal fields read and native writes can land at incorrect or out-of-record guest offsets, preventing task setup or corrupting guest memory. Applies to the optional x86_64 m68kemu target; AArch64/RISC-V use a checked-in layout documented as needing regeneration, so their exact offsets are not asserted here. No maintained in-tree emulated guest caller was found; the registered public vectors provide the route for external guests. High confidence in the missing conversion and checked-in x86_64 offset mismatch. No task creation or memory access was run; source-only.

<a id="ek9278"></a>
### EK9278 — Near-maximum vector-allocation sizes wrap the hidden-header request and can return undersized storage.

`AllocVec()` adds `AROS_ALIGN(sizeof(IPTR))` to the caller's `byteSize` without checking overflow, allocates the wrapped value, stores that value in the hidden header, and returns after the header (`rom/exec/allocvec.c:57-79`). For an `IPTR`-width request of `IPTR_MAX - AROS_ALIGN(sizeof(IPTR)) + 2`, the backing request wraps to 1. If that small `AllocMem(1)` succeeds, `AllocVec()` returns non-NULL while the block does not contain the requested payload. A caller that uses the requested extent can access outside the allocation. There is also a concrete conditional effect with Exec MungWall enabled: the boot `mungwall` option makes `AllocMem()` reserve `MUNGWALL_TOTAL_SIZE` around its original one-byte extent, and `MungWall_Build()` places the post-wall immediately at `res + 1` (`rom/exec/allocmem.c:99-110`; `rom/exec/mungwall.c:63-67`; `compiler/arossupport/include/debug.h:224-235`). `AllocVec()` then writes its aligned hidden-size word at `res`; on 32-bit and 64-bit targets this store extends three or seven bytes into the 32-byte post-wall. `FreeVec()` passes the stored wrapped size of one to `FreeMem()`, whose MungWall integrity check detects the damaged post-wall and raises the memory-insane alert (`rom/exec/freevec.c:48-56`; `rom/exec/mungwall.c:125-154`). This guard corruption is limited to the optional MungWall configuration; without it, the confirmed consequence remains the undersized allocation and caller use beyond its extent.
